### Alpenbrevet
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 166 mi | 22,309 ft | Andermatt, Switzerland | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpenbrevet/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpenbrevet.md

Switzerland's ultimate Alpine pass conquest – brutal beauty that defines gran fondo greatness. Four route tiers out of Andermatt, in the central Swiss Alps: Platinum (267 km, 6,800m — five passes: Sustenpass, Grimselpass, Nufenenpass, Lukmanierpass, Oberalppass), Gold (212 km, 5,000m), Silver (108 km, 3,100m), and Bronze (68 km, 2,100m, including the cobbled Tremola ascent). The vitals on this profile describe the Platinum route, the event's hardest and longest option. Roads are not closed to traffic on any tier — riders share the passes, including tunnels, with normal Swiss road traffic and must run lights and follow standard rules throughout. Signature challenge: Five Alpine passes in one day on the Platinum route — Sustenpass, Grimselpass, Nufenenpass, Lukmanierpass, and Oberalppass — with a 21:00 finish cutoff and intermediate cutoffs on the longer distances. Alpenbrevet has run since 1978 — the 2026 edition is its 48th, not a fully unbroken run, but still a genuinely long-lived Swiss Alpine institution that regularly sells out its 3,250 places within about two weeks. But it's explicitly built as a 'no-race': the organizer times riders but publishes finishers alphabetically, not ranked, and holds no winners' ceremony. Four route tiers (Bronze through Platinum) make it accessible to a wide range of ability, and the passes themselves — Sustenpass, Grimselpass, Nufenenpass, the cobbled Tremola on Bronze — are the real Alpine deal. The catch: roads stay open to ordinary traffic throughout, including in tunnels, so this is a personal-challenge ride through real Alpine road conditions, not a closed-course race. Yes if you want a genuine multi-pass Alpine day with nearly 50 years of organizational pedigree and don't need ranked results. Skip if you specifically want a closed-road, competitively timed race.

### Dolomitenradrundfahrt / SuperGiroDolomiti
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 135 mi | 16,597 ft | Lienz, East Tyrol, Austria | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/dolomitenradrundfahrt/

Legendary Austrian road ultra with epic Dolomites climbing and 70+ years of history. Two distinct races out of Lienz, East Tyrol: the 112 km Classic Dolomitenradrundfahrt (~1,870m) and the 218 km SuperGiroDolomiti (~5,060m) that this profile's vitals describe. The SuperGiro crosses the Austria-Italy border into Carinthia and Friuli, taking in Monte Zoncolan alongside the passes shared with the Classic route, before returning to Lienz. The Dolomitenradrundfahrt itself is Austria's oldest cycling marathon, first held in 1951; the SuperGiro is a later addition, launched in 2014 as the harder long-distance option (the 2026 editions were the 38th Dolomitenradrundfahrt and 11th SuperGiroDolomiti). Signature challenge: Monte Zoncolan — one of cycling's hardest climbs, tackled only on the 218 km SuperGiroDolomiti alongside a double ascent of the Plöckenpass. First run in 1951, the Dolomitenradrundfahrt is a genuine Austrian institution — 38 editions deep by 2026 and billed as the country's oldest cycling marathon. The 218 km SuperGiroDolomiti, added in 2014, is the race this profile's numbers describe: a border-crossing route into Italy that tackles Monte Zoncolan, one of cycling's hardest climbs, alongside a double Plöckenpass ascent. More than 2,000 riders from 26 countries took part across both distances in 2026. The organizer's own material has minor inconsistencies (a one-year gap in founding-year claims, some pages still citing the SuperGiro's older 228-240 km course length), which is worth knowing but doesn't undercut the core event's substance. Yes if you want a genuinely historic Alpine marathon with a world-class signature climb (Zoncolan) and don't mind firm time cutoffs. Consider the shorter Classic route if 218 km/5,060m is more than you want to take on.

Eroica Japan is the real thing — a licensed outpost of the Eroica family that started in Tuscany in 1997, running in Japan since 2013 and marking its tenth anniversary in 2024. ### The Flandrien Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 254.8 mi | 18,176 ft | Oudenaarde and Heuvelland, Flanders, Belgium | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/flandrien-ride/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/flandrien-ride.md

Ultimate Flandrien proving ground – suffer on hallowed cobbles, claim immortality in stone. Not a course in the normal sense — a permanent, self-guided Strava challenge across 59 designated segments split between two regions: nine around the Kemmelberg/Heuvelland area in West Flanders and fifty around Oudenaarde and the Flemish Ardennes, the beating heart of the Tour of Flanders cobbled climbs. There is no fixed route; riders choose how to connect the segments, and published routings range from a single ~304 km day to a standard three-day itinerary of roughly 410 km and 5,540 m. The only fixed rule is the clock: all 59 segments must register on Strava within a rolling 72-hour window. Signature challenge: The 72-hour Strava clock across all 59 segments — not any single climb, but the logistics of covering two separated regions and dozens of short, brutal hellingen before the window closes. Read this carefully before you file it next to a gran fondo: The Flandrien Challenge is not an organized event. There's no start line, no field, no closed roads, no date. Visit Flanders launched it in November 2020 as a permanent, self-guided Strava challenge — ride all 59 designated segments across the Flemish Ardennes and Kemmelberg/Heuvelland areas, upload them to Strava, and complete the first-to-last interval inside a rolling 72-hour window. The climbs themselves are the real thing — Oude Kwaremont, Paterberg, Koppenberg, the Kapelmuur — roads the Tour of Flanders has made famous. But you're riding them alone or with friends on open Belgian roads, on your own schedule, racing a clock against yourself rather than a field. It is not a gran fondo. Attempt it if you want a self-directed, bucket-list tour of the actual Tour of Flanders cobbled climbs and don't need an organized-event atmosphere. Skip it if you're looking for a scored, dated gran fondo — this is a permanent Strava challenge, not a race.

### Galibier Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 71 mi | 10,991 ft | Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne, Savoie, France | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/galibier-challenge/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/galibier-challenge.md

A prestigious Alpine cyclosportive that delivers authentic Tour de France climbing on two of cycling's most iconic passes, ideal for experienced riders seeking high-altitude challenge with strong community atmosphere. Two formats out of Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne: the main 110 km cyclosportive (~3,350m) taking in Montée d'Orelle, Col de Beau Plan, Col du Télégraphe, and Col du Galibier, and a separate 35 km 'La Grimpée' timed ascent (~2,100m) linking just Télégraphe and Galibier from Saint-Michel. On the main route, timing and classification stop at the Galibier summit or tunnel — the descent back to Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne is untimed, free-pace riding, not part of the race result. Most of the route stays open to ordinary traffic with riders given passage priority, but the upper Galibier climb itself is closed to motor traffic during set event hours (9:00am-3:00pm in 2026). Signature challenge: Col du Galibier — 18 km from Valloire, 1,239m of gain to the 2,642m summit, the finale of both the full cyclosportive and the standalone Grimpée. Only six years old (founded 2021), Galibier Challenge has already built real demand — 1,326 starters in 2026, a record, up from roughly 1,000 in 2025, and the event sold out. It earns that growth honestly: the Col du Galibier, one of the Tour de France's most storied climbs, is the genuine centerpiece, and the standalone 35 km Grimpée gives riders a shorter way to just do Télégraphe-Galibier without the full 110 km. The honest-critic catch: classification stops at the summit or tunnel. The descent and return to Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne — real kilometers, on a road shared with traffic — happen after the timing ends. Yes if you want a genuine, well-organized shot at the Col du Galibier with growing prestige and don't mind an untimed return leg. Consider the 35 km Grimpée if you want the climb without the full 110 km commitment.

### GFNY Grand Ballon

Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-grand-ballon/

The 2026 long course ran 146.8 km / 4,043m per the organizer's post-event report — noticeably more than the 145 km / 3,921m in the pre-race guide, a real gap worth noting rather than smoothing over. The medium course (~71 km, ~1,800m) is explicitly non-competitive — riders get a finish time but results are published alphabetically, not ranked. Signature challenge: The second ascent of the Grand Ballon, arriving after Le Markstein, Col du Firstplan, Petit Ballon, and Col du Platzerwasel have already taken their toll — climbing the same mountain twice in one day. GFNY Grand Ballon is a legitimate entry in the global GFNY series, now in its fifth edition (founded 2022) and included in the French Cycling Federation's Trophée Label d'Or calendar. The 2026 edition sold out at nearly 2,000 riders — real, growing demand for a race climbing the Grand Ballon twice through the Vosges. Like other GFNY events, it's honest about its two-tier structure: the long course is fully competitive with age-category classification, but the medium course, despite receiving a finish time, is explicitly non-competitive with alphabetical-only results. Course figures also shifted between the pre-race guide and the post-event report (145 km/3,921m planned vs. 146.8 km/4,043m actual) — worth knowing rather than treating either number as fixed. Yes for the long course if you want genuine GFNY competitive racing and a real double-summit test. Choose the medium course only if you're fine with a non-competitive, supported ride despite the finish-time format.

### GF Orcières
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 83.3 mi | 11,155 ft | Orcieres-Merlette, Hautes-Alpes, France | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-orcieres/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-orcieres.md

Alpine beast with Tour pedigree and Écrins majesty. The race starts and finishes at the 1,850 m Orcières-Merlette ski station, initially descending into the Champsaur before climbing toward Ancelle. It then crosses the Col de Moissière and follows panoramic mountain roads through Beaurepaire and Les Costes. The decisive back half stacks the Chaillol and Serre-Eyraud ascents, including extremely steep ramps, before the final climb back to Orcières-Merlette. It's a paved, climbing-dense Southern Alps route defined by repeated valley-to-resort elevation changes rather than one isolated giant col — four distinct late-race pressure points packed into 134 km. Roads stay open to normal traffic, with only temporary control at selected points. Signature challenge: The Serre-Eyraud ascent — 518 m gain, 7.6% average with ramps to 20%, the sharpest advertised wall on the course, arriving in the closing stages before the final climb back to Orcières-Merlette. This race ran as GFNY France-Orcières through 2025 as part of the global GFNY World Series; the 2026 edition dropped GFNY entirely, rebranding as GF Orcières on a new domain (gforcieres.com) with its own 'new event' positioning. That's a real separation, not a rename — riders expecting GFNY's competitive age-category format and global series ranking should verify current rules before entering. What hasn't changed is the terrain: 134 km/3,300-3,400 m through the Southern Alps, with four genuine late-race pressure points (Col de Moissière, Chaillol, Serre-Eyraud, and the Orcières-Merlette finish climb) and real Tour de France heritage at the resort itself. The old GFNY domain is still live even though it no longer represents the current event, which is its own source of confusion for anyone searching for it. Yes for the climbing density and Écrins scenery. If you specifically want GFNY World Series competitive status, verify current rules first — this event separated from GFNY for 2026.

### Giro delle Dolomiti
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 214.9 mi | 31,247 ft | Bolzano, South Tyrol, Italy | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/giro-delle-dolomiti/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/giro-delle-dolomiti.md

Historic 5-day Dolomites road epic blending social rides with brutal timed climbs. A five-day amateur road-cycling tour based around Bolzano that combines controlled-speed group riding with traffic-free timed uphill sections on each mountain stage. Those Crono sections count toward daily and overall classification while riders regroup for the untimed portions in an escorted convoy. The organizer confirms the same five-stage competitive format for July 19-23, 2027; the exact 2027 stage itinerary is not yet published, so the latest delivered 2026 route (345.8 km and 9,524 m) is a scale reference rather than a promise of identical passes. Signature challenge: Five consecutive Dolomite mountain stages with a classified uphill Crono each day — recovery and repeatable climbing matter more than one isolated summit. The 2026 Sellaronda queen stage (107 km, 3,102 m) is the latest official scale reference while the 2027 stage itinerary remains forthcoming. The 49th Giro delle Dolomiti (13-17 July 2026) is a genuinely unusual format: five days of controlled-pace group riding through South Tyrol's most famous passes, but only one traffic-free uphill Crono per stage actually counts for time. That means the overall classification is the sum of five short climbing efforts, not a continuous race — riders get the Sellaronda, Passo Rolle, and San Pellegrino under their wheels without needing to hold a race pace for 345.8 km. It's 49 editions deep (2020 cancelled due to COVID-19, resuming in 2021), runs on roughly 60 volunteers, and includes meals, mechanical support, luggage transfer, and massage — real infrastructure, not just a start list. But it isn't cheap (EUR 550-650 for the entry alone) and it isn't hub-and-spoke: stage starts shift between Bolzano, Ponte Gardena, and Predazzo, adding logistics most single-town gran fondos don't have. Yes if you want a supported week accessing the Sellaronda, Passo Rolle, and San Pellegrino without racing full distance. Skip it if you want a continuous, fully timed stage race — only short uphill Cronos count here.

### Gran Fondo Suisse

Vaud Alps' brutal UCI gem redefines fondo suffering. Grand Tour mountain stage disguised as fondo—starts Villars, warms with Croix/Pillon double, dives Hongrin low at 690m via Mittelberg wilds. Signature challenge: Triple Croix motif—opener, mid-link, summit killer—embodies Vaudois relentless vert. 7.4km TT variant pure climber duel. Grand Tour DNA in amateur flesh. Gran Fondo Suisse delivers Grand Tour pain in Vaud's hidden Alps—150km shredding Croix, Pillon, Mosses with 3,700m that humble even pros. UCI pedigree near HQ plus gravel twin makes ultimate Swiss weekend. Offroad kicks and time trial genius elevate beyond standard fonda drudgery. Young event punches like veteran; if you climb, this owns your soul. Yes if you're a climber chasing World Series glory and 3,700m badges. ### Granfondo La Nucia
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 82 mi | 7,464 ft | La Nucia, Alicante, Spain | October | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-la-nucia/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-la-nucia.md

Indurain-designed Costa Blanca beast: UCI qualifier with Aitana summit suffering. A 132 km loop starting and finishing at La Nucia's Camilo Cano Olympic Stadium, heading inland through Finestrat and Relleu before climbing into the Sierra de Aitana toward the Safari Aitana area, just above 1,000 m. The organizer markets this high point as "Alto de Aitana," but it's not the 1,558 m Aitana summit — riders top out at Safari Aitana, roughly 1,000 m, on a long ascent that's mostly a moderate 3-4%, not a genuine HC wall. A long middle section links small valleys and villages — Gorga, Fageca, Famorca, Castell de Castells — over repeated rolling climbs, before the decisive late feature: the timed Coll de Rates ascent at km 99-105, followed by a technical descent and rolling return to La Nucia. Signature challenge: The timed Coll de Rates climb (6.6 km at 5.4% average) arriving at km 99-105, roughly 20 km from the finish — the course's genuine late-race benchmark test. Granfondo La Nucia is a genuine UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier — men 19-59 and women 19-49 earn a shot at the 2027 Worlds over the 132 km/2,275 m Gran Fondo course, with a 71 km Medio Fondo for older age brackets. That's real stakes, not borrowed branding. But the marquee name doesn't match the terrain: "Alto de Aitana" implies the 1,558 m Aitana summit, and riders actually top out at Safari Aitana around 1,000 m on a long, mostly 3-4% grind — a solid climb, not the HC wall the name suggests. Official data hygiene is also shaky this early in the event's life: the UCI's own summary lists 131 km against the organizer's 132 km, and Medio Fondo elevation figures conflict by a few meters depending on the source. Yes if you want a real UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier on quiet Alicante mountain roads and understand the climb is Safari Aitana, not the true Aitana summit. Confirm your age/sex qualifying category before entering — Open riders don't qualify.

### Granfondo Livigno Alè
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 103.7 mi | 14,108 ft | Livigno, Italy | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-livigno-ale/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-livigno-ale.md

Ultimate high-alpine road suffering with notable scenery and climbs. An all-asphalt loop leaving Aquagranda in Livigno (already at 1,816 m), crossing the town and climbing the Forcola di Livigno into Switzerland to reach Passo Bernina. The route continues through the Upper Engadin to Zernez, crosses Pass dal Fuorn and the Umbrail Pass, then descends toward the Bormio/Valdidentro side of the Rhaetian Alps. The decisive return climbs Passo del Foscagno and Passo d'Eira before a steep finishing road alongside the Mottolino ski slope. Classification is the sum of designated climbing-sector times — between timed climbs, riders ride under normal road rules, not a continuous race clock. Signature challenge: The Eira-Mottolino finale (1.9 km at roughly 9.3%) to the 2,385 m Mottolino gondola station — the same finish where Tadej Pogačar soloed the 2024 Giro d'Italia queen stage, now the granfondo's dedicated closing test. Livigno sits at 1,816 m and is a legitimate high-altitude training hub, which gives this granfondo a genuine cycling identity rather than a manufactured one — the 166.8 km/4,300 m route links major Rhaetian Alps passes across Italy and Switzerland with sustained riding above 2,000 m, and the Eira-Mottolino finale climbs the exact slope where Tadej Pogačar soloed the 2024 Giro d'Italia queen stage. But it's a modestly sized field (850+ starters in 2026) for a heavily promoted international event, and the branding has been inconsistent — 2024's 'Granfondo Alé La Merckx' became 2026's 'Granfondo Livigno Alé,' with older pages and search results for the old name still circulating. Classification only counts designated climbing sectors, not the full 166.8 km, so this isn't a continuous timed race either. Yes if you want genuine high-altitude Rhaetian Alps climbing and the real Pogačar finishing slope. The field is modest and only climbing sectors are timed, not the full route.

### Granfondo Serra da Estrela
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 82 mi | 13,780 ft | Manteigas, Serra da Estrela, Portugal | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-serra-da-estrela/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-serra-da-estrela.md

Portugal's toughest granfondo: epic climbs to Torre with stunning Serra da Estrela views. Starting in Seia, the route enters the Serra da Estrela's steep, twisting mountain roads and accumulates an unusually dense 4,170 m of climbing in just 115 km — roughly 36 m of ascent per kilometer. The 2026 route introduced a new ascent to Portela de Folgosinho before descending toward Manteigas, then tackles the defining final climb through the Zêzere glacial valley to Torre, mainland Portugal's highest point at 1,993 m. Timing stops at the summit; riders then descend and return to Seia for the finish-line services. It runs on roads open to traffic, and despite being formally a non-competitive cicloturismo, the event uses chip timing, classification, and a timed mountain prize. Signature challenge: The Manteigas-Torre ascent — 20.7 km at 5.6% average, roughly 1,151 m of gain, finishing at 1,993 m, mainland Portugal's highest point. The 11th Granfondo Serra da Estrela (28 June 2026) delivers something few European gran fondos can claim: a genuine timed finish at mainland Portugal's highest point, 1,993 m at Torre, reached via a 20.7 km/1,151 m climb through the Zêzere glacial valley. At 115 km and 4,170 m of climbing, it's exceptionally dense — about 36 m of ascent per kilometer. But its identity is a little muddled: it's formally a non-competitive cicloturismo event, yet it runs full chip timing, classification, and a timed mountain prize, and the roads stay open to traffic throughout. Field counts are also inconsistent — 1,142 finishers reported post-race versus 1,113 confirmed registrations on the timing platform, both well short of the pre-event 1,500 forecast. Yes if you want a genuine summit finish at mainland Portugal's highest point and dense, sustained climbing. Know it's formally a non-competitive cicloturismo on open roads, not a closed-road race.

### Hærvejsløbet — The Viking Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 186.4 mi | 8,202 ft | Flensburg, Germany to Viborg, Denmark | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/haervejslobet/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/haervejslobet.md

Viking-fueled endurance test blending history, hills, and high-quality organization. The full route starts on Flensburg's waterfront, crosses the German-Danish border at Rønsdam after roughly 9 km, and follows the historic Hærvejen corridor north along Jutland's glacial ridge. Open South Jutland countryside gradually gives way to the rolling hills of Vejle Ådal, the Jelling monuments, forests around Vrads, and the glacial terrain of Dollerup Bakker. It's an endurance course rather than an alpine gran fondo — 2,500 m of climbing is accumulated through repeated short rollers over 300 km, not one dominant pass. The road component is now co-branded L'Etape Denmark by Tour de France (only the 5 road routes carry L'Etape status; MTB and gravel remain plain Hærvejsløbet), with genuine timed yellow/green/polka-dot jersey competitions. Roads are open or only partially closed — riders must obey normal traffic law. Signature challenge: The sheer distance and cumulative rolling terrain over 300 km rather than any single climb — four named KOM climbs are spread across the route, with the final one only ~12 km from the Viborg finish. Hærvejsløbet is DGI's mass-participation cycling weekend through Jutland, and its road routes now carry official L'Etape Denmark by Tour de France status — timed jerseys, priority L'Etape du Tour registration access, the works. That's a real ASO partnership, not borrowed branding. But it's co-branding, not a full rebrand: only the five road distances belong to L'Etape; the MTB and gravel events (also part of the same weekend, all converging on Viborg) stay under the plain Hærvejsløbet name, which makes the naming feel inconsistent depending on which page you land on. The flagship 300 km route is brutally long — 2,500 m of climbing sounds modest for the distance, and it is: this is a distance-and-wind test with four modest KOM climbs, not an alpine L'Etape. It also runs on open or only partially closed roads, a real gap from the closed-road experience the Tour branding might suggest, and the 'since 1985' founding date on file doesn't hold up — DGI's own history points to a 2012 test ride and 2013 launch. Yes if you want a genuine L'Etape-branded endurance ride through Jutland's countryside and don't need major mountain climbs. Expect open roads and a distance/wind test, not an alpine challenge.

### Hotter'N Hell Hundred
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 100 mi | 1,700 ft | Wichita Falls, Texas, USA | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/hottern-hell-hundred/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/hottern-hell-hundred.md

100 miles. 100 degrees. 10,000 riders. The largest and most hostile century ride in America, where the heat is the course and survival is the victory. One hundred miles of flat, exposed North Texas prairie in conditions that redefine the word 'hot.' The course loops through Wichita and Clay counties on paved farm-to-market roads, starting and finishing in downtown Wichita Falls. There are no climbs worth naming, no technical features, no scenic distractions — just relentless sun, wind, and heat radiating off pavement. The challenge is entirely atmospheric. The route's most famous feature is Hell's Gate at mile 61, where riders must arrive by 12:30 PM or be diverted to the shorter 75-mile route. Everything about this course is designed to test whether you can manage your body temperature, hydration, and pacing across 100 miles of hostile conditions. Signature challenge: The heat. Full stop. One hundred miles on flat roads is a standard century. One hundred miles on flat roads at 100-108F with a heat index over 111F and relentless wind is a survival exercise that tests hydration strategy, heat acclimatization, and mental resilience in ways that climbing and technical terrain cannot. CamelBak was invented here because the conditions demanded a solution that did not yet exist. That tells you everything. Hotter'N Hell Hundred is not the hardest century in America. It is not the most scenic. It is not the most technical. It is the most hostile — and that hostility is the entire point. Every late August, 10,000+ cyclists assemble in downtown Wichita Falls, Texas, and voluntarily ride 100 miles through conditions that would make a sensible person stay indoors with the air conditioning on full blast. Temperatures crack 100F by mid-morning. The heat index exceeds 111F. The wind blows hot and gritty across flat, shadeless prairie. And yet they come — year after year, decade after decade, since 1982 — because surviving HHH is a cycling rite of passage that no other event replicates. This is the ride that made a paramedic duct-tape an IV bag to his jersey and accidentally invent CamelBak. If that does not tell you everything you need to know about the conditions, nothing will. If you live in Texas or the southern plains, this is a mandatory bucket-list century. If you are flying in from out of state, it is worth the trip exactly once — to prove to yourself that you can ride 100 miles when the thermometer says you should not. Train your heat tolerance for at least 6 weeks beforehand. Arrive hydrated, start early, respect Hell's Gate at mile 61, and do not underestimate the Texas wind. The multi-day festival and Friday criterium make it a worthy cycling weekend even beyond the century ride.

### Iron Horse Bicycle Classic
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 50 mi | 6,000 ft | Durango, Colorado | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/iron-horse-bicycle-classic/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/iron-horse-bicycle-classic.md

Fifty-three years of man versus machine through the San Juan Mountains — Colorado's definitive cycling tradition. A point-to-point mountain road race on closed US Highway 550 through the heart of the San Juan Mountains. Two passes above 10,000 feet, a net elevation gain of 2,806 feet, and the narrow gauge train running alongside for the first 10 miles. Simple concept, demanding execution. Signature challenge: The double pass crossing — Coal Bank (10,640 ft) and Molas (10,910 ft) — with no recovery between them. At altitude, your power drops 10-15% from sea level values, and the thin air makes the descents feel faster than they are. The Iron Horse Bicycle Classic is not just a road race — it's an American cycling institution. Since 1972, the concept of racing a steam train through the San Juan Mountains has created something genuinely irreplaceable. Two 10,000-foot passes on a closed US highway, a point-to-point finish in Silverton, and more than half a century of tradition make this Colorado's definitive cycling event. The road race itself is demanding without being destructive, and the surrounding festival has grown into a weekend celebration of everything on two wheels. If you love mountain road racing and want an event steeped in history with a genuinely unique concept, absolutely. If you need flat-course speed or a pure criterium experience, this is not your race. The altitude and climbing demand respect — prepare accordingly.

### L'Ariégeoise Cyclosportive
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 113.1 mi | 13,615 ft | Tarascon-sur-Ariège, France | June | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/lariegeoise-cyclosportive/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/lariegeoise-cyclosportive.md

Pyrenean climbing showcase, France's 5th largest gran fondo. The planned flagship route runs from Tarascon-sur-Ariège to Auzat through the wooded, often narrow Ariège Pyrenees, climbing the Col du Portel via Péguère, Col de la Core, Col de Latrape, Col d'Agnes, and Port de Lers — a course defined by cumulative climbing and repeated valley-to-pass transitions rather than extreme altitude. Weather can materially rewrite the event: in 2026, extreme heat forced the flagship onto the shorter 124 km Mountagnole course, dropping Core and Latrape and leaving the Portel/Péguère and Agnes-Lers sequences as the principal tests. A separate non-competitive XXL ultra (298 km/7,500 m, run over two days) exists alongside the main timed field and should not be conflated with it. Signature challenge: Col d'Agnes — 10 km at 8.2% average, a sustained first-category-grade effort that survives even when the flagship route is shortened. Thirty editions and 100,000+ cumulative starters give L'Ariégeoise genuine institutional depth in the French Pyrenees, with a large registration ceiling and route choice spanning the 298 km non-competitive XXL down to a 74 km entry option. But 2026 exposed how much the event bends to conditions: extreme heat forced the flagship off its planned 182 km/4,150 m course and onto the 124 km Mountagnole route, dropping the Core and Latrape climbs entirely. Official data hygiene doesn't help — the same regulations document lists conflicting distance figures for the flagship route, and there's no verified, consolidated 2026 starter count to confirm the oft-repeated '5th largest gran fondo in France' claim, which reads as promotional language rather than a sourced ranking. Yes for genuine Pyrenean climbing with real institutional history. Check the current-year route before you commit — the flagship distance can and does change with conditions.

### L'Etape du Tour de France Femmes
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 75 mi | 9,843 ft | Route changes annually (2026: Vaison-la-Romaine to Mont Ventoux, Provence) | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-du-tour-femmes/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-du-tour-femmes.md

The official Tour de France Femmes amateur stage. ASO-organized. Closed roads. Mont Ventoux via Bedoin. 3,000m of climbing through Provence. A Provencal masterpiece that builds from gentle beauty to savage finality. The route from Vaison-la-Romaine winds through the sun-baked vineyards and lavender fields of the Comtat Venaissin, with the limestone Dentelles de Montmirail and the white dome of Mont Ventoux dominating the horizon throughout. The approach is rolling but manageable — this is the calm before the storm. Then Bedoin arrives, and the real race begins. Mont Ventoux via Bedoin is 21.8 km of relentless climbing: gentle through the village, savage through the dark forest at 9%, then the barren exposed moonscape above Chalet Reynard where the wind howls and the summit observatory beckons. One climb. 1,617 meters of vertical. No hiding. Signature challenge: Mont Ventoux via Bedoin — 21.8 km at 7.4% average. The three-phase structure is what makes Ventoux unique and devastating: gentle village approach that lulls you, the savage forest section at 9% that breaks you, and the barren exposed moonscape that finishes you. One climb. No recovery. No hiding. This is the climb that killed Tom Simpson and terrified Eddy Merckx. It is cycling's most feared mountain for a reason. L'Etape du Tour de France Femmes is not just another sportive — it is a statement. When ASO launched the Tour de France Femmes in 2022, it corrected a century-long omission in cycling's most important race. The amateur L'Etape edition, inaugurated in 2025 with 7,000 riders, extends that revolution to anyone willing to suffer up the same mountains as the professional women. The 2026 route delivers cycling's ultimate single-climb challenge: 120 km from ancient Vaison-la-Romaine through Provencal vineyards and lavender fields, building toward 21.8 km of Mont Ventoux via Bedoin. The forest section averages 9%. The barren moonscape above Chalet Reynard offers no shade, no shelter, and no mercy. And the next day, Demi Vollering and Katarzyna Niewiadoma will ride the same road. Yes if you want to be part of the most important development in women's cycling — the Tour de France Femmes brand, in amateur form. Yes if Mont Ventoux via Bedoin is on your lifetime cycling list. Yes if you want the prestige of L'Etape du Tour with a more accessible distance. Skip if you want a mature, established event with decades of history — this is only its 2nd/3rd edition. Skip if extreme heat is a dealbreaker.

### L'Etape Slovakia by Tour de France

### LoToJa Classic
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 203 mi | 9,800 ft | Logan, Utah to Teton Village, Wyoming | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/lotoja-classic/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/lotoja-classic.md

America's longest one-day road race. Three states. Three passes. One unforgettable day. An odyssey across three states and three mountain passes. The front half punishes you with climbing; the back half tests whether anything remains. At 203 miles, LoToJa is not about any single climb or feature — it is about the accumulation of everything across an entire day. Signature challenge: Three mountain passes in the first 110 miles — then 90+ miles on depleted legs. The front-loaded climbing ensures that the 'flat' back half of the course is anything but easy. At mile 150, every false flat feels like a climb. At mile 180, you still have a marathon of cycling remaining. The signature challenge is not any single climb — it is the relentless accumulation of 203 miles. LoToJa is the American one-day classic that European cycling traditions inspired but the Mountain West made its own. Two hundred three miles from a Utah college town to the foot of the Tetons, across three states and three mountain passes, in a single day. It is not the hardest race in America. It is not the most famous. But it might be the most audacious — a race conceived in 1983 when two Logan cyclists decided that Americans deserved their own Paris-Roubaix and built it through sheer mileage. LoToJa is for riders who want more than a century ride — who want a genuine odyssey. If you can sustain moderate effort for 10-13 hours, have a reliable crew, and want a finishing story that few other events can match, this is your race. But be honest with yourself: 203 miles is a very long day, and the three mountain passes in the first half ensure you will face the final 90 miles on tired legs.

### Bob Cook Memorial Mt. Blue Sky Hill Climb
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 27.4 mi | 6,590 ft | Idaho Springs, Colorado | July | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-evans-hill-climb/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-evans-hill-climb.md

27 miles. 6,590 feet. Summit at 14,130 ft. The highest paved cycling race in North America since 1962. One direction: up. The Mt. Evans Hill Climb is 27.4 miles of continuous ascending from the town of Idaho Springs at 7,540 feet to the summit parking area at 14,130 feet. The gradient is never savage — averaging 4.5% with a maximum around 10% — but the relentlessness is the point. There are no descents, no flat recovery sections (save a brief respite at Echo Lake), and no escape from the altitude that builds with every pedal stroke. The course passes through three distinct life zones: montane forest, subalpine forest with ancient bristlecone pines, and finally barren alpine tundra where nothing grows and mountain goats outnumber cyclists. Above treeline at 11,500 feet, the landscape transforms into an exposed, wind-blasted moonscape. The final miles above 13,000 feet are ridden in a hypoxic fog where your body is operating on roughly 60% of sea-level oxygen. Signature challenge: The final 5 miles above Summit Lake. From 12,830 feet to 14,130 feet, exposed switchbacks climb through alpine nothing. The oxygen is gone. The trees are gone. The gradient is honest (5.7% average) but your body has been robbed of its ability to process it. This is where the Mt. Evans Hill Climb separates itself from every other cycling event on the continent. There is no higher paved road you can race a bicycle on in North America. That sentence is the entire sales pitch, and it is enough. Since 1962, cyclists have lined up in Idaho Springs to ride 27 miles straight up into oxygen debt, hypothermia risk, and the company of mountain goats. The race honors Bob Cook, a five-time winner who died at 23 — a reminder that the mountain does not care about your credentials. At the summit, you will stand at 14,130 feet with 40% less oxygen and 100% more perspective. The Mt. Evans Hill Climb is not the hardest race. It is not the longest. It is not the most prestigious. But it is the highest, and nothing else comes close. Yes if you want the most extreme altitude experience available in competitive cycling on paved roads. Yes if you have trained for altitude or can arrive early enough to acclimatize. Skip if you have altitude sickness history, need technical terrain variety, or want a mass-participation atmosphere.

### Mt. Fuji Hill Climb
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 14.9 mi | 4,118 ft | Fujiyoshida, Yamanashi, Japan | June | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-fuji-hill-climb/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-fuji-hill-climb.md

Brutal paved assault up Mt. Fuji—Japan's signature sufferfest. Riders leave Fuji Hokuroku Park (1,035 m), complete an untimed parade approach to the timing start near the Tainai intersection (1,050 m), then climb the paved Fuji Subaru Line continuously to Mount Fuji's 5th Station at 2,305 m — 1,255 timed meters over 24 km on broad, moderate gradients rather than alpine-style walls. The Subaru Line is fully closed to ordinary traffic during the event, an unusually clean mass-participation climbing course by hill-climb standards. Only the ascent is timed; there is no competitive descent, and riders return in controlled groups afterward. Signature challenge: The Mountain Split — a separately timed, steep one-kilometer sector at 19-20 km carrying the course's hardest gradients, arriving after riders have already spent over an hour above 2,000 m. The 22nd Mt. Fuji Hill Climb (7 June 2026) is a fully closed-road climb up the paved Fuji Subaru Line to the 2,305 m 5th Station — 1,255 timed meters over 24 km at a broad, moderate 5.2% average with a 7.8% max, not an alpine-style wall. With 8,810 starters in 2026, it's one of Japan's largest hill climbs and a recognized national benchmark with finisher-ring time standards. But it's a one-day, ascent-only effort: there's no competitive descent, riders return in controlled groups afterward (with a real cold-wait risk at 2,305 m), and international logistics — mandatory prior-day registration, bike transport, limited transit, early starts — effectively require a multi-day trip for a single climb. Yes if you want a genuinely prestigious closed-road climb and don't mind a single ascent-only effort with real trip logistics. Plan for a multi-day visit, not a fly-in-fly-out race weekend.

### Race Across France
Tier 2 | Score: 74/100 | 1553.4 mi | 93,832 ft | Hendaye to Mandelieu-la-Napoule, France | June | gran_fondo

Ultimate French ultra-road odyssey: suffer the miles, conquer the cols, celebrate on the Riviera. IMPORTANT — the route changes by edition; this profile previously described the 2025 course (Dinan/Brittany start, Cime de la Bonette, Massif Central) which is NOT the 2026 route. The 2026 flagship crossed France from Hendaye on the Atlantic to Mandelieu-la-Napoule on the Mediterranean: Basque foothills and Pyrenees, then Gascony, Saint-Emilion, and the Loire, continuing through the Morvan, Jura, Grand Colombier, and Bauges toward the Alps. From Albertville it turned through the Drôme and Provence before a late Mont Ventoux ascent and the run to the Riviera. The format is semi-autonomous, not fully unsupported: riders are self-sufficient between staffed bases, but outside assistance and drafting are prohibited except at bases, where food, rest, showers, charging, drop bags, and limited assistance are available, with mandatory GPS tracking throughout. Signature challenge: Mont Ventoux from Malaucène (21.2 km at 7.2%) — the final marquee climb, arriving after roughly 2,160 km already ridden, before the run to the Riviera finish. Race Across France's 2026 flagship crossed the country coast to coast, Hendaye to Mandelieu-la-Napoule, 2,500 km and 28,600 m+ of climbing with a 240-hour cutoff and mandatory rest every 36 hours — this is a serious, well-organized ultra with GPS-tracked semi-autonomy (staffed bases, not full self-support) rather than a pure unsupported race. But the route is not fixed: the 2025 edition started in Dinan and climbed the Cime de la Bonette; 2026 started in Hendaye and climbed Mont Ventoux instead. Don't trust last year's course description for this year's race. The 2026 heatwave also forced real disruption — some 1,000 km riders had their start relocated to Albertville, and some 2,500 km riders faced stoppages and restarts, meaning not every finisher rode the identical advertised course that year. Yes if you want a genuinely severe, well-supported French ultra and can handle a route that changes materially year to year. Confirm the current edition's actual start city and marquee climbs before committing — don't assume last year's course.

It's a 118-mile conversation between you and the Rocky Mountains, starting in the dark foothill pines of Evergreen and ending with a 28-mile victory lap descent into the Vail Valley. Over $4.6 million donated to community nonprofits. 37 years without interruption. This is what cycling for something looks like. Yes if you want to cross the Continental Divide on a bicycle and experience the full spectrum of Colorado mountain riding in a single day. Signature challenge: The Keutenberg. 22% gradient on narrow tarmac through the Limburg countryside. The steepest paved climb in the Netherlands, and a moment where the gap between reading a gradient number and riding one becomes vividly, painfully clear. The Amstel Gold Race Toerversie puts 15,000 riders on the steepest roads in the Netherlands, riding the same Limburg hills that define cycling's Ardennes classic. Thirty climbs on the 240 km route — none longer than 2 km, many steeper than 15%, the Keutenberg touching 22%. ### Bergen-Voss
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 107.5 mi | 6,890 ft | Bergen to Voss, Norway | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/bergen-voss/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/bergen-voss.md

Norway's iconic Fjord Classic: breathtaking scenery meets solid challenge on roads. A 173 km point-to-point ride from central Bergen to Voss station (about 11 km longer than the usual 162 km course in 2026). The new opening heads south through Os and Rolvsvågen, adding a scenic Bjørnafjord section before climbing toward the Kvamskogen plateau. Riders then descend to Norheimsund and follow the narrow, twisting Hardangerfjord road through Kvanndal toward Voss. The defining challenge is repeated climbing and descending — 2,100 m total — combined with long, narrow fjord-side roads with oncoming traffic, rather than one dominant alpine pass. Significant sections are not closed to traffic, and several descents are neutralized with speed caps and no-passing rules for safety. Signature challenge: The Kvamskogen-Norheimsund descent — a steep, twisting run through dark tunnels, neutralized as a single-file, no-passing timeout zone rather than a free-for-all descent. Bergen-Voss is a genuinely historic Norwegian sportive — 50 continuous editions under Bergen CK, tracing a 173 km fjord-to-mountain route from Bergen to Voss through Bjørnafjord, Kvamskogen, and the Hardangerfjord. Kondis calls it one of Norway's most traditional sportives, and the scenery is real: fjords, mountain plateau, a historic finish town. But it's not a closed-road event — long stretches share the road with normal traffic, several descents are neutralized with speed caps and no-passing rules, and there's no finish sprint. Participation has also fallen a long way from its historical peak: roughly 1,395 finishers in the 50th-anniversary edition against a near-5,000 peak in 2011/2013, which makes any '4,000+ participants' marketing figure misleading for the event as it exists today. Yes for genuine fjord-to-mountain scenery and 50 years of history. Know it's open-road with neutralized descents, not a closed-course race, and participation is well below its historical peak.

### GFNY Bogota
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 62.8 mi | 7,615 ft | Zipaquira, Cundinamarca, Colombia | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-colombia/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-colombia.md

Start inside a salt cathedral. Climb into the thin Andean air above 3,000 meters. Race where Egan Bernal learned that oxygen is optional. A high-altitude road race that uses moderate gradients and paved Colombian mountain roads to deliver a physiological challenge that the course profile alone cannot explain. The route starts inside the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquira at 2,650m — an underground cavern carved from a salt mountain — before climbing through the Cundinamarca highlands to summits above 3,000m. The terrain is not technically demanding and the gradients are not extreme by European standards, but every effort is amplified by the 27% reduction in available oxygen. A 3.3% average gradient at 3,000m delivers the suffering of a 6% climb at sea level. The course rewards acclimatized climbers, punishes sea-level sprinters, and humbles everyone who arrives thinking fitness alone will suffice. Signature challenge: Altitude. Not the climbing gradient, not the distance, not the technical terrain — the air. GFNY Bogota starts at 2,650m and races above 3,000m. At these elevations, atmospheric oxygen is 25-30% lower than sea level, your VO2max drops 15-25%, and physiological systems that function flawlessly at sea level begin to fail. Heart rate creeps higher at the same power output. Lactate accumulates faster. Recovery between efforts takes longer. A 3.3% gradient that you'd spin up at sea level becomes a gasping, vision-narrowing ordeal. The course doesn't need steep grades or long distances to destroy you — it has physics. No amount of sea-level fitness compensates for unacclimatized lungs at 3,000 meters. GFNY Bogota is what happens when you take a franchise gran fondo template and drop it into one of cycling's spiritual homelands at an altitude that reduces your VO2max by 20% before you even clip in. The course itself is straightforward — paved roads, moderate gradients, 100 km — but the 2,650m starting elevation transforms every watt into an existential negotiation with the atmosphere. You warm up inside a salt cathedral carved from a mountain, emerge into the Andean dawn in Egan Bernal's hometown, and climb into mountains where the air gets noticeably thin. The Colombian cycling culture does the rest: crowds that actually care, a nation that treats cyclists as heroes, and a post-race atmosphere that feels earned in a way that manufactured expo-village celebrations never do. The franchise format is the ceiling — this is still a GFNY satellite, not a standalone institution — but the Colombian setting is the floor, and that floor is higher than most events' ceilings. Yes if you want to experience the world's highest gran fondo and test yourself at extreme altitude. Yes if Colombian cycling culture — the passionate crowds, the heritage of Bernal and Quintana and Forero — means something to you. Yes if you want a destination gran fondo that costs half of what European events charge. Skip if you haven't acclimatized to altitude and don't plan to arrive early — sea-level fitness is worthless above 3,000m. Skip if you want technical terrain, gravel, or a course that challenges handling. Skip if you need a massive international field.

### Gran Fondo Utah

### GranGuanche Audax Road
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 466 mi | 55,774 ft | Lanzarote to La Gomera, Canary Islands, Spain | February | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granguanche-audax-road/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granguanche-audax-road.md

Epic island-hopping Audax on volcanic roads with ferry chases and Teide summit. IMPORTANT — this is not a conventional gran fondo. GranGuanche Audax Road is a self-supported, single-stage, fixed-route audax across five Canary Islands (Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Tenerife, La Gomera) — organized and tracked, with published classifications, but governed by inter-island ferry timing rather than a start list and finish clock in the conventional sense. The road edition covers roughly 750 km and 17,000 m of gain almost entirely on paved, low-traffic roads and major mountain passes, though one Gran Canaria climb runs on deteriorated tarmac that can carry loose gravel after rain. There are separate trail and gravel editions of the same event on different surfaces/months; this profile is specifically the road edition. Signature challenge: The Tauro Pass-GC-210 leg on Gran Canaria — roughly 245 km and 5,500 m of gain on a steep, narrow, partly deteriorated mountain road, the hardest single-island leg of the crossing. GranGuanche Audax Road is exactly what its name says: a self-supported audax, not an organized race, and it doesn't belong in a database of scored, dated gran fondos the way this profile presents it. It IS organized and tracked — published classifications, a one-week cutoff window (24-31 January 2026) — but the format is fundamentally a personal-challenge crossing of five Canary Islands (roughly 750 km, 17,000 m gain, ~100 riders) governed by inter-island ferry timing rather than a mass-start field with a shared finish clock. The terrain is genuinely demanding — the Tauro Pass/GC-210 leg on Gran Canaria alone is 245 km/5,500 m on steep, partly deteriorated tarmac — and the volcanic island-hopping concept is distinctive and well-regarded among ultra-distance/audax riders. But it has no start list in the conventional sense, no ranked results comparable to a gran fondo, and no fixed daily distance — everything bends around ferry schedules. Attempt it if you want a self-supported, ferry-timed island-crossing challenge and are an experienced ultra-distance/audax rider. Skip it if you're looking for a scored, mass-start gran fondo with a conventional finish clock.

### La Leggendaria Charly Gaul
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 88 mi | 13,123 ft | Trento, Trentino-Alto Adige, Italy | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-leggendaria-charly-gaul/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-leggendaria-charly-gaul.md

141 km and 4,000m of climbing to the summit where Charly Gaul collapsed into legend in the 1956 Giro — UCI-caliber racing at a regional gran fondo price, while it ran through 2019. A gran fondo that builds toward a single, defining moment: the summit finish on Monte Bondone at 1,650m. The granfondo route from Trento loops through the Valle dei Laghi and Cembra Valley before climbing Monte Bondone twice — once as an intermediate test, once as the grand finale. The course design is classical Italian: a long day through varied terrain, building toward a decisive summit finish that rewards the strongest climbers. The emotional weight of finishing at the exact spot where Charly Gaul collapsed in 1956 elevates the physical challenge into something more meaningful. Signature challenge: The second ascent of Monte Bondone: 22 km at 7.6% average after 120 km of riding and 3,000m of prior climbing. The same climb you did 60 km ago, but on legs that have nothing left. Summit finish at 1,650m at the exact spot where Charly Gaul became a legend. La Leggendaria Charly Gaul exists because of one day in cycling history: June 8, 1956, when Luxembourg's Charly Gaul — the 'Angel of the Mountains' — rode alone through fog and ice to the summit of Monte Bondone, collapsing at the finish and securing the Giro d'Italia. Seventy years later, 2,000-5,000 riders retrace his path from Trento's Cathedral Square to the same summit at 1,650m, now in the July heat rather than June snow.

The granfondo is not gentle about it. 141 km and 4,000 meters of climbing, including Monte Bondone done twice — once as a warm-up that ends with a descent back to the valley, and once as the final 22 km summit finish that decides the race. The climb averages 7.6% for 22 km with sections punching to 15%. On the second ascent, after 120+ km of riding in July heat through the Valle dei Laghi and Cembra Valley, those 15% sections feel like walls. The mediofondo at 57 km with 2,000m of climbing offers a more direct path to the emotional summit finish.

UCI Gran Fondo World Series status gave the event competitive teeth while it ran. Age-group riders were genuinely racing for World Championship qualification slots, and the field reflected this — La Leggendaria itself hosted the actual UCI Worlds in 2013 (Trento separately hosted the UCI Worlds again in 2022, on the same roads, after the granfondo had already folded — see history for the distinction). The Luxembourg connection (the ACC Contern club co-organizes) adds a unique cross-border dimension. Trento as a host city provides excellent infrastructure, cultural depth, and accessibility. This is not the most dramatic landscape in the Italian Alps — the Dolomites are 50 km north — but the Monte Bondone summit finish, at the exact spot where Gaul collapsed into legend, delivers an emotional punch that no amount of scenery can replicate. No — this race hasn't run since its final edition in 2019 (2020-2021 were pandemic cancellations), and the organizing committee confirmed in February 2022 it would not return. When it operated, it delivered exactly what the name promised: a UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier with genuine competitive depth, a summit finish at the exact spot where Charly Gaul collapsed into legend in 1956, and results that counted toward UCI World Championship qualification. If that Trentino climbing and qualifying pathway is what you're after today, check the current UCI Gran Fondo World Series calendar for an active Italian stop rather than assuming this one still runs.

### La Ruta de los Conquistadores
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 162 mi | 32,300 ft | Jaco to Turrialba area, Costa Rica (2026 total distance/elevation not published — figures below are historical, vary by edition) | October | multi_stage
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-ruta-de-los-conquistadores/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-ruta-de-los-conquistadores.md

Legendary brutal coast-to-coast MTB epic across Costa Rica's wild heart. IMPORTANT — this is a mountain bike (MTB) stage race, not a road cycling event, and does not belong in a road-cycling database's active catalog. La Ruta traditionally traverses Costa Rica from the Pacific side toward the Caribbean through mountains, tropical forest, and volcanic country, on gravel roads, technical singletrack, banana plantations, dense jungle, river crossings, and climbs above 3,000 m — with some paved connectors, but never a road-surface event. The announced 2026 sequence runs Jaco-San José, Tres Ríos-Turrialba, then Turrialba toward Limón and back to the Casa Turire/Turrialba area over 3 stages (29-31 October). Total 2026 distance, elevation, and surface percentages are not published by the organizer as of this research; historical editions have varied substantially (a widely-cited 2016 edition ran 217 km with 343 entrants — treat any single historical total as edition-specific, not a fixed course figure). Signature challenge: The Tres Ríos-Turrialba volcanic mountain stage — historically crosses toward Irazú/Turrialba near 3,000 m, though the organizer has not explicitly confirmed this alignment for 2026. La Ruta de los Conquistadores is a pioneering three-stage mountain bike race, founded in 1993, that crosses Costa Rica from the Pacific to the Caribbean through jungle, volcanic terrain, mud, and river crossings. The New York Times called it one of the world's toughest bike races, and it remains a well-regarded MTB expedition three decades on. But it is a mountain bike race, run predominantly on gravel roads, technical singletrack, and jungle trail with some paved connectors — not a road cycling event, and this database's prior 'Paved roads' surface classification and gran_fondo framing misrepresented it entirely. The 2026 edition (29-31 October, US$575 base entry) remains thinly documented on the organizer's own site: no total distance, elevation gain, field cap, or surface percentages are published, and the English page even carries a conflicting date header alongside the correct October dates. Not applicable to a road-cycling audience — this is an MTB stage race, not a road event. If you ride mountain bikes and want a demanding, historic expedition-style challenge, it's worth serious consideration on its own terms.

Discontinued — Tour de France-branded gran fondo that ran two editions in Parma's food hills before A.S.O. relocated L'Étape Italy to Piedmont. The 2025 (final) edition started and finished inside Parma's Parco Ducale. It crossed the plains and foothills south of Parma before entering the Emilia-Romagna Apennines around Lesignano de' Bagni, Neviano degli Arduini and Tizzano Val Parma. The defining section climbed through Lagrimone to Schia-Monte Caio and Passo dei Caprioli before descending back toward Parma — long flat urban approaches bookending a concentrated, repeatedly rolling mountain middle. Signature challenge: The Lagrimone-Schia/Monte Caio climb (km 56.8-63.9, 7.1 km at roughly 7.3% net average, cresting at 1,228 m before continuing to Passo dei Caprioli at 1,273 m) — the high point of the course, arriving with the finish still 30+ km away. L'Étape Parma ran for exactly two editions (2024, 2025) before A.S.O. moved L'Étape Italy out of Emilia-Romagna entirely. The official 2026 announcement (27 December 2025) lists two new Piedmont stops — Entracque in May and Mondovì in September — with no Parma date anywhere on the calendar. While it ran, it was a legitimate Tour de France-branded event: closed/controlled roads, real climbing through the Apennines (Lagrimone, Schia, Monte Caio, Passo dei Caprioli), and a genuinely international field (20 countries in 2025). But its own published figures didn't agree with each other even in its final year — the organizer's course guide said 134 km/2,660 m while the municipal roadbook filed for road closures said 133.4 km/3,167 m, a 507 m gap in the same edition's stated climbing. No — this event does not exist for 2026 or beyond. If you want the current L'Étape Italy experience, look at L'Étape Piemonte (Entracque, May) or Granfondo Alpi del Mare/L'Étape Mondovì (Mondovì, September).

### Manali-Khardung La Cycling Championship
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 313.8 mi | — | Manali to Leh, Himachal Pradesh / Ladakh, India | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/manali-khardungla-cycling-championship/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/manali-khardungla-cycling-championship.md

An extreme Himalayan high-altitude stage race on paper — but unverified since 2015, so confirm it's actually running before you book. Starts in Manali, crosses from Himachal Pradesh over the Great Himalaya into the Trans-Himalayan terrain of Ladakh, passes through Leh, and finishes atop Khardung La. It covers roughly 500-510 km of the Manali-Leh-Khardung La corridor over multiple stages (nine in the last independently verified 2015 edition — not a fixed seven-day cutoff, despite marketing copy suggesting one). The surface is predominantly paved high-altitude highway, interrupted by sand, gravel and rocky stretches. Repeated high passes, large daily altitude changes and a final ascent above 5,300 m define it — this is a supported high-altitude endurance/expedition race, not a conventional one-day mass-start road event, and the promoter runs a competitive timed format alongside a parallel untimed adventure-tour option for the same route. Signature challenge: The Leh-Khardung La finale, finishing around 5,359-5,375 m, where hypoxia compounds the final climb after days of accumulated high-altitude fatigue. This is a genuinely demanding high-altitude, multi-stage cycling event on the Manali-Leh-Khardung La corridor — but its current operating status cannot be confirmed. The last independently verifiable edition finished on 3 August 2015 with a real 63-rider field and named winners. The promoter (Northern Escapes Outdoors) has since advertised further editions, including a claimed 2022 running and a 2024 edition scheduled for 7-16 August, but no independent source confirms either actually took place — the official site itself has remained frozen on the 2024 dates with no post-event report. Promoter marketing also overstates the route: distance is claimed at 558.4 km against the promoter's own more conservative 500-510 km figure, and Khardung La is still billed as the 'world's highest motorable pass,' a claim Guinness World Records no longer supports (that title now belongs to Umling La at 5,798 m). Treat every current-year claim from this promoter with real skepticism until a 2026 edition is independently verified. Only after independently confirming a current edition is scheduled and has run recently — the promoter's marketing has outpaced verifiable results for over a decade.

### Marmotte Granfondo Pyrenees
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 110 mi | 18,701 ft | Argelès-Gazost / Luz-Saint-Sauveur, Hautes-Pyrénées, France | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/marmotte-pyrenees/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/marmotte-pyrenees.md

Five Pyrenean cols. Double Tourmalet. 5,700m of climbing. Summit finish. The Marmotte's Pyrenean sister hits harder per kilometer than the Alpine original. The Marmotte Pyrénées is the event that cycling insiders know but the broader world has not fully discovered yet. On paper, it is the younger sister of the legendary Alpine Marmotte. In practice, it might be the harder ride. The numbers do not lie: 5,700m of climbing in 177 km gives it a higher elevation-per-kilometer ratio than the Alps. The double Tourmalet — climbing the most storied mountain in the Pyrenees from both sides in a single day — is an act of organized cruelty that, after 120 km, will have you questioning the sanity of the route designers. And then, when the Tourmalet has taken everything, they send you up Hautacam with its irregular gradients that refuse to let you find a rhythm.

The Pyrenees are darker, wilder, and less forgiving than the Alps, and this event embraces that character completely. Where the Alpine Marmotte finishes on the iconic 21 hairpins of Alpe d'Huez with crowds four deep, the Pyrénées edition sends you up a ski station road where the only witnesses are sheep and your own suffering. The Tourmalet at dawn, with mist rolling off the Pic du Midi and the road rising endlessly above the treeline, is one of cycling's great sensory experiences. Doing it a second time, 100 km later on legs that have already climbed three other mountain passes, is one of cycling's great tests of character.

If the Alpine Marmotte is the bucket-list mountain sportive, the Pyrénées edition is the insider's version — harder per kilometer, less crowded, and set against the wild, dark drama of the Tour de France's spiritual home. Give it ten more years and this event will be spoken about in the same breath as its Alpine sibling. For now, it remains the connoisseur's choice. Yes if you want the intensity of the Alpine Marmotte with more climbing per kilometer and fewer crowds. Yes if the Tourmalet means something to you — doing it twice in one day is a career cycling memory. Skip if you want the prestige and global atmosphere of the Alpine original. Skip if you need technical terrain — this is pure road climbing on tarmac.

### Gran Fondo Milano-Sanremo
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 184 mi | 14,474 ft | Milan to Sanremo, Liguria, Italy | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/milano-sanremo-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/milano-sanremo-gran-fondo.md

La Classicissima — 296 km from Milan to the Ligurian Riviera. The Turchino, the Capi, Cipressa, Poggio, Via Roma. The longest day in amateur cycling. A race of three acts across three regions of Italy. Act One: the Lombardy and Piedmont plains — 100+ km of flat, fast, relentless agricultural roads where the peloton moves at 40+ km/h and the only challenge is staying in the group and out of the wind. Act Two: the Turchino — the first real climb, the passage through the Apennines where Lombardy becomes Liguria and the grey plains give way to the blue Mediterranean. Act Three: the Ligurian coast — 100 km of increasingly dramatic riding as the three Capi, the Cipressa, and the Poggio pile suffering onto legs that have already ridden 200+ km. The course is deceptive in its simplicity. No individual climb is fearsome. The Poggio averages 3.7%. The Cipressa averages 4.1%. But at kilometer 270 and kilometer 280, those modest percentages become the hardest climbs of your life. The pro peloton calls this phenomenon 'the course that bites you at the end.' For amateurs riding 2-3 hours longer than the professionals, the bite is sharper. Signature challenge: The distance. 296 kilometers. Not the Turchino, not the Cipressa, not the Poggio — those are just climbs. The signature challenge of the Gran Fondo Milano-Sanremo is the distance itself. It is the longest one-day amateur cycling event in the world, and there is no way to simulate it in training. You can ride 200 km. You can ride 250 km. But the zone between 250 km and 296 km is uncharted territory for nearly every rider who lines up. The legs stop working normally. The nutrition strategy that seemed bulletproof starts to fail. The mind begins its negotiations with the body. The Poggio at kilometer 280 is the cruelest joke in cycling — a climb that would be trivial at kilometer 80, transformed by distance into a monument of suffering. There are five Monuments in professional cycling. Milan-Sanremo is the longest, the oldest continuously run, and — for many — the most beautiful. La Classicissima. The Spring Classic. 296 kilometers from the industrial flatlands of Lombardy across the Apennines to the flower-scented Riviera di Ponente. The gran fondo version has been running since 1970, making it older than most of the riders who line up for it. You leave Settala at dawn and ride through the flat agricultural plains, the Turchino pass, the Ligurian coast, the three Capi, and then — with nearly 280 km in your legs — you climb the Cipressa and the Poggio. Two climbs that are not objectively hard. Two climbs that, after 280 km, will feel like the steepest roads you have ever ridden. Then you descend to the Via Roma in Sanremo and you are done. You have ridden La Classicissima. The same road Merckx rode seven times to victory. The same Poggio where Cancellara attacked from the front. The same Via Roma where van der Poel sprinted. No other amateur event in the world offers 296 km of Monument history in a single day. Yes if you are an endurance cyclist who wants the ultimate one-day road challenge — 296 km is a threshold experience that changes how you think about distance. Yes if you care about cycling history and want to ride every meter of the oldest, longest Monument. Yes if you have the discipline to train specifically for ultra-endurance and the self-sufficiency to manage nutrition for 10-13 hours with minimal feed station support. Skip if 296 km genuinely exceeds your ambition or your available training time. Skip if you want a well-serviced, festival-atmosphere sportive with aid stations every 30 km. Skip if you are looking for technical terrain or off-road riding — this is road cycling, pure and relentless.

### Race Across America
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 3000 mi | 175,000 ft | Oceanside, CA to Atlantic City, NJ | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-america/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-america.md

3,000 miles. Coast to coast. 12 days. The most extreme endurance cycling race on Earth. A 3,000-mile transcontinental odyssey across the full diversity of the American landscape. Desert, mountains, plains, ridgelines, and coastline — all in a single continuous effort. Signature challenge: 3,000 miles across the entire continental United States — desert heat, Rocky Mountain passes, Great Plains wind, Appalachian climbs, and 175,000 feet of elevation gain — all in a single continuous, nonstop effort under 12 days. Race Across America is not a bike race in any conventional sense. It is a 3,000-mile, coast-to-coast war of attrition against sleep deprivation, extreme climate, and the fundamental limits of the human body. Running since 1982, with fewer than 300 solo finishers in history and a 50% DNF rate, RAAM occupies a category of one. The logistics are staggering — you need a crew, vehicles, and a budget that rivals a small expedition. The experience is transformative. The prestige is unmatched in ultra-cycling. This is not an event most people should attempt. It is an event everyone should know about. If you are an elite ultra-endurance cyclist with $15,000-$100,000 to spend, a crew of 8-12 people willing to sacrifice two weeks, qualifying results from approved ultra events, and the physical and mental capacity to ride 20+ hours a day for 8-12 consecutive days across the entire continental United States — yes. For everyone else, RAAM is best appreciated from the crew van, the documentary couch, or the dot-watching screen.

### Race Through Poland
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 1118.5 mi | 88,583 ft | Nowy Targ, Poland | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-through-poland/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-through-poland.md

A genuine self-supported ultra-distance bikepacking race through the Carpathians — not a mass gran fondo, and the '7 countries' branding overstates the actual route. This is a one-stage, self-supported, Transcontinental-style bikepacking race, not a mass gran fondo. Race No.8 (2026) started and finished at Rynek in Nowy Targ, linking four mandatory control points and parcours through the Western Carpathians using rider-selected roads — because riders choose their own connections between controls, full-route finishers actually logged anywhere from 1,681 to 1,876 km in 2026, so any single distance figure is a nominal estimate, not a fixed course measurement. Documented geography centers on Poland, Slovakia and the Czech Republic; despite the organizer's broader PL/SK/CZ/DE/AT/HU/RO branding header, Germany, Austria, Hungary and Romania were not part of the actual No.8 route. Signature challenge: The Low Tatras crossing — explicitly designated the race's main mountain course, combining difficult routing choices with sustained Carpathian climbing between controls. Race Through Poland is a genuine, currently active self-supported bikepacking race, now on its eighth edition. It is not a mass-participation gran fondo and shouldn't be evaluated as one: there's no closed course, no fixed distance, no aid stations beyond four mandatory control points, and riders choose their own roads between them. The 2026 field of 78 starters produced only 44 finishers — a real, demanding event with a genuine attrition rate, verified by public GPS tracking and manually checked results rather than a self-reported honor system. The branding overstates the geography: despite a marketed 'seven-country' framing, the actual No.8 route stayed within Poland, Slovakia and the Czech Republic. Only if you want genuine self-supported ultra-distance racing with route-choice strategy and are prepared for a real chance of not finishing — 44 of 78 starters finished in 2026. This is not an entry-level gran fondo.

### Raid Pyreneen
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 447 mi | 36,100 ft | Hendaye (Atlantic) to Cerbere (Mediterranean), France | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/raid-pyreneen/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/raid-pyreneen.md

Ocean to ocean. 18 cols. 100 hours. The Pyrenees crossing that's been humbling cyclists since 1950. Epic. Point-to-point, ocean to ocean, 18 mountain passes over 3-5 days. The Pyrenees from west to east, starting in the green, rain-prone Basque country and finishing on the sun-baked Mediterranean coast. Each day brings a new set of cols, a new landscape, and a new challenge. The format — self-navigated with a stamped logbook — strips cycling back to its essentials: you, the mountains, and the road. Signature challenge: The Tourmalet at 2,115m is the symbolic peak, but the real challenge is the cumulative toll of 18 passes over 3-5 days with no support. The Raid tests self-reliance as much as fitness. The Raid Pyreneen is not an event. It's a tradition. Since 1950, cyclists have collected stamps in a logbook as they cross the Pyrenees from ocean to ocean — no timing chips, no aid stations, no spectators. Just you, 18 mountain passes, and 100 hours. The format hasn't changed because it doesn't need to. In an era of sold-out sportives with Instagram hashtags and finisher's beer gardens, the Raid stands apart as a declaration of what cycling adventure was always meant to be: self-reliant, mountain-focused, and earned. Yes if you want cycling's most authentic mountain challenge — no frills, no crowds, pure self-supported adventure. Yes if you value tradition over Instagram. Skip if you need organized support — this is fully on you. Skip if you want a single-day event.

### Sierra Nevada Límite Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 73.9 mi | 10,890 ft | Cenes de la Vega, Granada, Spain | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/sierra-nevada-limite/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/sierra-nevada-limite.md

Dense Sierra Nevada climbing test finishing at Pradollano — legitimately hard, but verify the current course, the organizer's own site disagrees with itself. A point-to-point road route starting at the Cenes de la Vega sports centre and finishing at Pradollano ski station, around 2,100 m altitude — not at the Veleta summit itself; the separate Subida al Veleta timed climb (38 km, 2,236 m, run the following day) is a different event, not part of this Gran Fondo. The route traverses mountainous roads east of Granada through the Sierra Nevada foothills, climbing Puerto de Blancares twice — once from Quéntar, once from La Peza — before turning through Güéjar Sierra toward El Duque and Las Sabinas. 2026 course figures (119 km / 3,319 m) run materially shorter than the 146.4 km / 3,353 m previously on file; the organizer's own site is internally inconsistent, with current Spanish-language pages giving 119 km/3,319 m and older English/homepage material still showing 140 km/3,200 m or other stale figures. Signature challenge: The dense 3,319 m of climbing packed into 119 km, capped by a classified high-mountain timed ascent on the Hotel El Duque-Las Sabinas segment (roughly 15 km, 1,177 m+) that alone decided the 2026 overall classification. Sierra Nevada Límite is a real, well-organized gran fondo with exceptional climbing density — 3,319 m packed into just 119 km for the 2026 edition, finishing at the Pradollano ski station east of Granada. It has genuine high-mountain roads, aid stations, medical teams, bag transfer, timing and finish food for 500+ riders. The problem is the organizer's own website: the current Spanish-language pages give one set of vitals (119 km/3,319 m, Cenes-Pradollano) while stale English/homepage material shows a different, larger course (140 km/3,200 m or other retained figures) — and the finish is at Pradollano, not the Veleta summit itself, despite marketing occasionally implying otherwise. The separate Subida al Veleta (38 km, 2,236 m) run the following day is the actual timed ascent to altitude, and it's a different event from this Gran Fondo. Yes if you want an exceptionally dense climbing test near Granada with solid event support. If you specifically want the Veleta summit and Europe's-highest-finish bragging rights, that's the separate Subida al Veleta event, not this Gran Fondo.

### Struggle Dales
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 102.5 mi | 10,223 ft | Harrogate, North Yorkshire, England | May | gran_fondo

A genuinely tough, well-supported Yorkshire Dales sportive marking its tenth anniversary — the 2026 route was redesigned and the organizer still hasn't published official elevation for it. Struggle Dales is a redesigned-for-2026, three-distance sportive (250 km Ultra, 165 km Classic, 120 km Short) based near Harrogate, running on paved roads through the Yorkshire Dales National Park's steep, rolling terrain. The 165 km Classic route contains six principal climbs; the 250 km Ultra contains ten. Signature challenge: The organizer has not published individual climb gradients for the redesigned 2026 route — the difficulty comes from the accumulation of six (Classic) or ten (Ultra) named climbs rather than one standout ascent. Struggle Dales is a real, well-supported UK sportive marking its tenth anniversary in 2026, offering three distances (120/165/250 km) through the Yorkshire Dales with route-switching permitted on the day. Cycling Weekly reviewed an early edition favorably, and the organizer backs the event with marshals, medical/mechanical support, a hotline, broomwagon, signposted courses with GPX files, and instant results. The route was redesigned for 2026 with new named climbs (Langbar, High Hill, Norwood Edge), but the organizer publishes rounded distances only — no official elevation or detailed climb-gradient data for the current route, so riders are left triangulating difficulty from other entrants' GPS tracks rather than the organizer's own materials. Yes if you want a legitimately hard, well-marshalled UK sportive with route-switching flexibility.
