### TORTOUR Ultracycling
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 621 mi | 45,932 ft | Schaffhausen, Switzerland | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tortour/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tortour.md

1,000 km non-stop across Switzerland. Alpine passes by starlight. The world's ultimate ultra-endurance cycling test. The TORTOUR 1000 route traverses Switzerland in a massive loop, changing year to year but always incorporating multiple Alpine passes, Swiss lowland roads, and urban transitions. The character is defined not by any single climb or descent but by the accumulation: 1,000 km of terrain changes, day-to-night-to-day temperature cycles, the psychological battle of sustained effort, and the Swiss Alps appearing on the horizon when your body is already finished. The route takes riders through multiple cantons, language regions, and climate zones. It is Switzerland distilled into a 48-hour continuous experience. Signature challenge: The second night. After 24+ hours and 500+ km of continuous riding, darkness falls again and the body demands sleep. Pushing through the second night — often on Alpine terrain — is the defining challenge of the TORTOUR 1000. Everyone can ride the first 500 km. The TORTOUR is decided in the dark hours. The TORTOUR is not a bike race. It is a 1,000 km argument with yourself about whether you can keep pedaling through the night, over Alpine passes, across an entire country, for 48 straight hours. The world's largest multi-day non-stop ultra-endurance cycling event takes everything Switzerland throws at you — 12,000m of climbing, 30-degree temperature swings, complete darkness, Alpine dawn — and compresses it into a single continuous effort.

Solo unsupported is the purest form: you, your bike, and whatever you can carry for 1,000 km. Solo with support gives you a crew car and checkpoint assistance. Teams of 2-6 relay the distance. Every format is punishing. The TORTOUR 1000 solo finisher has earned something that no one-day sportive can replicate.

The 2026 edition returns to Schaffhausen, the event's birthplace, after six years in the Zurich canton. The prologue, pasta party, and finisher's brunch return to the original format. This is a homecoming for an event that has grown into the defining ultra-cycling challenge in Europe. Yes if ultra-endurance cycling is your discipline and you want to test yourself against 1,000 km of Swiss terrain in 48 hours. Yes if the idea of Alpine passes at 3 AM excites rather than terrifies you. Skip if you have never ridden through the night or covered more than 300 km in a single effort. Skip if the budget (CHF 3,000-5,000 all-in) is prohibitive.

### Tour du Mont-Blanc Cyclo
Tier 2 | Score: 73/100 | 205 mi | 26,247 ft | Les Saisies, Haute-Savoie, France | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-du-mont-blanc-cyclo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-du-mont-blanc-cyclo.md

Circumnavigate Mont-Blanc through France, Switzerland, and Italy. 330 km. 8,000m of climbing. Dawn to dusk. One mountain. Three countries. Epic in scale, relentless in execution. The 330 km route is a circumnavigation — you are literally riding around a mountain massif, and the sense of circling Mont-Blanc drives the entire experience. The six major cols are not stacked as brutally as the Marmotte or Gavia events — there are valley recovery sections between climbs — but the sheer accumulation of climbing over 15+ hours creates a unique kind of attrition. The middle section through Switzerland and Italy, with the Great St. Bernard as the high point, is the psychological crux. The Cormet de Roselend as the final major col, when 260 km are in the legs, is the physical crux. Signature challenge: The 330 km distance with 8,000m of climbing through three countries creates a unique attrition challenge. No single climb is as brutal as the Mortirolo or as iconic as Alpe d'Huez, but the accumulated effect of 6+ cols over 15+ hours, with the Great St. Bernard at 2,469m as the high point after 130+ km, is the defining challenge. The Tour du Mont-Blanc Cyclo is not for the majority of cyclists. It is for the minority who have looked at the map, seen that you can ride around Western Europe's highest mountain through three countries in a single day, and thought: yes. 330 km. 8,000 meters. Six major cols. Dawn to dusk. France, Switzerland, Italy, and back to France. The Great St. Bernard Pass at 2,469m is a crossing that Napoleon used to invade Italy — you're doing it on a road bike with 200 km already in your legs. This is not a sportive. This is a geographical statement. Yes if you have deep ultra-endurance fitness and want the most epic single-day cycling adventure in Europe. Yes if riding through three countries around Western Europe's highest peak speaks to your sense of journey. Skip if you haven't completed at least one 200+ km mountain sportive. Skip if the logistics of a 15-hour day across three countries overwhelm rather than excite you.

### Tour of the Peak

Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-of-the-peak/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-of-the-peak.md

Peak District climbing on historic roads, undercut by the organizer's own inconsistent route data. Both the Long and Medium routes start and finish at Bakewell Showground in Derbyshire's Peak District. After a gentle opening, climbing begins just beyond Ashford-in-the-Water and stays frequent. Both routes cross Winnats Pass; the Long route adds Holme Moss before rejoining the Medium course, and Cat and Fiddle supplies the major late climb before the return to Bakewell. Organizer pages themselves aren't fully consistent — the linked Long-route detail page gives a slightly different 182.8 km/3,701 m — so treat these as best-available, not exact, figures. Signature challenge: Winnats Pass' timed 'Killer Mile' closed-road section, with ramps reportedly reaching 28% — the defining early test that splits Medium from Long routes. Tour of the Peak has real pedigree: it revives the 1943-2005 Tour of the Peak road race, and the current sportive delivers three major, nationally recognized climbs (Winnats Pass, Holme Moss, Cat and Fiddle) across the Peak District — with Winnats specifically run as a closed-road, separately timed 'Killer Mile' section. The event is well-organized on race day — chip timing, feed stations, that one closed-road timed climb — but its own published route data doesn't agree with itself: the main event page and the linked Long-route detail page give materially different distance and elevation figures for the same course. Entry also requires a narrow Tuesday-Thursday booking window with a mandatory questionnaire, and no day-of entries are accepted. Yes if you want a historically rooted, genuinely hard Peak District sportive with three major climbs. Book inside the Tuesday-Thursday entry window — there are no day-of entries.

### The Assault on Mt. Mitchell
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 102.7 mi | 11,000 ft | Spartanburg, South Carolina to Mt. Mitchell, North Carolina | May | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/assault-on-mt-mitchell/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/assault-on-mt-mitchell.md

102.7 miles. 11,000 feet. The highest summit east of the Mississippi. The Beast of the East since 1975. The Assault on Mt. Mitchell is a study in patience and delayed devastation. The first 80 miles lull you into thinking this is a pleasant century ride — rolling Piedmont roads through South Carolina and the North Carolina foothills, gaining barely 500 feet of net elevation as you pass through rural towns between Spartanburg and Marion. The road is flat enough to make you forget what you signed up for. Then mile 85 arrives, and the road tilts upward, and it does not stop tilting for the next 18 miles. The climb to the Blue Ridge Parkway gains over 1,000 feet in under 2 miles. The Parkway itself is a sustained grind at 3,000-5,000 feet with no flat recovery. At mile 98, you turn off the Parkway toward Mt. Mitchell State Park, and those final 5 miles to the summit are the cruelest on the course — steep, relentless grades through ancient spruce-fir forest to the summit at 6,684 feet. The air is cooler. The trees are different. You are standing at the highest point east of the Mississippi River, and your legs stopped working two miles ago. Signature challenge: The final 18 miles from Marion to the summit. After 80+ miles of rolling Piedmont riding, the course demands 5,000+ feet of climbing in the final stretch — a backloaded elevation profile that punishes anyone who did not respect the first 80 miles. The last 5 miles up the Mt. Mitchell summit road, on legs that have been working for 7-10 hours, through gradients that would be hard on fresh legs, is where the Beast of the East earns every letter of its name. There is no higher point east of the Mississippi River. There is no older cycling challenge to reach it. Since 1975, when John Bryan and a handful of Freewheelers pedaled from Spartanburg into the clouds above western North Carolina, the Assault on Mt. Mitchell has been the defining endurance cycling event east of the Rockies. The Beast of the East does not care about your FTP, your Strava KOMs, or your deep-section carbon wheels. It cares about whether you can ride 102 miles through the Carolina Piedmont, turn upward at mile 85 when your legs are already spent, and then climb 5,000 feet to the summit of a mountain that has no business being this tall on the East Coast. The first 80 miles are a long, hot warm-up. The last 20 are the ride. At the top, you stand at 6,684 feet in a spruce-fir forest that looks like it belongs in Canada, not North Carolina. You rode there from South Carolina. That fact will matter to you for a very long time. Yes if you want the defining climbing challenge east of the Rockies. Yes if a century ride with 11,000 feet of backloaded climbing and a geographic superlative finish appeals to you. Yes if you value tradition and community over timing chips and podiums. Skip if you need competitive structure, technical terrain, or cannot handle 80 miles of rolling warm-up before the real climbing begins.

### Formosa 900
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 559.2 mi | — | Circumnavigation of Taiwan | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/formosa-900/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/formosa-900.md

A well-supported circumnavigation-of-Taiwan tour category, not one standardized race — compare operators, don't trust a single '900 km' figure. 'Formosa 900' is a category name, not a single fixed event — there is no closed course, no start list and no unified date. Groups depart representative Taiwanese cities and circumnavigate the island using Cycling Route No. 1 plus organizer-selected variants, run as fully supported, non-competitive multi-day group tours rather than a mass-start race or self-supported challenge. The standard Taipei framework starts near Songshan Station, follows the urbanized western side south through Pingtung, crosses the southern mountains, then returns north through the Pacific coast and Huadong Rift Valley. Terrain combines river bikeways, cities, agricultural plains, coast roads, rolling hills and the Shouka mountain crossing. Published distances for '900' vary from roughly 900 to 950 km depending on operator and itinerary, and the full Cycling Route No. 1 measures 960.8 km — treat '900' as branding, not a fixed measurement. Signature challenge: The Shouka crossing (County Highway 199, climbing to roughly 450 m) — a representative day totals about 1,300 m of ascent before descending to the east coast, the main geographic pinch-point of the loop. Formosa 900 is a legitimate, well-supported circumnavigation-of-Taiwan cycling product — 1,268 riders including 381 international participants took part in 2025 — but it is not a single race or standardized event. It's a collection of paid, fully supported group-tour packages sold by different operators (Giant and others) under a shared '900' brand, each with its own dates, starting city, exact route and difficulty. Full support (bilingual guides, two support vehicles, luggage transport, meals, lodging, mechanical assistance) is genuinely strong, and the full-island format delivers unusually varied urban, rural, mountain, coastal and cultural landscapes in one trip. But comparing date, route, difficulty or field size across 'Formosa 900' entries is not meaningful — they're different products under one name. Yes if you want a fully supported, non-competitive multi-day tour around Taiwan with strong logistics. Compare specific operator packages carefully — dates, exact routes and distances vary meaningfully under the shared '900' branding.

### Gran Fondo Jordan
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 47.2 mi | 4,921 ft | Dead Sea, Jordan | January | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-jordan/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-jordan.md

A geographically stunning and physically brutal three-day climbing challenge that rewards serious cyclists willing to travel. Gran Fondo Jordan is a three-day stage race that weaponizes geography. The Dead Sea's position as Earth's lowest point becomes the launching pad for sustained climbing that tests every system in your body. Stage 1 is a deceptively simple time trial along the lake—flat but windy, a tactical opener. Stages 2 and 3 are climbing masterclasses: relentless ascents with variable gradient patterns, steep sections that demand pacing discipline, and descents that offer brief respite before the next push. The course is fully paved but feels raw and exposed, with Dead Sea views that are simultaneously beautiful and humbling as you suffer upward. This is climbing-focused cycling at its most unforgiving. Signature challenge: The 30 km Mount Panorama climb on Stage 3 is the event's defining challenge. Divided into three steep steps (first 5-6 km steep, second steep section after 10 km, third steep part at km 18), with moderate recovery sections and even short downhills between them, this climb demands tactical pacing and mental toughness. Riders must manage their effort across three distinct steep sections while managing fatigue from the previous day's climbing. The final 6 km flatten out slightly, but by then most riders are operating on empty. This is climbing that breaks riders mentally and physically. Gran Fondo Jordan is a rare breed: a genuinely distinctive cycling event that justifies the logistical effort to reach it. The elevation profile is legitimately brutal, the location is unforgettable, and the UCI credentials are real. This isn't a mass-participation gran fondo—it's a curated challenge for serious cyclists willing to travel. The small field creates intimacy but limits competitive depth. If you're seeking a cycling adventure with genuine geographic and physical challenge, this delivers. If you want a casual weekend ride with thousands of peers, look elsewhere. Yes if you're a strong climber seeking a unique, UCI-sanctioned challenge with genuine adventure and don't mind international travel logistics. Skip if you prefer mass-participation events, casual weekend rides, or budget-friendly racing.

### L'Étape Mondovì by Tour de France
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 68.7 mi | 7,451 ft | Mondovì, Piedmont, Italy | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-alpi-del-mare/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-alpi-del-mare.md

A well-attended gran fondo through the Alta Langa and Monregalese hills — now officially L'Étape Mondovì by Tour de France as of its 2026 second edition. Starts in central Mondovì at Piazza Ellero and finishes uphill in Mondovì's Piazza. The route loops through the Alta Langa and Monregalese valleys, including Murazzano, Vicoforte, Frabosa Soprana/Sottana and numerous smaller communes. The defining character is persistent rolling terrain — repeated panoramic climbs, descents and rhythm changes rather than one enormous Alpine pass — returning to Mondovì after approximately 110.5 km and 2,271 m of climbing. Now in its second edition (2026), the event was rebranded L'Étape Mondovì by Tour de France after debuting in 2025 as Granfondo Alpi del Mare — the same race, course region and organizer, under official Tour de France/L'Étape branding for its second year. Signature challenge: The Alta Langa/Monregalese 'sawtooth' — continuous climbing and descending throughout the route, making pacing and repeated accelerations the decisive factor rather than any single summit. This race debuted in 2025 as Granfondo Alpi del Mare and drew 2,400 riders in its first year through the Alta Langa and Monregalese valleys — the organizer's 2026 target of 'over 2,000' is actually a step down from that actual 2025 turnout. For 2026, it was absorbed into the official L'Étape Italy calendar and rebranded L'Étape Mondovì by Tour de France — the same course region and organizer, now carrying Tour de France/L'Étape closed-road protection and chip timing. As a second-year event under new branding, it lacks a long operating history, and its own official pages already disagree with each other on the basics: the event homepage shows 2,201 m of climbing while the route page, FAQ and regulations all say 2,271 m. Yes if you want genuine Alta Langa/Monregalese climbing with new Tour de France/L'Étape pedigree. Confirm current-year climbing figures directly — the organizer's own pages disagree by 70 m.

### Granfondo Antalya
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 65.2 mi | 2,158 ft | Kadriye/Belek, Antalya, Turkey | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-antalya/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-antalya.md

Warm late-season UCI qualifier on Antalya's flats near a major resort corridor — but check the current year's course, it moves every edition. Start and finish sit outside The Land of Legends resort in the Kadriye/Belek district east of Antalya. The route stays in the Turkish Riviera's low, rolling hinterland rather than climbing into the Taurus Mountains — the 2025 long course (92.6 km/512 m) ran from Prof. Dr. Erdal İnönü Kent Parkı to Düden Waterfall through the Lara–Aksu/EXPO corridor and Kurşunlu-area backroads, mixing fast flat/rolling tempo sections with a handful of short, sharper rises around Aksu and Kurşunlu. The course has changed materially edition to edition — 98 km/517 m in 2024, 92.6 km/512 m in 2025, a reported 105 km/658 m for 2026 — so treat any single year's vitals as edition-specific, not fixed. Signature challenge: No single decisive climb — the course rewards sustained bunch speed across repeated shallow rollers rather than a marquee mountain pass; the closest thing to a defining test is the string of short Kurşunlu-area rises (documented 2025 examples run roughly 1.4-4.0 km at 2.8-6.0%). UCI Gran Fondo World Series Antalya (formerly branded Nirvana Granfondo Antalya, after title sponsor Nirvana Hotels) is a real, currently active UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier held every November in the Kadriye/Belek resort corridor east of Antalya. It delivers what it promises: closed-road racing, genuine UCI World Championships qualification for the top 25% of finishers by age group, and warm late-autumn weather on the Turkish Riviera. What it does not deliver is a stable course — published distance and elevation have shifted every year on record (98 km/517 m in 2024, 92.6 km/512 m in 2025, a reported 105 km/658 m for 2026), and even within a single season the organizer's own pages have disagreed with the federation calendar and the UCI listing on both distance and dates. This is a fast, rolling course for rouleurs, not a mountain test — 658 m of climbing across 105 km is thin for a 'gran fondo' billing, and the organizer publishes no detailed climb map or gradient breakdown for the current route. Yes if you want a genuine UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier on fast, flat-to-rolling roads with warm November weather and convenient resort/airport logistics. Skip it if you want real Turkish mountain climbing — this course stays in the coastal hinterland, not the Taurus range.

### Granfondo San Gottardo
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 71 mi | 10,656 ft | Ambri, Ticino, Switzerland | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-gottardo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-gottardo.md

115 km, 3,248m climbing, three HC passes, 1832 cobblestones. Switzerland's most beautiful suffering. The course is a clockwise loop from Ambri through three distinct Alpine worlds. It opens with the Tremola — the cobblestone ascent of the Gotthard Pass through 24 hairpins of 1832 granite, a road monument unlike anything in cycling. After summiting at 2,106m, a fast descent drops into the Urseren valley and the base of the Furka Pass. The 12.2 km Furka climb at 7.3% average takes you past the famous Goldfinger filming location and the Rhône Glacier viewpoint to the summit at 2,429m. The descent into the Valais is fast and exposed. Then comes the Nufenen — 13.7 km at 8.3% average, the hardest climb of the day, saved for when your legs have nothing left. The summit at 2,478m is the second-highest paved road in Switzerland. The reward is a 26 km descent all the way back to the finish in Ambri. Signature challenge: The Nufenen Pass. At 13.7 km and 8.3% average, it is the steepest and highest of the three passes — and it comes last, after 80+ km and two HC climbs have already emptied your legs. The Tremola is the spectacle. The Nufenen is the reckoning. The Granfondo San Gottardo packs three of Switzerland's most legendary Alpine passes into 115 km of pure, concentrated suffering and beauty. The Tremola cobblestones — 4 km of 1832 granite through 24 hairpins — are cycling's most photogenic climb. The Furka Pass descent past the Rhône Glacier is James Bond's literal road. The Nufenen, at 2,478m and averaging 8.3% over 13.7 km, is the silent assassin that breaks you when you thought the hard work was done.

Cycling Plus voted this the best 100 km loop in Europe. It is hard to argue. The variety is extraordinary — cobblestones to smooth tarmac, Italian-speaking Ticino to German-speaking Uri, valley warmth to Alpine cold, history to cinema. And all of it compressed into a day's ride that starts and finishes in a small Ticino village.

The event itself is Swiss-organized and appropriately precise. Three feeding zones, mechanical support, professional timing, finisher meal. No unnecessary frills, no corporate bloat. Just an honest sportive on extraordinary roads. Yes if you want concentrated Alpine climbing on three legendary passes in a single day. Yes if the Tremola cobblestones and Goldfinger's Furka road are on your cycling bucket list. Skip if you need a large, competitive field or global prestige. Skip if Switzerland's prices and the Nufenen's 8.3% average after two prior passes sound like punishment rather than purpose.

### Cycle to the Sun
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 36 mi | 10,023 ft | Pa'ia, Maui, Hawaii | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/haleakala-cycle-to-the-sun/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/haleakala-cycle-to-the-sun.md

Sea level to 10,023 feet. One climb. One volcano. The House of the Sun. Pure uphill. There is no flat. There is no descent. The road leaves Pa'ia at sea level and climbs continuously for 36 miles through four distinct climate zones to the summit of Haleakala at 10,023 feet. The average gradient is 5%, but sections through Makawao hit 10% and the final summit approach reaches 10-18% in oxygen-depleted air. The landscape transforms completely as you climb: tropical vegetation gives way to eucalyptus, then pine, then barren volcanic rock above the treeline. You will ride above the clouds. You will arrive at the rim of a volcanic crater. Every foot of elevation is earned. Signature challenge: The final 8 miles above the park entrance. Above the cloud line, through barren volcanic landscape, with 70% oxygen and gradients hitting 18%, you grind to the summit crater of Haleakala at 10,023 feet. It is the closest thing to riding on another planet. Cycle to the Sun is not the hardest race in the world, or the most prestigious, or the most competitive. It is, however, one of the most extraordinary cycling experiences on the planet. You start at sea level on a tropical island and ride continuously uphill for 36 miles until you're standing at 10,023 feet on the rim of a volcanic crater, above the clouds, in 40-degree air that was 80 degrees when you started. You traverse every climate zone Hawaii has to offer — tropical, temperate, alpine, volcanic — in a single effort. The name Haleakala means 'House of the Sun,' and when you reach the summit, you understand why. This is not a race you enter to win. This is a ride you do to remind yourself that cycling can take you to places that feel like the edge of the Earth. Yes if you want one of cycling's most extraordinary single-climb experiences. Yes if riding through four climate zones to the summit of a Hawaiian volcano sounds like a lifetime memory. Skip if you need competitive depth or can't justify Hawaii travel costs for a single 36-mile uphill ride.

### Granfondo Nove Colli
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 124 mi | 12,513 ft | Cesenatico, Emilia-Romagna, Italy | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/nove-colli/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/nove-colli.md

The queen of granfondos — 9 Romagna hills, 200km, Pantani's hometown, and the event that invented the gran fondo format in 1971. 200km of relentless Romagna hills from the Adriatic coast into the Apennine foothills and back. The course starts with a flat 28km coastal section at 40+ km/h with echelons, then hits 9 named climbs in succession. No single climb is alpine, but the cumulative effect of 3,814m over 200km with pitches of 18% is enormous. Barbotto (18% max) is the signature, Gorolo (17-20% finale) is the final sting. The food stations serve actual Romagna cuisine — this is a culinary tour as much as a cycling event. Signature challenge: Barbotto — 5.5km at 6.9% average with a devastating final kilometer of 14-18% gradients. The crowd atmosphere at the summit, with an announcer calling every rider's name, is one of the great moments in amateur cycling. Nove Colli is where the gran fondo was invented. 17 riders in 1971, 12,000 today. The course is not alpine — max altitude 791m — but the relentless succession of 9 hills with pitches to 18% over 200km creates genuine suffering. Barbotto with the announcer calling your name is one of the great moments in amateur cycling. The Pantani connection is everywhere — you're riding his training roads in his hometown. EUR 120 including a Gobik jersey and 9 food stations serving actual Romagna cuisine is exceptional value. Yes, if you appreciate cycling heritage and Italian food culture as much as course difficulty. The 200km long route with 3,814m of climbing is genuinely tough, but the altitude is modest. The medium route (137km) includes the iconic Barbotto. Come for the history, the Pantani connection, and the 9 food stations.

### Omloop Het Nieuwsblad Sportive
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 93 mi | 3,996 ft | Ghent, Belgium | March | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/omloop-het-nieuwsblad-sportive/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/omloop-het-nieuwsblad-sportive.md

Essential Flemish classics cyclo for cobbles lovers. Cobbled Flemish hellingen and pavé sectors mimicking pro Omloop; new additions for 2026. Signature challenge: Muur van Geraardsbergen cobbles This sportive captures the soul of Flemish cycling—cobbles, wind, and bergs that humble even pros. Starting from 't Kuipke the day after MVDP's win? Pure magic for €25. Shorter Ninove options make it accessible, but 150km is the real test of Vlaamse koersbeleving. Iconic routes matching the pro race with new challenges like Haaghoek and Leberg. Excellent value, strong community, weather adds adventure. T2 tier gran fondo with top cultural punch.

### RAGBRAI
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 391 mi | 16,027 ft | Across Iowa, USA (Missouri River to Mississippi River, west to east) | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/ragbrai/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/ragbrai.md

America's oldest, largest, and longest multi-day bicycle ride. 53 years of Iowa towns turning themselves inside out for 10,000+ riders. RAGBRAI is not a race. It is not even really a ride, in the way most cyclists understand rides. It is a 400-mile rolling block party across the entire state of Iowa, powered by pedals and sustained by the most extraordinary host community in sports. You will ride through towns where the entire population has turned out to feed you pie, spray you with garden hoses, and blast classic rock from a flatbed trailer. You will camp in church yards, drink beer at breakfast, and discover that Iowa is not flat. You will dip your tire in the Missouri River on Saturday and the Mississippi River the following Saturday and wonder where the week went.

Since 1973, RAGBRAI has defined American recreational cycling. It inspired over 200 similar events worldwide. It has been visited upon all 99 Iowa counties. Nearly half a million riders have completed it. The oldest, largest, and longest multi-day bicycle ride in the world is not a race — and that is precisely why it matters. RAGBRAI proves that the best reason to ride a bicycle is to ride a bicycle, preferably through a small town that has been waiting all year for you to arrive.

Do not come to RAGBRAI expecting a challenge. Come expecting a transformation. Come expecting the farmer playing saxophone on the hilltop at sunrise, the 90-year-old woman handing out cookies from her porch, and the moment on Day 5 when you realize you have been smiling for five straight days and you cannot remember the last time that happened. That is RAGBRAI. That is Iowa. That is cycling at its most fundamentally, unapologetically joyful. You do not race RAGBRAI. You ride it. You experience it. You eat pie at every stop and drink beer before noon and sleep in a tent in a stranger's yard and discover that Iowa is hillier, friendlier, and more beautiful than you imagined. If you have ever wanted to know what happens when an entire state decides to throw a week-long party for cyclists, register for RAGBRAI. Registration opens November each year and fills steadily. $250 for the week. Bring a bike, a tent, sunscreen, and an appetite. Leave the power meter at home.

### RAMROD — Ride Around Mount Rainier in One Day
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 154 mi | 10,000 ft | Enumclaw, Washington, USA | July | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/ramrod/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/ramrod.md

154 miles. 10,000 feet. One active volcano. The Pacific Northwest's defining cycling challenge since 1984. RAMROD is a circumnavigation. You ride all the way around an active volcano and come back to where you started. That simple premise — one loop, one mountain, one day — produces one of the most varied and rewarding days you will ever spend on a bicycle. The ride begins in the agricultural lowlands east of Tacoma, where Enumclaw sits at the Cascade foothills. Depending on the route edition, you may head counterclockwise toward the Nisqually Entrance and Paradise (the classic route) or clockwise toward Crystal Mountain and Cayuse Pass (the modern bypass). Either way, the terrain transitions dramatically: flat farmland gives way to rolling foothills, which give way to towering old-growth forest, which gives way to alpine passes where the air cools and the mountain dominates the sky. Stevens Canyon Road — when permitted — is the emotional heart of the ride: a 1930s-era park road through a glacial valley with stone bridges and tunnels. Cayuse Pass at mile 100+ is the physical heart: 8 miles at 6% when your legs have nothing left. The long descent back to Enumclaw in the Pacific Northwest's extended summer twilight is the reward. The mountain was always there. You rode all the way around it. Signature challenge: Cayuse Pass at mile 100. Eight miles at a constant 6% grade in afternoon sun with no shade, on legs that have already climbed 6,000-7,000 feet over 100 miles. Every RAMROD veteran knows the name. The rest stop halfway up Cayuse is the most grateful you will ever be for a cup of water and a folding chair. The climb is not technically difficult — it is 6% and relentless — but arriving at its base after 100 miles of riding around a volcano transforms a moderate climb into a test of will. Cayuse Pass is where RAMROD separates the people who trained for 150 miles from the people who trained for 100. Forty years ago, a cyclist named John Dixon convinced 51 other people to ride their bicycles all the way around Mount Rainier in a single day. Forty-one editions later, 800 people win a lottery each year for the privilege of doing the same thing. RAMROD is the Pacific Northwest condensed into a single day on a bicycle: old-growth forest, alpine passes, glacial rivers, quiet foothills towns, and a 14,411-foot active volcano that is always there — above the treeline, above the clouds, above everything. The ride starts in the dark of Enumclaw at 5 AM with breakfast cooked by the local Rotary club. It climbs to Paradise through cathedral forests with the mountain overhead. It crosses Stevens Canyon on 1930s stone bridges through a glacial valley. It grinds up Cayuse Pass at mile 100 on legs that stopped cooperating 20 miles ago. And it returns to Enumclaw 150 miles later, in the long Pacific Northwest twilight, with the mountain still watching. RAMROD is not the hardest ride in America. It is not the longest. But it may be the most complete — a full orbit of something genuinely magnificent, earned one pedal stroke at a time. Yes if you want to circumnavigate an active volcano in a single day on one of America's most storied cycling routes. Yes if 150+ miles through national park alpine passes, old-growth forest, and glacial valleys is your idea of a perfect day. Yes if you value community tradition over timing chips and age-group podiums. Enter the lottery every year and volunteer when you can. Skip if you need competitive structure, technical terrain, or a ride shorter than 150 miles. Skip if you cannot handle uncertainty — the route changes annually and the event's future depends on National Park Service permitting decisions.

### Ride Across Britain
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 970 mi | — | Land's End to John O'Groats, UK | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/ride-across-britain/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/ride-across-britain.md

A fully supported nine-day Land's End to John O'Groats ride through varied UK scenery — a supported endurance tour, not a competitive race. A fully supported, signposted end-to-end ride rather than a race — Ride Across Britain travels north from Land's End, Cornwall, to John O'Groats, Scotland, crossing 23 counties across England, Wales and Scotland over nine consecutive riding stages. It links Cornwall and Devon's steep lanes and moorland with Cheddar Gorge, the Severn crossing, the Wye Valley, northern England and Shap Fell, before the Scottish stages cross the Grampians and Cairngorms to the remote Strathnaver Valley and North Atlantic coast. No official 2026 elevation total is published; official distance materials themselves disagree, with the website's rounded '980 miles' headline against the 2026 event sheet's more specific 970 miles. Signature challenge: Stage 7, Hopetoun House to Strathdon — 180.2 km with approximately 2,449 m ascent, rated 5/5 by the organizer, crossing the Cairngorms and climbing Glenshee late in the day. Ride Across Britain is a genuine, well-established fully supported traverse of the UK, run by Threshold Sports over nine consecutive riding days. It delivers exceptional geographic variety — Cornwall's steep lanes, the Wye Valley, the Grampians and Cairngorms, the remote Scottish north coast — with extensive support: route signage, regular rest stops, medical and mechanical assistance, chaperones, baggage transport, meals, showers and pre-pitched tents. This is explicitly a supported, non-competitive challenge ride, not a race with a field to compete against. Even the organizer's own materials aren't fully consistent — the main site advertises a rounded '980 miles' while the 2026 event sheet specifies 970 miles, and no verified elevation total is published. Yes if you want a genuinely demanding, exceptionally well-supported nine-day traverse of Britain. This is a challenge ride, not a competitive race — go in with that expectation.

### Sellaronda Bike Day
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 33 mi | 5,413 ft | Sella Group, Dolomites, Italy | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/sellaronda-bike-day/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/sellaronda-bike-day.md

Four car-free Dolomite passes, 20,000 cyclists, zero entry fee — the purest cycling experience in the mountains, twice a year. A counterclockwise circuit around the Sella Group — the massive limestone massif at the junction of four South Tyrolean valleys. The route links four Dolomite passes in a continuous loop of climbing and descending through some of the most dramatic mountain scenery on Earth. On Sellaronda Bike Day, the absence of motor traffic transforms this circuit from a challenging road ride into a transcendent cycling experience. The terrain is constantly undulating — you are either climbing a pass or descending one, with minimal flat valley transitions. Signature challenge: Not a single climb but the totality: four passes in 55 km with 1,780m of climbing, experienced in silence on car-free roads through the most dramatic mountain landscape in Europe. The physical challenge is modest; the experiential impact is extraordinary. Sellaronda Bike Day is the simplest concept in cycling events: close the roads around the Sella Group to cars for one day and let cyclists ride. No registration, no timing, no fees, no bibs. Just 55 km of four legendary Dolomite passes — Sella (2,240m), Pordoi (2,239m), Gardena (2,136m), and Campolongo (1,875m) — in complete silence. The result is one of the most magical cycling experiences on Earth.

The numbers are modest — 55 km and 1,780m of climbing is a half-day ride for any fit cyclist. But the numbers miss the point entirely. This is about the silence. On any other day, these roads carry cars, buses, and motorcycles through some of the most dramatic mountain scenery in Europe. On Sellaronda Bike Day, 20,000+ cyclists of every age and ability share these roads without a single engine noise. The only sounds are tires on tarmac, wind through the Dolomite spires, and the spontaneous cheering at pass summits.

The event runs twice annually — June and September — offering two different Dolomite experiences. June delivers wildflower meadows, long daylight, and occasionally lingering snow at the highest elevations. September brings autumn colors, stable weather, and a gentler light. Both are extraordinary. The 20th edition in 2026 is a celebration of a concept so pure it has not needed to change since its inception: close the roads, open the mountains, and let bicycles be bicycles. Ride this if you love cycling as pure experience — car-free Dolomite passes in UNESCO World Heritage scenery with zero bureaucracy. Skip it if you need competitive structure, timing, results, or a challenging distance (55 km is short). If you want a competitive Dolomite event, enter the Maratona dles Dolomites lottery instead.

### Velo Vietnam Northern Frontier
Tier 2 | Score: 71/100 | 331.2 mi | 29,035 ft | Northern Vietnam (Hanoi to Ha Giang) | October | gran_fondo

Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/velo-vietnam-northern-frontier.md

A premium guided multi-day tour through Vietnam's northern border highlands with sustained climbing and karst scenery — the organizer is explicit that it's not a race. This is a bookable guided challenge tour, not a mass-participation race — the organizer explicitly states 'this is not a race,' and timed climbing/GC standings are optional. Riders assemble in Hanoi, transfer beyond the capital, then ride through Bắc Kạn and Cao Bằng toward the Chinese-border highlands and Hà Giang. The route uses paved mountain roads, long passes, quiet valleys, switchbacks, and the Đồng Văn Karst Plateau/Happiness Road, finishing at a traditional ethnic-minority house in a village outside Hà Giang city before a transfer back to Hanoi. Seventeen designated uphill segments provide optional competition while the group otherwise rides together. Signature challenge: The Stage 3 centerpiece — 17.4 km at 5% followed by 4.15 km at 8% on/near Happiness Road — the longest sustained optional-competitive climbing block of the tour. Velo Vietnam Northern Frontier is a premium, fully guided multi-day cycling tour through Northern Vietnam's border highlands — not a sanctioned road race, and the organizer says as much directly. Full guide, motorcycle, mechanic, van, meal, transfer, GPS-route and photography support back four riding stages between Hanoi and Hà Giang, with 17 optional timed climbing segments determining an informal, non-binding leaderboard for riders who want it. An independent rider report from the 2019 pilot described near-perfect pavement, reliable hydration/regrouping support, strong local knowledge and exceptional limestone-mountain scenery — genuine praise for a genuinely different category of event than the mass-start gran fondos elsewhere in this database. Yes if you want a genuinely well-supported guided tour through remote mountain terrain with optional informal competition. Not for riders who want a sanctioned race with a real field and official results.

### Alpen Challenge Lenzerheide
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 117.4 mi | 14,435 ft | Lantsch/Lenz, Graubünden, Switzerland | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpen-challenge-lenzerheide/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpen-challenge-lenzerheide.md

A real 25-edition-deep Swiss Alps gran fondo over the Albula, Splügen and Julier passes — open roads and genuine high-pass weather risk, not a closed-course event. Both routes start and finish in Lantsch/Lenz, in the Lenzerheide region of Graubünden. The long course crosses the Albula Pass, the Upper Engadine and Maloja before descending through Bergell into Italy, then climbs the Splügen Pass and returns through Viamala. The short course shares the Albula/Engadine opening before turning over the Julier Pass and returning via Savognin and Salouf, with route-switching permitted at Silvaplana. This is an open-road granfondo — roads are not closed to traffic — defined by major Alpine passes, long descents and a final uphill return to Lantsch/Lenz. Signature challenge: The Splügen Pass — 30.4 km and 1,842 m of continuous climbing from Chiavenna, 500 m more ascent than the Albula, arriving deep into the long route after the Engadine and Bergell have already taken their toll. Alpen Challenge Lenzerheide is a legitimate, long-running Swiss Alpine gran fondo — the 2026 edition marks its 25th year — offering two genuinely major routes through some of Graubünden's most scenic terrain: the Albula Pass, Upper Engadine, Bergell, and either the Splügen Pass (long) or Julier Pass (short). It's a UNESCO-adjacent ride through the Albula railway landscape with timed classification, aid stations and medical support. But it is not a closed-road event — riders share the route with normal traffic throughout — and high-pass Alpine weather is a real operational risk, not just marketing language: the 2024 edition was cancelled minutes before the start due to snow cover. Yes if you want genuine Alpine passes (Albula, Splügen or Julier) with real organizational depth. Come prepared for open-road traffic and real weather risk — the 2024 edition was cancelled for snow.

### Bike Abu Dhabi Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 93.2 mi | 5,988 ft | Hazza bin Zayed Stadium, Al Ain to Sheikh Zayed Festival, Al Wathba, Abu Dhabi, UAE | December | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/bike-abu-dhabi-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/bike-abu-dhabi-gran-fondo.md

Prize-laden desert road epic for community cyclists. Fast desert roads with long straights, gentle rises, and light inclines; fully supported with 5 water stations. Signature challenge: 150km UAE inter-city haul with speed-group competition. A standout road gran fondo in the desert, blending massive prizes, pro-amateur racing, and UAE hospitality into an accessible yet challenging event. Perfect for speed-focused endurance riders seeking value and adventure without gravel or climbs. The Bike Abu Dhabi Gran Fondo delivers a fast 150km road challenge across UAE deserts, backed by top support and AED 2M prizes. Ideal for speed groups from elites to recreational riders, it's a cornerstone of Abu Dhabi's cycling rise.

### Boone Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 94 mi | 8,432 ft | Boone, North Carolina, USA | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/boone-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/boone-gran-fondo.md

Fun, scenic high-country gran fondo with timed segments and mountain challenges in cooler summer temps — an open-road, segment-timed format, not a closed race. Start and finish are at 164 South Depot Street in downtown Boone, near Appalachian Voices/FizzED. The paved route crosses Appalachian State University before entering the wooded, rolling roads of North Carolina's Blue Ridge High Country. The Gran route runs past Grandfather Mountain through Linville, Newland, the North Toe River Valley, Beech Mountain, Bethel Valley, Sugar Grove and Valle Crucis — repeated short climbs, twisting descents and limited recovery define it, not one single giant ascent. This is not a closed course; riders must obey traffic controls, and only timed segments determine results, with a 10 mph progression-speed cutoff (including stopped time) that can force Gran/Medio riders onto a shorter route. Signature challenge: Shull's Mill-Hwy 221 — a climb past the Blue Ridge Parkway followed by a paved 'roller-coaster' traverse of Grandfather Mountain, the course's signature terrain feature. Boone Gran Fondo offers real Blue Ridge High Country scenery and three difficulty choices through terrain shaped by Grandfather Mountain, the North Toe River Valley and Beech Mountain. It's honest about what it is: not a closed-course or start-to-finish race, but a marked route with timed segments where riders must obey normal traffic controls between them. A 10 mph progression-speed cutoff (including stopped time) can force slower Gran/Medio riders onto a shorter route mid-ride. Published course figures conflict across the organizer's own pages and local tourism sites, and 2026 route details remain labeled provisional. Yes if you want genuine Blue Ridge scenery with flexible difficulty options. Understand it's open-road and segment-timed, with a real progression-speed cutoff that can shorten your day.

### Cycling Shimanami
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 43.5 mi | 2,417 ft | Onomichi, Hiroshima Prefecture to Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan | October | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/cycling-shimanami/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/cycling-shimanami.md

Japan's most prestigious international cycling event offering unparalleled logistics, scenery, and cultural immersion across the Seto Inland Sea. The IMABARI 70 is a one-way island crossing from Onomichi to Imabari over six islands and nine bridges. Its advertised distance is about 70 km; the organizer-linked route measures roughly 66 km with about 737 m of climbing. Paved island roads alternate with normally car-only expressway sections opened to cyclists for the event, and the elevation accumulates through repeated bridge approaches rather than one major climb. Signature challenge: Nine bridge crossings and their repeated approaches. The route never has one defining mountain, but the short climbs to bridge level keep returning while the open-water setting leaves pace exposed to wind. Cycling Shimanami represents the gold standard for mass-participation cycling events in Asia. The combination of world-class organization, stunning scenery, and genuine cultural integration makes it exceptional for riders seeking an unforgettable experience rather than a competitive challenge. The event's biennial schedule and international draw create a unique atmosphere where thousands of cyclists from around the world share the road simultaneously, with locals cheering from sidewalks and photographers lining the route. The rolling bridge approaches add real climbing without turning the IMABARI 70 into a mountain event. For those prioritizing logistics, experience quality, and community engagement over raw difficulty, this is a premier destination event. Cycling Shimanami 2026 stands as a masterclass in event organization and cyclist-centric infrastructure. The event's strength lies in its holistic experience: stunning bridge crossings, event-only expressway access, volunteer support, and authentic cultural integration. The October timing and biennial schedule create a genuine international gathering. The repeated bridge approaches make the 70 km target rolling rather than flat, but this still appeals primarily to experience-seekers rather than riders chasing a competitive mountain challenge. For international cyclists planning a Japan cycling pilgrimage, this is non-negotiable; for those seeking a hard race, look elsewhere.

### Love Tiles Douro Granfondo

Portuguese granfondo blending Douro climbs with wine-country scenery — genuinely well-attended, but the organizer's own course figures don't agree with each other. All three routes start and finish in Peso da Régua. The Granfondo heads south through Lamego, Tarouca, Moimenta da Beira, São João da Pesqueira, Tabuaço and Armamar on paved, hilly Douro roads, following the EN226 toward Faia and the Vilar reservoir before returning through vineyard villages and Tabuaço to the Douro-side EN222. Terraced vineyards, river valleys, sustained climbing and steep descents define the route; the southern alignment was introduced after winter landslides damaged the traditional northern roads, and total elevation gain remains unpublished by the organizer. All three distances start together with only about 2 km controlled, creating a potentially crowded opening. Signature challenge: The Tabuaço climb — 9 km at 5.6% average, the principal quantified climb on the course, followed by a steep, technical descent through Barcos, Adorigo and Tedo. Love Tiles Douro Granfondo is a legitimate, well-attended event through UNESCO-listed Alto Douro vineyard country, drawing roughly 2,000 riders from 25 nationalities and carrying real competitive credibility through Portugal's Superprestígio series — Rui Costa and Pepe have both been associated with the event. But the organizer's own published course figures don't agree with each other (140.3/105.4/71.1 km in official documentation versus 135/100/69 km elsewhere in the same narrative materials), and total elevation gain for the Granfondo route is not published anywhere found. The southern route alignment used in 2026 was itself a reroute forced by winter landslide damage to the traditional course. Yes for the scenery, international field and Superprestígio pedigree. Confirm the current year's exact route and distance directly — recent landslide damage forced a reroute, and published figures conflict.

### Dragon Ride L'Etape Wales
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 143 mi | 11,483 ft | Margam Park, Port Talbot, South Wales, UK | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/dragon-ride/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/dragon-ride.md

The UK's oldest and hardest sportive. 230 km through the Brecon Beacons. Devil's Elbow at 10.3%. L'Etape by Tour de France branding earned through 22 years of Welsh mountain suffering. The Dragon Ride is the event that invented the UK sportive scene. Before it existed, British cyclists went to France to suffer on mountain roads. Lou Lusardi looked at the Brecon Beacons in 2004, saw Italian gran fondo terrain hiding in plain sight, and built an event that has drawn 4,700+ riders annually for over two decades. The Gran Fondo at 230 km with 3,500 m of climbing is a legitimate monster — longer and harder than most L'Etape du Tour editions. The Brecon Beacons deliver climbing that riders describe as the closest the UK gets to the Alps: Rhigos grinds on for 11 km, Black Mountain feels like the end of the world, and Devil's Elbow hits you with 10.3% through hairpins that would not look out of place on the Stelvio. Welsh weather adds a dimension that Italian gran fondos never deliver — you might get baked in June sunshine or hammered by horizontal rain, and the organisers tell you to pack for both.

The 2016 ASO partnership brought L'Etape by Tour de France branding and international credibility, but the Dragon Ride had already earned its reputation the hard way: 22 years of riders crawling up Welsh mountains and declaring it the hardest thing they have ever done on a bike. Starting from the gothic grandeur of Margam Park's Tudor mansion, climbing through increasingly wild terrain until you are alone on a windswept mountain with sheep for company, then descending through valleys that feel like they belong in Middle-earth — this is an experience that no amount of branding can manufacture. It is authentically, brutally, beautifully Welsh. The 2027 Tour de France Grand Depart will include a stage cresting Rhigos mountain, bringing international attention to climbs Welsh cyclists have known for decades. Yes if you want to ride Britain's most iconic sportive on roads that rival Alpine passes for scenery and suffering. Yes if a 230 km day with 3,500 m of climbing through Welsh mountain weather sounds like your definition of a good time. Skip if you need competitive racing — this is participatory, not a race. Skip if you cannot handle unpredictable weather — Welsh mountains do not care about your forecast. Skip if you demand continental European sportive prestige — this is the biggest fish in the UK pond.

### Gran Fondo Collado del Condor
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 76.4 mi | — | Merida, Venezuela | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-collado-del-condor/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-collado-del-condor.md

Guinness World Record holder for longest hill climb bicycle race — a genuine altitude monument, though international riders should check current Venezuela travel advisories before booking. A point-to-point Andean road ascent beginning at Estanques, approximately 426 m above sea level, passing through Mérida's Sierra Nevada corridor (shorter-distance fields join from Mérida, Valle Hermoso and Mucuchíes) and finishing at Collado del Cóndor/Pico El Águila at 4,118 m — not the 4,200 m previously on file, which appears to have rounded the finish altitude rather than measuring it precisely. The defining feature is the roughly 3,692 m lowland-to-páramo altitude transition from start to finish, with some descents interspersed before the final high-altitude climb rather than one uninterrupted ascent. Total climbing gain (as opposed to net elevation change) is not independently confirmed. Signature challenge: Mucuchíes-Collado — the final 26 km, climbing from 2,983 m to 4,118 m (about 1,135 m net), increasingly exposed to hypoxia and low páramo temperatures as the finish approaches. Gran Fondo Collado del Condor delivers a real and exceptional altitude test: a roughly 3,692 m net lowland-to-páramo climb from Estanques (426 m) to Collado del Cóndor/Pico El Águila (4,118 m). Guinness World Records recognizes it (with Ultrabikex) for the 'Longest hill climb bicycle race,' set at 123.5 km on 23 March 2025. The 2026 sixth edition drew 1,000+ riders across four distance options with full event-day road closure and security. What sets this event apart from most others in this database isn't the course — it's the destination. As of this research, UK Foreign Office travel advice recommends against all but essential travel to Mérida and most of Venezuela, with limited flights and constrained emergency support. That's a genuine, practical planning factor for international riders considering this event, separate from the course itself. Yes for the altitude test itself, which is genuinely exceptional. Check current government travel advisories for Venezuela independently before planning international travel — this is a real logistical factor separate from the race.

### Granfondo Felice Gimondi
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 92 mi | 9,186 ft | Bergamo, Lombardy, Italy | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-felice-gimondi/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-felice-gimondi.md

30 years in the saddle of a legend. Six valleys. Selvino's 19 hairpins. Bergamo's cycling soul, named for the man who won all three Grand Tours. Six Bergamasque valleys connected by sustained climbs, starting and finishing in the cultural city of Bergamo. The climbs are not short punchy walls — they are genuine valley ascents of 7-11 km at 5-7% average gradients, with steeper pitches up to 12%. Selvino's 19 hairpins are the signature feature: nearly 11 km of climbing through switchbacks named after local cycling legends, reaching 946m above sea level. Between climbs, the valleys offer rolling terrain through stone villages, river gorges, and alpine meadows. The rhythm is valley-floor recovery, gradual approach, sustained climb, hairpin descent, repeat. The long route does this six times across 148 km. Signature challenge: Selvino's 19 hairpins — 10.9 km of sustained climbing through switchbacks named after Bergamasque cycling legends. It is not the steepest climb on the route (Colle Gallo has steeper pitches), but it is the most sustained and the most iconic. The 19 bends create a hypnotic rhythm that either carries you upward or slowly grinds you down. On the long route, Selvino comes early enough to be manageable but late enough that the remaining four climbs are ridden on Selvino-depleted legs. The Granfondo Felice Gimondi is what happens when a cycling-obsessed city names its signature ride after its greatest son. Felice Gimondi — born in Sedrina, 10 km from Bergamo — won the Tour de France, the Giro d'Italia three times, and the Vuelta a Espana. One of only seven riders to complete the Grand Tour triple crown. The event bearing his name threads through six Bergamasque valleys, climbs 19 hairpins up to Selvino where each bend carries a local cycling legend's name, passes the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Cyclists at Colle Gallo, and returns to a medieval city that breathes cycling the way other cities breathe football. Thirty years of continuous operation. Bianchi co-branding. A EUR45 entry fee that feels like a gift. This is not the most famous gran fondo in Italy — it is perhaps the most authentically Italian. Yes if you want an authentically Italian gran fondo in cycling's heartland — great value, deep heritage, and honest climbing through beautiful pre-Alpine valleys. Yes if Gimondi's name means something to you. Yes if EUR45 for a well-organized FCI event with a Santini jersey option sounds like a bargain. Skip if you want Alpine drama at 2,500m — Selvino tops out under 1,000m. Skip if you need a massive international field and English-language everything — this event is proudly Italian first.

### La Vaujany Cyclosportive
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 93.8 mi | 13,688 ft | Vaujany, Isère, France | June | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-vaujany/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/la-vaujany.md

A GFNY chapter built on a full L'Alpe d'Huez ascent — clearly disclosed two-tier format, documented Alpine heat risk. GFNY's Alpine chapter in the Oisans massif, built around one of cycling's most famous climbs. The long course opens with roughly 30 km of descending from Vaujany toward Séchilienne before Col de la Morte (15.1 km at 6.7% average, 10% max) starts the climbing; Col d'Ornon follows, then the course tackles L'Alpe d'Huez itself — the 21 hairpins straight from the Tour de France — before descending through Villard-Reculas and Pas de la Confession to a final, deceptive ~5 km kicker into Vaujany with pitches up to 14%. The planned long-course figures are 151 km / 4,172 m (raced in 2025, planned for 2026); a stale 170.6 km / 3,962 m figure previously on file was not supported by the GFNY sources reviewed and has been corrected. Know before you register: GFNY's medium course (60.8 km) normally gets a finish time but non-competitive, alphabetical-only results — standard GFNY two-tier format. 2026 was an exception worth flagging: an Orange Heat Alert forced organizers to put every rider, long-course and medium-course alike, onto the ~60 km medium route (roughly 2,000 m of climbing) — and for that one edition it was run fully timed with overall classification and podiums, not the usual alphabetical listing. Treat published course figures as edition-specific until you've checked the current year's actual route. Signature challenge: L'Alpe d'Huez's 21 switchbacks arriving after Col de la Morte and Col d'Ornon have already taken a bite out of your legs — then a final, unglamorous ~5 km climb into Vaujany with 14% pitches that punishes anyone who celebrated too early on the Alpe. GFNY La Vaujany – L'Alpe d'Huez is a six-edition entry in the global GFNY series (founded 2021), and its long course delivers exactly what the name promises: Col de la Morte, Col d'Ornon, and a full ascent of L'Alpe d'Huez's 21 hairpins, capped by a nasty, unglamorous kicker into Vaujany. The long course carries GFNY's standard age-group classification; the medium course (60.8 km) gets a finish time but non-ranked, alphabetical results — a clearly disclosed two-tier format. What you need to know before registering: this is a weather-exposed Alpine event, and the 2026 edition (21 June) proved it — an Orange Heat Alert led organizers to scrap the long course entirely and put every rider on the ~60 km medium route, run fully timed with overall classification for that one year, but not the Alpe d'Huez long-course day riders signed up for. It's also easy to confuse with a second, separately-listed GFNY event sharing the same town — GFNY Alpes Vaujany – Croix de Fer, which currently has no 2026 date on GFNY's calendar; prior conflicting audits in our own research trail turned out to be tracking these two different events. Yes if you want a competitively-classified ride up L'Alpe d'Huez's 21 switchbacks in a clearly disclosed GFNY two-tier event. Go in aware that heat forced the 2026 edition onto the shorter medium course — pack for variability, and confirm you're registering for this event and not the separate, differently-routed Alpes Vaujany–Croix de Fer race in the same town.

### Maraton Franja BTC City
Tier 2 | Score: 70/100 | 97 mi | 4,281 ft | Ljubljana, Slovenia | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/maraton-franja/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/maraton-franja.md

Europe's oldest gran fondo. 43 editions since 1982. UCI World Series founding member. EUR 44 entry. The Slovenian institution that proves longevity beats hype. A 156 km loop through the Ljubljana Basin and Julian Alps foothills. The route leaves Ljubljana, climbs gently over the Vrhnika Hill, traverses the Logatec Plateau, descends through the historic mercury-mining town of Idrija, then tackles the defining Kladje climb — 7 km at 6.3% average with a 10% maximum pitch. After a long, rough descent through alpine forest, the route passes through medieval Skofja Loka before rolling back to Ljubljana across pastoral terrain. The course is diverse: urban start, rolling plateau, alpine forest climbs, historic towns, and flat agricultural finish. Maximum elevation is 801m — this is a foothills event, not an Alpine epic. Signature challenge: The Kladje climb: 7 km at 6.3% average with a maximum gradient of 10%. It arrives at approximately km 90 after the plateau crossings and the Idrija valley, on legs that have already absorbed 60+ km of rolling terrain. The climb itself is honest — no false flats, no respite sections. But the real test comes immediately after: a 10 km descent on rough road surface that demands concentration when you most want to coast. Maraton Franja is not the hardest gran fondo, not the most scenic, not the most famous. What it is, without qualification, is one of the most genuine. Running since 1982 — before 'gran fondo' was even a recognized category — this Slovenian institution has quietly built a 43-year legacy of accessible, well-organized road cycling through the Ljubljana Basin and Julian Alps foothills. Named after a secret WWII partisan hospital hidden in a mountain gorge, the event carries historical weight that no Italian monument or French classic can replicate. The Kladje climb will test you. The descent will scare you. The finish in Ljubljana will satisfy you. And the EUR 44 entry fee will make you wonder why everyone else charges three times as much. Yes if you want a well-organized UCI gran fondo qualifier at a fraction of the cost of Italian or French alternatives. Yes if the historical connection to a WWII partisan hospital resonates. Yes if you want to discover Slovenia — an underrated European cycling destination. Skip if you need Alpine drama — the maximum elevation is 801m. Skip if you need a globally recognized name on your cycling resume.

This is run by ULTRAGRÜN GmbH, a small independent German team, on a fixed organizer-supplied GPX course with no staffed life-bases: riders choose between a genuinely self-supported 'Nonsupported' category and a bring-your-own-crew 'Supported' category. ### Cyclassics Hamburg
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 96 mi | 1,150 ft | Hamburg, Germany | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/cyclassics-hamburg/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/cyclassics-hamburg.md

Free entry. 22,000 riders. Closed roads through Germany's second city. The Waseberg at 16%. Europe's biggest cycling party — not its hardest ride. The Cyclassics Hamburg is not a race that tests your body. It tests your appreciation for what cycling events can be. Twenty-two thousand riders on closed roads through a major European city, alongside a UCI WorldTour professional race, with free registration — that combination exists nowhere else in the world. The physical challenge is minimal by any serious cyclist's standard: 109 km of flat roads with one 700-meter climb on the Waseberg, which is over before your heart rate settles into zone 5. You will not suffer here. You will not dig deep into reserves you did not know you had. What you will do is experience cycling as a mass cultural event — a city that shuts its streets for bikes, spectators lining the Waseberg and Mönckebergstraße, the energy of twenty thousand riders rolling through Hamburg's best scenery.

The prestige comes from the pro race connection. Since 1996, the Cyclassics has been Germany's flagship professional road race — the country's only event at cycling's highest level since the Deutschland Tour disappeared in 2009. Elia Viviani, Andre Greipel, Tyler Farrar, Peter Sagan, Alexander Kristoff — the sport's greatest sprinters have won on these roads. Riding the same tarmac, on the same day, on closed roads, with the same finish line on Mönckebergstraße: that means something. The Waseberg climb in Blankenese — 700 meters at gradients touching 16%, rising sharply from the Elbe's north bank — is the one moment where the amateur and professional experiences converge in physical effort. The rest is about the atmosphere, the city, and the sheer improbability of free entry to an event of this caliber.

If you want a cycling challenge, go elsewhere. If you want to experience European cycling culture at its most accessible and democratic — the biggest party on two wheels, in one of Europe's great cities, for zero euros — Hamburg in August is the answer. Yes if you want to experience the scale and energy of one of Europe's largest mass-participation cycling events. Yes if the WorldTour pro race connection matters to you. Yes if free registration and world-class ASO organization sound too good to pass up. Yes if a cycling festival weekend in Hamburg appeals. Skip if you need climbing, technical terrain, or a genuine physical test — this is flat and short. Skip if you want adventure, wilderness, or remoteness — this is a city sportive.

The Cyclotour du Léman is exactly what it says it is, which is rarer than it should be: a 176 km lap of Lake Geneva with roughly 3,500 starters, no timing, no ranking, and a 2026 slogan that spells it out — 'NO RACE, JUST PACE.' Official event materials describe it as Switzerland's largest non-competitive cycling event, and the recent sold-out fields (3,800-4,000+ registrations each year 2023-2025) confirm it operates at serious national-event scale across its 22 completed editions, with the 23rd scheduled for 2026. With no results published, you get nothing to measure yourself against except your own computer. For 2026 the event also moved from its traditional late-May date to October 18 because of anticipated G7-summit restrictions around Évian — an autumn slot this event has not used before. If you need a scored result, this will feel hollow. If you want a well-organized, supported long day around one of Europe's great lakes, it delivers exactly that. Yes if you want a supported, well-marshalled full lap of Lake Geneva and don't need a result: there is no timing and no ranking, by design, and the roads stay open to normal traffic. Ford RideLondon was the cycling equivalent of the London Marathon — a mass-participation event where the experience of riding through the capital on closed roads mattered more than your finishing time. The move from Surrey to Essex removed the dramatic hills but kept the unique thrill of London's streets without traffic. If RideLondon returns from its indefinite pause, it is an automatic yes for anyone who wants to ride through central London on closed roads surrounded by 25,000 other cyclists. Routes emphasize the Kemmelberg's notorious 20% cobbled gradient and multiple ascents of Baneberg, Monteberg, and Plugstreets' unpaved sections. Finish is flat after final Kemmelberg descent, allowing for sprint finishes. Strong headwind exposure and echelon-forming conditions typical. Signature challenge: The Kemmelberg: A steep (20% gradient), cobbled climb ascended twice in the race finale. The descent is notoriously technical and dangerous, with unpredictable terrain and tight turns. Riders must manage both the physical demand and technical bike-handling skill; crashes are common in the professional race. Gent-Wevelgem Cyclo is the thinking cyclist's spring classic—a chance to suffer on the same cobbles and climbs that define professional racing's most storied one-day event. The Kemmelberg will humble you, the Plugstreets will test your bike handling, and passing through Ypres's Menin Gate adds gravitas that most sportives lack. Late March weather is unpredictable and often brutal, but that's part of the Flemish classic experience. If you want to understand why cyclists revere the spring classics, this is essential. Not the easiest or most scenic ride, but undeniably authentic. Gent-Wevelgem Cyclo delivers what few sportives can: direct access to a legendary professional race's course, complete with the Kemmelberg's infamous cobbles, Plugstreets' technical unpaved sections, and the emotional weight of riding through Ypres's Menin Gate. The 2026 edition's alignment with the pro race's new Middelkerke-to-Wevelgem route ensures you're riding current UCI WorldTour terrain. Multiple distance options (70–225 km) make it accessible to various fitness levels, though even the shortest routes include serious climbing and technical descents. Late March conditions are typically cool, wet, and windy—classic Flemish spring racing weather that adds authenticity but demands preparation. At tiered entry fees of €25–45 depending on distance, with an estimated 5,000 participants (40% international), it offers strong community and prestige without premium pricing. Best suited for riders who value cycling history, don't mind suffering on cobbles, and want to experience the spring classics' soul rather than chase personal records.

### GFNY New York
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 85 mi | 6,380 ft | Fort Lee, New Jersey / Hudson Valley, New York, USA | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-new-york/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-new-york.md

100 miles from the George Washington Bridge to Bear Mountain and back. The world championship of gran fondos, started by two people who paid $50K to close the busiest bridge in America. An out-and-back loop that starts with one of cycling's most dramatic send-offs — 5,000 riders rolling across the closed George Washington Bridge — and then heads north through the Hudson Valley's mix of river flats, suburban rollers, and genuine mountain terrain. The first half builds toward Bear Mountain, the course's physical and emotional apex. The second half punishes you with the Rockland County ridgeline — a relentless sequence of sharp climbs and technical descents that hit when your legs are already compromised. The final miles back along 9W are a flat-road time trial to the finish in Fort Lee. The course rewards riders who can climb, recover on descents, and still produce power in the final 30 miles. Signature challenge: Bear Mountain gets the name recognition, but the Rockland County ridgeline is the real race-breaker. Gate Hill and Cheesecote hit when you're 55-65 miles deep with 5,000+ feet already in the legs. The 18% maximum on Cheesecote stops riders who are already cooked. The course is designed to punish poor pacing — it's back-loaded by design. GFNY New York is the race that proved American gran fondos could be taken seriously. When Uli and Lidia Fluhme paid the Port Authority $50,000 to close the George Washington Bridge for a cycling event in 2011, they were making a bet that the US market wanted European-style competitive cycling with real timing, real anti-doping, and real racing — not another charity ride with a fruit cup at the finish. Fifteen years and 30+ global editions later, that bet has paid off spectacularly. The NYC World Championship draws 5,000 riders from 90+ countries to race 100 miles through the Hudson Valley, summit Bear Mountain, and grind through the Rockland County ridgeline. The course is demanding without being mythical. The organization is professional without being corporate. And that start on the closed GWB — with the Manhattan skyline receding behind you as 5,000 riders roll out together — remains one of the most visually stunning moments in amateur cycling. Yes if you want the most competitive, most international gran fondo in North America. Yes if starting on a closed George Washington Bridge with the NYC skyline behind you is on your bucket list. Yes if you want anti-doping, real timing, and a world championship classification. Skip if you want Alpine grandeur — this is the Hudson Valley, not the Dolomites. Skip if NYC-area costs are a dealbreaker.

Ride with a legend. 138 km through the Costa Blanca mountains, alongside the man who won the Tour, the Giro, and the Vuelta — and still shows up to pedal with the field. A circular route from the Mediterranean coast into the limestone mountain passes of the Costa Blanca interior and back. The first kilometers are flat — the Valencian coastal plain around Oliva is rice-paddy territory, sea-level warm-up before the mountains begin. Coll de Rates is the signature — the most famous cycling climb on the Costa Blanca, a timed section that separates those who paced wisely from those who did not. Sa Creueta is the high point, with its sharp final kilometer and panoramic ridge views. The Vall d'Ebo descent through bare limestone landscape feels like riding through a geology textbook. The return to Oliva via Pego is mercifully flat, a Mediterranean homecoming with the salt air announcing the finish before you see it. Signature challenge: Coll de Rates — the timed section that defines the competitive day. 6.6 km of consistent climbing at 5.3% average, arriving early enough in the route (km 30) to tempt riders into going too hard. The climb itself is not the hardest on the route — Sa Creueta is steeper, Vall d'Ebo is longer — but the timed section creates a race-within-a-race dynamic. Ride it as a time trial and pay later. Ride it as a tempo effort and carry strength through the remaining ~108 km. Every year, Coll de Rates sorts the field into those who raced the climb and those who raced the event. The Gran Fondo Alberto Contador is the rare event where the name on the marquee actually shows up and rides with you. Alberto Contador — two-time Tour de France winner, two-time Giro champion, three-time Vuelta conqueror, one of the seven members of the Grand Tour triple crown club and arguably the most devastating pure attacker of his generation — does not just lend his name to this event. He starts at the front, drops back to wait for the last rider, and works his way through the entire peloton, greeting cyclists, posing for photos, and probably putting in a few accelerations that remind everyone within visual range exactly why he won seven Grand Tours. The route through the Costa Blanca's interior mountains — Coll de Rates, Sa Creueta, the Vall de Gallinera — is a concentrated dose of Mediterranean climbing at its finest. The Fundacion Alberto Contador channels the event's proceeds into cycling development, stroke awareness, and providing bikes to disadvantaged communities. This is not a vanity project. It is a UCI-sanctioned event with real competitive structure, ridden through genuinely beautiful mountains, organized by professionals, and anchored by a champion who clearly still loves the bike. Yes if you want the once-in-a-lifetime experience of riding alongside Alberto Contador through Mediterranean mountain passes. Yes if a UCI-sanctioned event with timed climbing sections suits your competitive instincts — note this is UCI 'Cycling For All' Road, not a UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier. Yes if the Costa Blanca's combination of mountain cycling and beach recovery sounds like the perfect September weekend. Skip if you want pure mountain extremity — the passes top out under 800m. ### Granfondo Eddy Merckx

Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-eddy-merckx/
