The greatest cyclist's namesake gran fondo. 162 km, 18 climbs, 2,644m of Walloon Ardennes punishment. The Cannibal's roads. A race of 18 successive walls through the Walloon Ardennes, bookended by the Meuse river valley at Andenne. The route begins with an immediate climb — the Cote de Peu d'Eau, 2.7 km of La Fleche Wallonne terrain that sets the tone from the gun. There is no warmup. From there, the course winds through the Condroz plateau — the rolling upland between the Meuse and Ourthe valleys — hitting classified climb after classified climb in a rhythm that is uniquely Belgian: short, steep, partial recovery, repeat. The signature moment is the Triple Mur de Monty — 1.9 km with three successive ramps hitting 20-24%, each one arriving just as you think the worst is over. Between the named climbs, the terrain never flattens. The Condroz is a landscape of gentle ridges and hidden valleys, and every false flat tilts upward. The descents are fast but technical — narrow communal roads through forest, hedgerows tight against the tarmac, the occasional farm vehicle adding authenticity. The final approach back to Andenne delivers panoramic views over the Meuse valley, a finishing reward for six-plus hours of Ardennes punishment. On a clear June day, the green Walloon countryside — stone farmhouses, church spires, cows in fields that slope toward hidden streams — is hauntingly beautiful. On a wet one, it is Belgium. Signature challenge: The Triple Mur de Monty. Three successive walls hitting 20-24% gradient over 1.9 km. A sign at the steepest point reads 23.9%. Tougher than the Mur de Huy that decides La Fleche Wallonne. On the Granfondo Eddy Merckx, the Triple Mur is where you discover whether your training, your gearing, your body weight, and your willingness to suffer are sufficient for Belgian hills. The Cannibal would have attacked on the first ramp and been over the top before most riders reached the second. You are not The Cannibal. There is one name in cycling that sits above all others. Not Coppi. Not Anquetil. Not Hinault. Eddy Merckx — The Cannibal — won 525 races, 11 Grand Tours, all five Monuments at least twice, three World Championships, and the Hour Record. He was so dominant that rivals stopped trying to win and raced for second. And this gran fondo bears his name. The Granfondo Eddy Merckx sends you out of Andenne on the Cote de Peu d'Eau — La Fleche Wallonne terrain — and then hammers you across 162 km of Walloon Ardennes hills. Eighteen classified climbs. The Triple Mur de Monty with its three successive 20%+ ramps. 2,644 meters of climbing that never lets you recover. This is the terrain that forged Belgian cycling's greatest generation. Golazo runs it with typical Belgian efficiency. The UCI sanctions it for World Championship qualifying. And at EUR 44, it costs less than dinner in Brussels. No — this race hasn't run since its last known edition on June 22, 2014, and no return has been announced. When it operated, it delivered exactly what the name promised: a UCI World Cycling Tour qualifier through 18 Ardennes climbs including the Triple Mur de Monty, with genuine UCI age-group competition and World Championship qualifying on the line. If that terrain and qualifying pathway is what you're after today, check the current UCI Gran Fondo World Series calendar for an active Belgian stop rather than assuming this one still runs.

Highlands Gran Fondo is a consistently sold-out Gran Fondo National Series event in the hilly New Jersey Highlands, climbing toward the state's highest point and crossing the Appalachian Trail eight times on the Gran route. ### Inthanon Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 29.8 mi | 8,465 ft | Chom Thong, Chiang Mai, Thailand | February | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/inthanon-challenge/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/inthanon-challenge.md

A genuine, brutal summit climb to the roof of Thailand — smaller and quieter than its old 'thousands' framing suggests. A one-way, point-to-point summit race up Highway 1009 to the roof of Thailand, not a steady alpine grind. The first 8km from the start at km 0 is essentially flat warm-up. After the national park gate the road kicks with a short, sharp 1.3km at 7% (touching 13%), then settles into 10km of rolling false-flat. Near km 20 the road climbs 6km at 7% (ramping to 14%) through a forested gorge past Wachirathan waterfall, followed by a brief respite, then 3km at 9% to Ban Khun Klang around km 31. The road eases for two easier kilometers before another 3.3km at 10% (including roughly 800m at 16%). From about km 39, the final 9km averages roughly 9%, with a reported 3.5km stretch at 14% and pitches touching 25% before the summit. The route climbs from lowland deciduous forest through terraced paddies into cloud-covered montane evergreen forest above about 1,500m, passing twin royal stupas near the top. Signature challenge: The final 9km from roughly km 39 to the Doi Inthanon summit — averaging about 9% with a documented 3.5km stretch at 14% and pitches as steep as 25-23% above 2,000m, arriving as the air turns cold, damp, and frequently fogged in. The Inthanon Challenge is a genuine, currently active hill-climb race to the summit of Doi Inthanon, Thailand's highest point, now in its 17th edition. The database previously carried 48.3km/2,565m as course stats, but 2,565m is the mountain's summit elevation above sea level, not the race's climbing gain — the organizer has never published an official total-ascent figure, and the best route-specific estimate is closer to 2,580m of gain over roughly 48km. The 2026 field of 870 registered riders (against a 1,500 cap) is a fraction of the event's 2018-2019 peak, when it drew 6,000-7,500 entrants; the old 'thousands' field-size label describes a bigger, older version of this race. What hasn't diminished is the climb itself: a genuinely brutal final 9km averaging 9% with pitches over 20%, arriving in cold summit fog after riders start the day in Thai valley heat. Yes if you want a hard, scenic hill-climb race with a real summit finish and don't need a huge field. Prepare for the forecast valley-to-summit thermal contrast and confirm current road-closure and descent-safety measures — the descent has seen at least one serious traffic incident in 2018.

### Mt. Washington Auto Road Bicycle Hillclimb
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 7.6 mi | 4,618 ft | Gorham, New Hampshire | August | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-washington-hillclimb/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/mt-washington-hillclimb.md

7.6 miles. 4,678 feet. 12% average grade. Summit finish on the mountain with the worst weather in America. Since 1973. There is no subtlety to the Mt. Washington Auto Road Bicycle Hillclimb. It is 7.6 miles of going uphill at 12% average gradient until you reach the summit of the highest peak in the Northeastern United States, a mountain so hostile that it holds the world record for the highest wind gust ever directly measured on Earth's surface. Since 1973, cyclists have lined up at the base of the Auto Road to race the clock, the gradient, and whatever weather the mountain decides to deliver. Tom Danielson did it in 49:24. Tyler Hamilton did it four times (though his records were vacated). Ian Boswell set the current mark at 50:18. Most riders take 60-90 minutes. All of them suffer.

The Mt. Washington Hillclimb is not a long race. It is not a technical race. It is not an altitude race. It is a gradient race on a mountain with a personality disorder — a 6,288-foot peak in New Hampshire that produces weather systems normally reserved for peaks three times its height. The 2022 completion of the road paving project reset the records and the conversation: every time set on the fully paved road is a modern mark. The 50th edition that year was a line in the sand. Everything before it was a different race on a different surface. Everything after is the pure, paved truth: how fast can you ride uphill at 12% for 7.6 miles into the worst weather in America?

This is not a race you enter casually. The $350 entry fee, the remote New Hampshire location, and the single-digit mileage all conspire to make this a deliberate choice. You come to Mt. Washington because you want to test yourself against the steepest sustained road climb in the Eastern United States. You stay because the summit finish — fleece blanket in hand, legs destroyed, staring out across the Presidential Range — is one of the most earned moments in American cycling. Yes if you are a hill climb specialist, power-to-weight obsessive, or simply need to know if you can ride up the steepest sustained paved climb in the Eastern US. Yes if you want a bucket-list summit finish on the highest peak in the Northeast. Skip if you want distance, technical terrain, or a mass-participation festival atmosphere. Skip if remote New Hampshire logistics are a dealbreaker.

### Peaks Challenge Falls Creek
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 146 mi | 13,123 ft | Falls Creek, Victoria, Australia | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/peaks-challenge-falls-creek/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/peaks-challenge-falls-creek.md

Australia's definitive mountain challenge. Three alpine summits. 235 km. 4,000 meters of climbing in a single day. A linear epic across the Victorian Alps. The three-peak structure gives the ride a natural narrative: conquer Hotham, survive the valley heat, endure Tawonga, and somehow find the legs for Falls Creek at the end. The terrain alternates between long sustained climbs to cool alpine summits and hot, exposed valley roads where the sun beats down relentlessly. There is almost no flat ground — you are either climbing, descending, or wishing you were descending. Signature challenge: The cumulative weight of 235 km and 4,000m. No single climb is the hardest you'll ever ride, but stacking three alpine summits in a single day — with valley heat between them — creates an event where the whole is devastatingly greater than the sum of its parts. Peaks Challenge Falls Creek is Australia's answer to the great European mountain cyclosportives, and it holds its own. The format is brutally simple: climb three alpine summits, cover 235 km, gain 4,000 meters. The Victorian High Country provides the backdrop — eucalyptus forests, alpine meadows, panoramic ridgeline views — but the real story is the sheer physical and mental challenge of the day. Mount Hotham's 30 km climb is the physical crux. The final ascent to Falls Creek at kilometer 220, on legs that have been working for 10+ hours, is the emotional one. If you finish, you know exactly what you're made of. Yes if you want a genuine ultra-distance mountain cycling challenge outside Europe. Yes if completing Australia's most respected single-day cycling event is on your list. Skip if you can't commit to training for 10-14 hours in the saddle. Skip if the 4.5-hour drive from Melbourne (or long-haul flight from overseas) is a dealbreaker.

### Race Across Benelux

Formerly Race Across Belgium (2021-2025), renamed and expanded for 2026 into a full Amsterdam-to-Arlon-and-back Netherlands/Belgium/Luxembourg crossing — flat lowlands into a real Ardennes climbing loop. A fixed, organizer-supplied GPX course run by Race Across Series, formerly named 'Race Across Belgium.' For the 2026 season (ran May 27-31, now completed) the organizer renamed and geographically expanded the event: the flagship started at Amsterdam's Olympic Stadium, crossed the flat Dutch and Belgian lowlands to reach Arlon (533.5 km, ~4,700 m), then completed a significantly hillier Arlon loop through the Belgian Ardennes and into Luxembourg (515.3 km, ~7,165 m) — meaning nearly two-thirds of the route's total climbing was concentrated in the second half. This is a semi-autonomous format: riders are self-sufficient between staffed life-bases (food, rest, showers, charging, drop bags), not a fully unsupported race. The organizer's own published route-planning article (issued before the race) carried minor internal inconsistencies (a 1,048 km headline total against a 1,048.8 km leg-sum, and two slightly different figures for the Arlon loop within the same article); these are the organizer's published planning figures, and no post-event public final-GPX audit was found to confirm the exact ridden distance. Signature challenge: The Arlon loop through the Belgian Ardennes — roughly half the total distance but nearly two-thirds of the total climbing (~7,165 m of ~11,900 m), arriving after riders had already crossed the flat Netherlands-to-Arlon leg. Race Across Benelux is a genuine, semi-autonomous Race Across Series ultra with five prior editions of organizer track record — it ran as 'Race Across Belgium' from 2021 through 2025 before the organizer renamed and geographically expanded it for 2026, extending the course from a Belgium-only race into a full Netherlands-Belgium-Luxembourg crossing. This is not a mass-participation gran fondo: it's a fixed organizer-GPX ultra with staffed life-bases rather than aid stations, GPS-tracked riders, and a route that front-loads flat Dutch and Belgian lowland miles before a genuinely mountainous Ardennes loop around Arlon. The rename is real and well-documented on the organizer's own site, but it also creates real confusion risk — the event still occupies its old 'race-across-belgique-2025' URL, and legacy calendars and results archives still reference the retired 'Race Across Belgium' name. Yes if you want a proven Race Across Series ultra with real organizer track record — confirm the current year's route and entry details directly with the organizer, since even 2026's own pre-race planning materials weren't internally consistent.

### Sado Long Ride 210
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 130.5 mi | 7,277 ft | Sado Island, Niigata Prefecture, Japan | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/sado-long-ride-210/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/sado-long-ride-210.md

A genuine 210km island circumnavigation with real coastal scenery — but budget for the ferry, the backloaded hills after Ogi, and a smaller field than its old numbers suggest. A largely coastal, clockwise circumnavigation of Sado Island starting and finishing at Sawata: low in absolute altitude but relentlessly rolling. The first half follows the rugged Osado northern coast through Aikawa and outer-coast settlements, over the sharp Z-zaka/Hanezaka climb and past the Onogame and Futatsugame rock formations, reaching Ryotsu at 103km as the approximate halfway point. The second half follows the gentler Kosado southern coast through Tada and Ogi — the organizer specifically warns that the hardest sequence of steep hills on the whole route arrives after Ogi, late in the ride. The route threads gold-mining history at Aikawa (19km), preserved merchant-shipping port settlements like Shukunegi, and passes through numerous dark tunnels that require working lights. Osado Skyline, a separate ~30km mountain road exceeding 900m, is NOT part of this course — the mapped route tops out around 136m. Signature challenge: The Kosado coast climbs after Ogi (past km 163) — the organizer's own warning is that its steepest, most concentrated hill sequence is saved for the back third of the ride, well past the point most riders expect the hard part to be over. Sado Long Ride 210 is a real, currently active mass-participation long ride circling Sado Island, now in its 20th year. The 210km distance label is organizer-marketed rather than a survey-grade decimal figure (the database's prior 209.2km was unconfirmed), and the ~3,000m elevation figure long carried in this database does not match any organizer-published total — the best authoritative proxy for the coastal circuit is closer to 2,218m. Field size has fallen from a 2010 peak of over 3,000 starters to roughly 1,700 across all 2026 courses combined; the old '3,000+' label describes a bigger, older version of the event. The route itself is legitimate and demanding — 210km with a genuinely backloaded hill sequence after Ogi, real cutoffs, and mostly open roads shared with ordinary traffic — but reaching it requires a ferry or jetfoil crossing that the organizer can cancel independent of on-island conditions, and the 2026 edition itself had a documented aid-station food shortage. Yes if you want a genuinely long, scenic island ride with real cutoffs and don't mind open roads and ferry logistics. Prepare specifically for the hardest climbing to arrive after Ogi, well past the 160km mark.

### Tour de Big Bear
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 100 mi | 8,585 ft | Big Bear Lake, California, USA | August | gran_fondo

Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-big-bear.md

100 miles at 7,000 feet with legendary aid stations that serve ribs, have DJs, and make you forget you are dying on a bike. A deceptive course that lulls you with rolling lakeside roads for 50 miles before delivering the altitude hammer in the second half. The Onyx Summit climb at 8,443 feet is the crown jewel, and the Cedar Falls descent-and-return is where tired legs at altitude learn about humility. Signature challenge: Onyx Summit at 8,443 feet. The highest paved road in Southern California, reached after 50+ miles of riding at altitude. The KOM/QOM competition makes the climb honest. Then you descend 2,000 feet to Cedar Falls and must climb back up. The Tour de Big Bear is what happens when a Southern California cycling community builds their dream ride: 100 miles at 7,000 feet with 8,500 feet of climbing, legendary aid stations that serve BBQ ribs and have DJ booths, and a mountain lake setting that delivers 55-65F start temperatures while the rest of SoCal melts in August.

The climbing is real. Onyx Summit at 8,443 feet is the highest paved road in Southern California, and the KOM competition up its slopes draws genuine efforts. The profile is back-loaded and punishing: rolling lakeside roads lull you for 50 miles, then the Onyx push and Cedar Falls loop deliver the hurt. The 12:30 PM cutoff at Blue Sky Meadows is there for a reason -- undertrained riders bonk at altitude.

But the aid stations are what make this event legendary. Full buffets, DJs, couches, ribs, live music. The volunteers are locals who have been doing this for 15 years and take genuine pride in their hospitality. Named the #1 Gran Fondo in North America by Gran Fondo Guide in 2023. If you are a SoCal cyclist, this is your annual pilgrimage. Yes if you want the definitive SoCal mountain cycling experience with altitude, climbing, and aid stations that redefine hospitality. Skip if you cannot handle 7,000+ foot altitude, need a sanctioned race, or live far from California.

Genuinely scenic Scottish Borders sportive, predominantly (not fully) closed-road, that paused for a year in 2024 over local closure consultation. A locally organized Scottish Borders sportive run by Hillside Outside Ltd out of Peebles, offering two routes: a 120 km / 1,200 m Full route and an 88 km / 940 m Challenge route. It's marketed and legally managed as a closed-road event, but that's not edge-to-edge — Moffat town centre runs as a neutralized, untimed open-road section on the Full route, agricultural and local-service vehicles may still operate around Talla and Megget on the Challenge route, and the final stretch back into Peebles uses traffic-management measures rather than a hard closure. Riders behind the 16 km/h minimum pace may continue on public roads once closures lift. The event paused for 2024 following local consultation, community objections, and closure difficulties, then returned in 2025 with 2,234 participants recorded in the council-commissioned economic impact assessment; that same assessment's post-event survey still found parking/access delays (11%) and food/drink queue or setup issues (12%) among riders' top improvement themes. Signature challenge: The Wall of Talla on the Challenge route and the Devil's Beeftub climb and descent to Moffat on the Full route — run through genuinely quiet, scenic Borders country roads. Tour o' the Borders is a locally rooted sportive through some of Scotland's quieter Borders country, with two distance options and a charity tie-in to Sir Chris Hoy's Tour de 4. It's marketed as a closed-road event, but that claim needs a caveat: Moffat town centre runs open and neutralized on the Full route, and agricultural or local-service vehicles may still operate around Talla and Megget on the Challenge route — call it predominantly closed-road, not literally traffic-free. The event paused for 2024 following local consultation, community objections and closure difficulties, then returned in 2025 with 2,234 participants. The 2026 edition is confirmed and open for registration; the documented present-day frictions are narrower than the 2024 pause itself — the council-commissioned 2025 survey flagged parking/access delays (11%) and food/drink queue or setup issues (12%) as riders' top improvement themes. Yes for the terrain and the two route options — the 2026 edition is confirmed and open for registration, though the 2024 pause is worth knowing as recent history.

The SBS Bank Tour of Southland is a legitimate, fully organized, team-based national road stage race — commissaires, race radio, neutral technical support, and team-manager meetings are all part of the official regulations. It is not something an individual amateur can register for like a gran fondo: entry is by selected six-rider team, with 96 riders across 16 teams contesting the rescheduled 69th edition in January 2026. That edition itself was a genuine emergency response — the traditional November 2025 date was postponed after a regional storm triggered a state of emergency, pushing the race to January 2026 and forcing a course relocation away from storm-damaged Queens Park. A 70th edition returns to the traditional November slot in 2026, but as of the most recent federation announcement its course and exact distance were still pending. The tour no longer carries current UCI-calendar international classification, though it runs under UCI-style national regulations. Only relevant if you can field or join a selected six-rider team — this is not an individual mass-participation entry event. ### Tour of Thekkady — Kerala Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 90.1 mi | 9,843 ft | Kottayam to Anakkara/Thekkady, Kerala, India | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-of-thekkady/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-of-thekkady.md

India's highest-profile road gran fondo: four dam-side climbs and ~3,000m of gain through Kerala's Western Ghats, on open roads. A relentless climbing route through Kerala's plantation hills, running Kottayam - Ettumanoor - Pala - Neeloor - Muttam - Kulamavu - Cheruthoni - Kattappana - Puliyanmala - Anakkara, passing the Kulamavu Dam (~km 75), Cheruthoni (~km 103), and Idukki Dam (~km 105) en route to a finish at Anakkara (Race) or a further descent into Thekkady (Tour). The roads are paved and generally well maintained, but this is not a closed-road event — the organizer's own FAQ states riders share the route with normal traffic throughout, singling out a busier ~7km stretch between Kattappana and Puliyanmala, and a 2025 rider account separately describes buses, trucks, and several close calls in the dark early kilometers out of Kottayam. Signature challenge: Four named climbs and roughly 3,000+ meters of gain over 145km — a 4km opener at km 32, a 12km HC climb gaining ~750m, an 8km Cat 1 climb, and a final major climb from km 127 — plus, new in 2026, a King/Queen of Calvary Mount competition on the 8km climb to the Calvary Mount viewpoint near km 116. Tour of Thekkady is a legitimate, organizer-run road gran fondo in Kerala's Western Ghats, now in its fifth year and growing steadily from a 54-rider debut to roughly 240 riders in 2026. The route itself is genuinely tough — around 3,000m of climbing over 145km across four named climbs, passing the Kulamavu, Cheruthoni, and Idukki dams en route to a finish near the Periyar Tiger Reserve. To the organizer's credit, this isn't hidden: its own FAQ is explicit that Tour of Thekkady is not a closed-road event, and singles out a busier ~7km stretch between Kattappana and Puliyanmala. Riders still share the tarmac with normal Kerala traffic throughout, and a 2025 rider report separately flags buses, trucks, and close calls in the pre-dawn kilometers out of Kottayam. "Self-supported" here means riders handle their own food and mechanicals between checkpoints, not that this is an unsupported wilderness ride — the organizer still runs hydration stations, medical/ambulance coverage, and bag transfer. Yes if you want a genuinely tough climbing day in a scenic, growing Indian gran fondo and don't mind sharing the road with local traffic. The Tour option is a good lower-stakes entry point.

### UCI Gran Fondo World Championships
Tier 2 | Score: 69/100 | 87 mi | 7,776 ft | Venue rotates annually (2027: Thônes-La Clusaz, Haute-Savoie, France) | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/uci-gran-fondo-world-championships/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/uci-gran-fondo-world-championships.md

The only UCI World Championship for amateur road cyclists. Qualify through 36 global events. Race 2,000 riders from 58 countries. Win the rainbow jersey. Course character changes completely with each host venue, but the UCI imposes design principles that create consistency: the Gran Fondo road race must challenge climbing ability, reward tactical racing, and culminate in a decisive finale. The 2026 Niseko course epitomizes this: 140 km through Hokkaido's volcanic mountain landscape, starting near sea level, building to an 840m main climb at the halfway mark, and finishing with a steep final kilometer that rewards explosive power on tired legs. The Medio Fondo at 80 km delivers the same decisive finish with 1,572m of climbing. The individual time trial on a flat 16.3 km course tests pure power. Three disciplines, three different demands, one championship. Signature challenge: The qualification system IS the signature challenge. Before you even reach the start line, you must race a UCI-sanctioned qualifier event and finish in the top 25% of your age group. Then you must travel to the championship venue — a different country each year — and race against 2,000 of the best amateur cyclists from 58 nations. The course varies, but the depth of competition does not. Winning a rainbow jersey requires not just fitness, but a year-long competitive commitment. The UCI Gran Fondo World Championships are the only event in amateur road cycling where you can earn the rainbow jersey — the single most recognizable symbol of cycling supremacy. This is not a participation sportive. It is a qualified-entry world championship with anti-doping, commissaire panels, and age-group classifications that attract the strongest amateur road cycling field assembled anywhere on the planet. You earn your start by finishing in the top 25% of your age group at one of 36 qualifying events worldwide. Then you race 2,000 riders from 58 countries on a course that changes every year — from Italian mountains to Danish flatlands to Japanese volcanoes. The 2026 edition in Niseko, Hokkaido is the first ever held in Asia: 140 km with 2,370m of climbing through volcanic mountain terrain, 1.5 hours from Tokyo. The rainbow jersey awaits at the finish. One winner per age group. For the rest, there is the knowledge that you raced the deepest amateur field in the world. Yes if you are a competitive age-group cyclist who wants the ultimate test against your global peers. Yes if the rainbow jersey means something to you. Yes if you want a multi-year global cycling adventure — different country, different course, every year. Skip if you want a fixed, repeatable course to benchmark against. Skip if the qualification requirement and international travel expense are dealbreakers. Skip if you want a participation experience — this is a race.

### AIDS/LifeCycle
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 545 mi | 25,000 ft | San Francisco to Los Angeles, California, USA | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/aids-lifecycle/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/aids-lifecycle.md

The most emotionally powerful cycling event ever created. 545 miles of purpose, community, and remembrance down the California coast. Seven days of California coastal beauty and emotional intensity. The route traverses the full diversity of the state's Central Coast — from San Francisco fog through redwood forests, over mountain ridges, through agricultural valleys, past wine country, over coastal passes, and along the Pacific Coast Highway to a Santa Monica finish. The terrain is varied but always paved, with significant climbing concentrated on Days 1, 3, 4, and 6. The real challenge is cumulative: 545 miles over 7 consecutive days in the saddle, compounded by camping, emotional weight, and California's variable June weather. Signature challenge: The cumulative toll of 545 miles over 7 days. No single day is impossible, but the relentless accumulation of miles, climbing, weather, camping, and emotional weight creates an endurance challenge that transforms riders. The body adapts; the spirit grows. By Day 7, riding into Santa Monica feels like crossing into a different version of your life. AIDS/LifeCycle is not a race. It is not a gran fondo. It is not a charity ride in the way most people understand charity rides. It is 545 miles of collective grief, joy, defiance, and love, pedaled down the California coast by thousands of people who refuse to let a disease define or defeat their community. You will climb the Quadbuster with disco music blasting. You will cry at camp listening to names of the dead read aloud. You will finish in Santa Monica having raised thousands of dollars and having been fundamentally changed by the experience. Over 30 years, this event raised more than $300 million and created a community that transcends cycling. The 2025 final ride ended an era — but the legacy is permanent. AIDS/LifeCycle ended in 2025 after 30 years and $300 million raised. If you rode it, you know what it meant. If you never did, the successor event Cycle to Zero (3-day, SFAF-produced) launches in May 2026. The 545-mile journey from San Francisco to Los Angeles is gone, but the community and mission endure. This was never about the miles — it was about why you rode them.

### Les Cinglés du Mont Ventoux
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 85 mi | 14,436 ft | Bédoin, Vaucluse, Provence, France | June | hillclimb
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/cingles-du-mont-ventoux/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/cingles-du-mont-ventoux.md

Three faces. One mountain. 4,400 meters of climbing. The most honest challenge in cycling — EUR 20 and a brevet card against the Beast of Provence. Three ascents of the same mountain from three different directions, linked by rolling Provençal country roads through lavender fields and vineyards. Each climb has a distinct personality: Bédoin is the classic — dense forest giving way to exposed moonscape, the route the Tour de France made famous. Malaucène is the underestimated equal — steep early ramps, varied terrain, fewer cyclists. Sault is the long, deceptive approach — gentle gradients through lavender plateau that lull you before the final shared summit cone brutalizes you. All three routes converge in the last 6 km, where the trees vanish and the white limestone begins — a barren, lunar landscape that looks like no other place in cycling. The observatory tower at 1,912m is visible from kilometers away, growing imperceptibly closer with each pedal stroke. You pass the Tom Simpson memorial three times. You stand at the summit three times. And three times, you descend. Signature challenge: The third summit. The first ascent is excitement — the mountain is fresh, the legs are willing, the scenery is extraordinary. The second ascent is determination — the mountain is familiar, the legs are heavy, the summit seems farther away. The third ascent is reckoning. Your body has already climbed 3,150 meters. The Sault approach's gentle gradients offer false hope. The final 6 km of exposed limestone — the same white moonscape you have already climbed twice — must be climbed one more time. The observatory tower is visible. The Tom Simpson memorial is ahead. The wind is blowing. The third summit is where the Cinglés challenge becomes exactly what its name promises: crazy. Les Cinglés du Mont Ventoux is not a race. It is not a sportive. It is not an organized event. It is a personal reckoning with the most revered mountain in cycling, repeated until either you or the mountain blinks. Three ascents — Bédoin's relentless forest grind, Malaucène's savage opening ramps, Sault's deceptively gentle approach — each delivering you to the same barren, windswept summit at 1,912m where an observatory tower stands like a lighthouse above the clouds and Tom Simpson's memorial reminds you that this mountain does not care about your suffering. The genius of the Cinglés is in its simplicity: EUR 20, a brevet card, three stamps, three summits, midnight to midnight. No marshals. No aid stations. No chip timing. Just you, the mountain, and 4,400 meters of vertical truth. The Club des Cinglés has existed since 1988 because Christian Pic understood something fundamental: some challenges do not need organization. They need audacity. The word 'cinglé' means 'crazy' in French, and by the third ascent — when your legs remember the first two and the summit looks impossibly far and the Mistral is shredding your jersey — you understand that it is not a name. It is a diagnosis. Yes if you want to experience the most complete day possible on a single mountain — three ascents, three landscapes, one barren summit that never gets less shocking. Yes if you value self-reliance and the purity of a challenge that has no finish-line arch, no announcer, no medal ceremony — just a stamped card and the knowledge of what you did. Yes if Mont Ventoux means something to you. Skip if you need organized event support, medical coverage, and feed stations. Skip if Provençal summer heat is a deal-breaker. Skip if you want to race against other people rather than against yourself.

### Cycle Oregon
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 300 mi | 17,000 ft | Southern Oregon — Grants Pass and Jacksonville basecamps (2026). Route and region change annually. | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/cycle-oregon/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/cycle-oregon.md

Oregon's iconic multi-day touring event. 600 riders. Five days. A different Oregon every year. Cycle Oregon is Oregon distilled into a cycling event. Since 1988, this nonprofit organization has been taking riders into the corners of Oregon that most Oregonians have never seen — the Wallowa Mountains, the Applegate Valley, the high desert, the coast — and doing it with a level of care and support that turns five days on a bike into something approaching a life experience. The 2023 sunset of the legendary 7-day Classic was a genuine loss for American cycling, but the 5-day Rally format preserves the essence: a rolling community of 600 riders exploring Oregon's most spectacular landscapes, fully supported, with meals and camping and live music and the camaraderie that only comes from sharing the road for multiple days.

The price tag is real — $1,400-1,600 is not casual money — but what you get is five days of worry-free riding through terrain that will rearrange your understanding of Oregon. The route changes every year, meaning you could do Cycle Oregon for a decade and never repeat a mile. The Cycle Oregon Fund has donated millions to the rural communities that host the event, so your registration dollars are doing genuine good. The community is warm, the organization is impeccable, and the landscapes are world-class. If you want to race, go somewhere else. If you want to ride through one of the most beautiful states in America with 600 people who feel the same way, Cycle Oregon is it. You do not race Cycle Oregon — you experience it. Yes if you want a premium, fully supported multi-day cycling tour through some of the most beautiful scenery in the American West. Yes if you value community, adventure, and discovery over competition. Skip if you need a competitive event, if the $1,400+ price tag is prohibitive, or if you want a massive social scene (600 riders is intimate, not a festival).

5 passes. 14,000 feet. The California Alps' ultimate climbing challenge since 1978. Relentless climbing. The up-and-back format on each pass means you're constantly ascending or descending. There is almost no flat riding. The passes come in waves — each summit brings the descent that takes you to the base of the next climb. By pass 4, the cumulative altitude exposure and climbing fatigue make every gradient feel steeper. Signature challenge: Ebbetts Pass — the steepest, most dramatic, and highest summit. Climbing to 8,732 ft on tired legs in the Sierra Nevada is the Death Ride's defining moment. The Death Ride is American road cycling's ultimate climbing challenge. 5 passes. 14,000 feet. One of the least-populated counties in California. No prize money, no timing chips, no Instagram-ready finish line — just you and the Sierra Nevada. Since 1978, serious cyclists have made the pilgrimage to Markleeville to test themselves against the California Alps. The name isn't hyperbole — it's a warning and a promise. If you finish all 5 passes, you've earned something that can't be bought. Yes if you want the defining high-altitude climbing experience in the American West. Yes if you can handle sustained riding above 8,000 ft. Skip if you need race infrastructure or a competitive field.

### Epic Gran Canaria
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 116.2 mi | — | Maspalomas, Gran Canaria, Spain | February | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/epic-gran-canaria/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/epic-gran-canaria.md

Pre-season volcanic punchbowl opener that kicks off GFWT with island flair. A two-day, paved-road event on Gran Canaria starting and finishing at Hotel Riu Palace in Maspalomas: a 112km Saturday stage with two timed climbing sectors (Ayagaures and the long Pasito Blanco-Salto del Perro climb), and a 75km Sunday stage built around a single 22km climb to Tirajana/Tunte. The roughly 187km weekend total (regulations say 186km) includes only three individually chip-timed climbing sectors, about 63km combined, that count toward the overall classification — the rest of Stage 1 is documented as a neutralized descent toward Mogan followed by a regrouped return to Maspalomas; the organizer's published Stage 2 schedule doesn't document the same regrouping language for the untimed portion. It's a genuine mountain test on volcanic terrain, but not a continuously timed single-day race the way the name "Epic Gran Canaria" might suggest. Signature challenge: The Pasito Blanco to Alto Salto del Perro climb — 29km (from km 33 to km 62) and roughly 997m of gain, the longest single timed sector of the weekend. Epic Gran Canaria is a legitimate and growing event — 680 riders from 28 countries in its 2026 ninth edition, up from 500 the year before, and confirmed by GFWT's own calendar as the season opener of the Gran Fondo World Tour. But the format needs stating plainly: this is not one continuously timed 187km race. It's a two-day, 112km + 75km weekend where only three named climbs (about 63km combined) are individually chip-timed, and the overall result is the sum of those three sector times, not elapsed time over the full route. The organizer documents Stage 1's non-timed portion as a neutralized descent toward Mogan followed by a regrouped return to Maspalomas; the published Stage 2 schedule doesn't document the same regrouping for its untimed section, so treat that as unconfirmed rather than assuming an identical format. The organizer's own regulations file it under Spain's "Cycling for All" category, which is formally non-competitive, even though the event runs chip timing, classifications, and a leader jersey. Course figures also carry small internal inconsistencies: the event page says 187km/186km depending on document, and cutoff times differ between the homepage and PDF regulations for the second sector. Yes if you want a genuine climbing test with real GFWT-series stakes and don't mind a two-day, sector-timed format rather than a single continuously timed race.

### Eroica Dolomiti
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 73.3 mi | 8,990 ft | San Candido, South Tyrol, Italy | September | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/eroica-dolomiti/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/eroica-dolomiti.md

Vintage-bike heritage ride through the Dolomites — nearly half gravel, no clipless pedals allowed, no ranked finish. Eroica Dolomiti is a vintage-bike heritage ride (a ciclostorica in the L'Eroica family, distinct from the original L'Eroica in Tuscany) based in San Candido, South Tyrol. It is emphatically not a paved-road-only sportive: the long route runs 118km with roughly 55km of strade bianche (white gravel roads) against 63km of asphalt — about 47% unpaved — climbing to Prato Piazza and on toward Cornetto di Confine/Markinkele near the Austrian border, while the short route winds between Cortina d'Ampezzo, Passo Tre Croci, and Lake Misurina. On the long and medium routes, only vintage or vintage-style steel bicycles are permitted — pre-1987 steel road frames (with a narrow Alan/Vitus aluminium exception), downtube shifters, toe clips instead of clipless pedals, external brake cables, and low-profile wheels with at least 32 spokes; the short route additionally accepts other vintage bicycle types (service, postman, and general work bikes), and the regulations carve out exceptions for riders with motor or sensory disabilities. It is non-competitive: riders collect checkpoint stamps rather than race for a ranked finish, and the roads remain open to normal traffic throughout. Signature challenge: Roughly 55km of strade bianche white roads on the long route, ridden on a mandatory vintage steel bike with toe clips and downtube shifters — the surface and equipment combination, not any single climb, is what defines the day. Eroica Dolomiti is a vintage-bicycle heritage ride in South Tyrol's Val Pusteria — but it is not the paved-road event our prior profile described. Roughly 47% of the long route (55 of 118km) is strade bianche white gravel road, rising to about 59% on the short route. On the long and medium routes, riders must show up on a pre-1987 steel bike (or a vintage-style equivalent) with toe-clip pedals and downtube shifters — no clipless pedals, no modern groupsets; the short route accepts a wider range of vintage bikes, and the regulations include disability exceptions. It's explicitly non-competitive: there's no ranked finish, just a checkpoint stamp book. That makes it closer to a supported cycling festival than a race, and it belongs in a different conversation than a normal gran fondo or club sportive. The organizer's own published figures aren't fully consistent either — its regulations and route pages disagree on both the long route (118km vs. 110km) and the medium route (95km vs. 91km) — a minor but real data-quality gap worth flagging. Go for the experience and the terrain if you own or can source a compliant vintage steel bike and want a non-competitive, checkpoint-stamped ride. Skip it if you're looking for a scored, competitive road gran fondo.

### GFNY Belitung
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 85 mi | 7,316 ft | Tanjung Pandan, Belitung, Indonesia | February | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-belitung/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-belitung.md

Climb from Bali's black-sand coast to a volcanic crater rim through rice terraces and Hindu temples — the most spectacular setting in the GFNY franchise. NOTE: course details describe the Bali-era editions (Sayan/Lebih). The 2026 relocation to Tanjung Pandan, Belitung brings a new venue; course specifics pending re-research. A point-to-summit-and-back volcanic mountain gran fondo that starts at Bali's coast, climbs relentlessly through the island's cultural and agricultural heartland to the rim of the Kintamani volcanic caldera, then descends back to the sea. The course is defined by one sustained ascent and one sustained descent, bookended by rolling coastal terrain. The climbing is not Alpine-steep but it is Alpine-long, and the tropical heat transforms moderate gradients into savage efforts. The Kintamani crater rim provides the emotional and physical summit — a view of Lake Danau Batur and Mount Batur that rewards every watt spent getting there. Signature challenge: The Kintamani volcano ascent. A 25-30 km sustained climb from the lowland rice terraces to the volcanic crater rim at 1,500 meters, performed in equatorial tropical heat. The gradient is steady (4-6% average, 8-12% pitches) but the length and conditions make it brutal. This is where the race breaks apart every year — the lead group of 15-20 fragments to 5-7 by the summit. The crater rim view of Lake Danau Batur is the payoff: one of the most dramatic summit finishes (mid-course) in world gran fondo cycling. GFNY Bali is the rare franchise event that transcends its brand. Strip away the GFNY timing chips and age-group classifications, and you still have one of the most visually spectacular road cycling courses on earth: a 134 km loop from a black-sand volcanic coast through UNESCO-worthy rice terraces and Hindu temple villages to the crater rim of an active volcano, then back down through monkey forests and the cultural heart of Ubud. The Kintamani ascent — 25-30 km of sustained climbing in equatorial heat to 1,500 meters — is a genuine test that combines European mountain-pass difficulty with Southeast Asian thermal punishment. The field is regionally competitive but internationally thin, and the franchise structure means the prestige caps below what this setting deserves. But no other GFNY event — and frankly, very few road cycling events anywhere — can match the combination of volcanic terrain, tropical ecology, and living spiritual culture that Bali delivers from the saddle. Yes if you want a world-class adventure cycling experience wrapped in a GFNY competitive framework. Yes if volcanic terrain, tropical conditions, and Balinese culture sound like the ride of a lifetime. Yes if you're based in the Asia-Pacific region and want a serious climbing gran fondo with professional organization. Skip if field depth matters to you — the competitive front is thin. Skip if you can't handle sustained climbing in equatorial heat. Skip if 20-30 hours of travel from the Americas is a dealbreaker.

This is where the Gran Fondo Hincapie earns the right to carry a Tour de France veteran's name. ### Gran Fondo Marco Pantani
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 90 mi | 7,054 ft | Cesenatico, Emilia-Romagna, Italy | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-marco-pantani/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-marco-pantani.md

Il Pirata's training roads. His family's event. Cesenatico to the Romagnol hills and back. Since 2005. Three routes of increasing ambition, all starting from the Marco Pantani monument on the Cesenatico waterfront and heading inland through the Romagnol hills. The terrain transitions from flat Adriatic coastal roads to rolling countryside to the punchy, steep-gradient hills that characterize the pre-Apennine foothills. The Lungo route ventures into the Marche border country, adding the Botticella and additional climbing to the Ciola and Montevecchio that feature on all routes. The rhythm is distinctly Romagnol — short, sharp climbs separated by rolling valleys with small villages, vineyards, and stone walls. These are not long Alpine grinds; they are the repeated punchy efforts that Pantani used to build explosive power before translating it to the high mountains. Signature challenge: The cumulative climbing across the Ciola, Botticella, and Montevecchio is honest rather than heroic — 2,150m on the Lungo route. The real challenge is emotional. These are the roads where Marco Pantani trained. The gradients he ground out on winter mornings. The hills he repeated until his legs could dance on the pedals at 90 rpm uphill. Riding them with the knowledge of what he became — and how it ended — adds a dimension that no elevation profile can capture. The Gran Fondo Marco Pantani is not the hardest ride in Italy, not the most scenic, and not the most famous. It is the most personal. Organized by the Pantani family, starting from the bronze statue of Il Pirata on the Cesenatico waterfront, following the roads he rode as a teenager and as a Tour de France champion, passing the monument at Montevecchio where his spirit lives in the hills. Marco Pantani — born in Cesenatico 1970, dead in Rimini 2004, the last man to win the Giro and the Tour in the same year — built his legendary climbing legs on these Romagnol hills before he ever touched the Galibier or the Mortirolo. This event lets you ride in his ghost. The climbs are honest, the countryside is charming, and the emotional weight is unlike anything else in amateur cycling. Yes if Pantani's story moves you and you want to ride the roads where he built his legendary climbing engine. Yes if September in Italy with warm weather and honest Romagnol hills sounds like your kind of weekend. Skip if you want pure athletic challenge — Nove Colli in the same town offers more distance and climbing. Skip if you have no connection to Pantani's legacy — without that context, this is a pleasant but mid-tier Italian sportive.

### UCI Gran Fondo Brasil

### Gruyère Cycling Tour

A defunct Swiss cyclosportive — real pre-Alpine climbing, no current event to enter. IMPORTANT — this event no longer exists. In its final 2015-2016 editions the route started and finished in Charmey, opening with a controlled descent (Descente de Bataille) before the long course climbed Col des Mosses and Col du Pillon en route to a finishing ascent of Col du Mittelberg; the short course used the Mittelberg as its one major pass. The Pringy-to-Mittelberg section, including descents, was the fully timed portion in these final editions — not a simple start-to-finish clock. The event began in 1998 as 'La Pascal Richard,' honoring the Swiss Olympic road champion, before being renamed Gruyère Cycling Tour. There is no current Gruyère Cycling Tour to rate. The last confirmed edition ran September 4, 2016 in Charmey — its 19th — drawing 600+ riders on a course combining Col des Mosses, Col du Pillon and Col du Mittelberg on the long route. The planned 20th edition was cancelled in 2017 when the organizer lost its partners and funding, and no edition has run since. The event does not appear in the current Swiss Cycling calendar; it was included in the inaugural 2011 UCI World Cycling Tour qualifying series, the program now known as the UCI Gran Fondo World Series, but is absent from that series' current calendar too. A third-party aggregator lists a May 2026 date in Bulle, but it has no working organizer page, no registration, and no results; treat it as stale or erroneous, not a revival. No — this event does not exist. The 2016 edition was its last; the 2017 edition was cancelled and none has run since.

### Jedermann-Rennen Rund um Köln
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 75.2 mi | 3,839 ft | Cologne, Germany (Rheinauhafen start/finish, through Bergisches Land) | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/jedermann-rennen-koln/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/jedermann-rennen-koln.md

A real competitive Jedermann race on Germany's oldest professional cycling roads — bring race fitness, not tourist legs. Starts and finishes at Rheinauhafen in central Cologne, running out through eastern and northern Cologne into the Bergisches Land before returning. The Velodom 120 pushes further — through the airport area, Lohmar, Overath/Ferrenberg, Kürten and Wipperfeld — while the Velodom 60 takes a shorter loop through Bergisch Gladbach. Both routes share the race's signature obstacle on the way back: a cobbled climb up to Schloss Bensberg, the one non-smooth section on an otherwise fully paved course. The Granfondo waves start separately and earlier than the professional Rund um Köln classic (which begins at 11:30, hours after the Velodom fields), sharing roads and the Rheinauhafen finish line but running as their own timed, ranked races. Signature challenge: The cobbled climb to Schloss Bensberg, arriving on both routes after the Bergisches Land rollers have already worn riders down — the defining non-smooth section on an otherwise fully paved course. The Jedermann-Rennen at Rund um Köln is a genuine, competitively structured mass-participation race, not a curtain-raiser tacked onto a professional event. Riders start in speed-based blocks hours ahead of the professional race, run their own transponder-timed results with age categories and team classifications, and finish under a mandatory 25 km/h minimum average pace. The course shares real roads with Germany's oldest surviving professional race (founded 1908) — including the cobbled climb to Schloss Bensberg — but the modern open-entry Granfondo product itself dates only to 2004; don't confuse the parent race's century-plus pedigree with the amateur event's shorter history. The organizer trimmed its lineup for 2027, dropping the shorter Velodom 30 and offering only the 60 and 120. Yes if you want a genuinely competitive, well-organized German road race with historical roads and clear categories. Skip it if you want a casual group ride — the mandatory 25 km/h minimum average is enforced.

### London Edinburgh London
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 956.9 mi | 46,194 ft | London area, England, UK (start venue varies by edition — Loughton/Debden, Essex in 2022; Writtle, near Chelmsford, scheduled for 2029) | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/london-edinburgh-london/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/london-edinburgh-london.md

A historic quadrennial ultra-randonnée to Edinburgh and back — not a gran fondo, and not scheduled again until 2029. London Edinburgh London is Audax UK's flagship randonnée — a fixed, prescribed 1,500 km-class course (1,540 km / 14,080 m in the last completed 2022 edition) that riders navigate exactly as designed, not a route-choice ultra like a bikepacking race. It is genuinely self-supported between controls — no personal support vehicles are permitted — but the organizer runs 20 control visits across 13 staffed locations offering food, beds, showers, and limited mechanical/medical help, which is a materially different support model from a fully unsupported bikepacking event. There are no placings: riders either finish inside the time limit or don't, and official finishers are published alphabetically, not ranked. It runs once every four years — 2017, a COVID-delayed 2022 (standing in for 2021), and a 2025 edition that started but was abandoned mid-event due to Storm Floris with no official finisher list. The next edition is scheduled for August 5, 2029. Signature challenge: Simply finishing inside the time limit — 128 hours 20 minutes for the standard start group in 2022 — after nearly 1,000 miles and roughly 14,000 m of climbing with no personal support crew, just the control network. London Edinburgh London is a historically significant self-supported randonnée organized by Audax UK since 1989, and it deserves to be judged on its own terms — but those terms have almost nothing in common with a gran fondo. There is no field to compare yourself against competitively, no closed roads, no ranked result: riders navigate a fixed 1,540 km / 14,080 m course (2022 figures) within a 128-hour-plus time limit, resupplying at staffed controls between long, self-supported stretches. It runs once every four years, and even that cadence isn't reliable — the 2025 edition started and was abandoned mid-event to Storm Floris, producing no official finishers, and the next attempt isn't scheduled until August 2029. In the last edition that actually completed (2022), 41% of the 1,500 starters didn't make it back inside the time limit. This is not an event you can casually decide to enter next season; if the next edition happens on schedule, it's three years away. Only if you have self-supported multi-day cycling experience and want a navigation-and-endurance challenge rather than a competitive event. It won't run again until August 2029 at the earliest, so this isn't something to plan around for 2026 or 2027.

### Marmotte Granfondo Sestriere
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 64.4 mi | 10,400 ft | Cesana Torinese, Piedmont, Italy | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/marmotte-granfondo-sestriere/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/marmotte-granfondo-sestriere.md

The only granfondo in the world with Colle delle Finestre's legendary unpaved summit. Giro d'Italia dirt at 2,178 meters. A focused Alpine assault centered on one defining climb. The route through the Susa and Chisone Valleys is scenic and demanding, but everyone is here for the same reason: Colle delle Finestre. The course builds through steady valley climbs and fast descents before delivering you to the base of the Finestre's 18.5 km ascent. The first 10 km on tarmac are relentless (9.2% average), but the real event begins when the road surface changes. The final 7.8 km on dirt — switchbacking through larch forests with gradients reaching 14% — is the granfondo's entire reason for existence. The descent and return climb to Sestriere at 2,035m ensures the legs never fully recover. Signature challenge: The 7.8 km of unpaved road on Colle delle Finestre. The transition from tarmac to dirt at approximately 1,700m altitude — on gradients that reach 14%, at oxygen levels measurably reduced by altitude — is the single most distinctive feature of any road granfondo in the world. You can train for the climbing. You cannot fully prepare for the psychological impact of losing your road surface when the gradient kicks hardest. The Granfondo Sestriere exists for one reason: Colle delle Finestre. And that one reason is enough. This is the only organized cycling event in the world that sends you up the 7.8 km of unpaved road that has produced some of the most dramatic Giro d'Italia stages in modern history. The event itself is young and still finding its identity after splitting from the Marmotte brand, but the mountain does not care about branding. When the tarmac ends and the gravel begins at 1,700m, you are riding the exact surface that broke champions and made legends. Everything else — the Susa Valley, the Olympic infrastructure, the finish at Sestriere — is context for that singular experience. Yes if you want to ride cycling's most famous unpaved climb in an organized event. Yes if you value Giro d'Italia heritage and want to feel what the professionals felt on that dirt. Yes if you want a high-value Italian Alpine experience without the logistics of deep-Alpine events. Skip if you need a large, prestigious international granfondo. Skip if you want a 150+ km all-day epic — at 103 km, this is more focused than sprawling.

South Limburg's hilly touring sportive, riding real elite-race roads — explicitly a tour, not a race. ### Pan-Mass Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 177 mi | 6,800 ft | Worcester to Provincetown, Massachusetts, USA (multiple routes across Massachusetts) | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/pan-mass-challenge/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/pan-mass-challenge.md

6,500 riders. 177 miles. $1.125 billion raised. The bike ride that fights cancer. A two-day crossing of Massachusetts on paved roads, from the rolling hills of central Mass to the windswept tip of Cape Cod. Day 1 is the harder day — 100 miles from Worcester featuring genuine New England climbing in the first 50 miles (long, rolling ascents and fast descents), gradually flattening as the route approaches the Cape Cod Canal and the finish at Mass Maritime Academy in Bourne. The overnight at MMA is a PMC institution — thousands of riders sleeping in dorms, tents, and ship quarters, fueling for Day 2. Sunday's 77 miles from Bourne to Provincetown are rolling-to-flat Cape Cod terrain with ocean breezes, cranberry bogs, and the charming towns of the outer Cape, punctuated by short steep climbs in Truro before the emotional finish at the Provincetown Monument. Signature challenge: The emotional weight. The PMC's signature challenge is not a climb or a headwind — it is riding 177 miles while carrying the names and stories of people fighting cancer. The physical effort is real. The emotional effort is greater. The Pan-Mass Challenge is not a bike ride. It is a $78-million-a-year cancer research funding machine that uses bicycles as its engine. Since 1980, when Billy Starr convinced 36 riders to cycle from Springfield to Provincetown, the PMC has raised $1.125 billion for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute — 100% of every rider-raised dollar going directly to research, treatment, and patient care. Today, 6,500 riders cross Massachusetts on routes from 25 to 177 miles, supported by 3,500 volunteers and an organization refined over 46 years. The cycling is honest New England terrain — rolling hills, coastal roads, and a two-day format that demands real fitness. But the experience transcends sport. You ride past signs that say 'Thank you — my daughter is alive because of Dana-Farber.' You pedal alongside survivors wearing jerseys with their diagnosis dates. You finish in Provincetown knowing that your effort — every dollar you raised, every mile you rode — went directly to the fight. The PMC does not ask you to race. It asks you to matter. You do not race the PMC — you ride it with purpose. Yes if you are ready to commit to raising $2,000-$6,000+ for cancer research and want the most emotionally powerful cycling experience in America. Yes if you can handle 100+ miles of rolling New England roads in August heat. Skip if you need competitive cycling, dramatic terrain, or cannot commit to the fundraising requirement.

The West Maui Loop is one of Maui's best-known road rides, and its remote northern stretch on the Kahekili Highway — narrow, rough, partly single-lane, with short steep pitches and a documented participant crash on a wet corner — gives the day real teeth. Note the organizer's own page has run stale (still showing the 2025 edition well into 2026), and third-party calendars disagree on the exact 2026 date (December 5 vs December 6), which is sloppy for an event asking you to book flights to an island.
