### Suzuka 8 Hours Enduro
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 144.3 mi | — | Suzuka Circuit, Mie Prefecture, Japan | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/suzuka-endurance-road/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/suzuka-endurance-road.md

Japan's big amateur circuit enduro on the Suzuka F1 track — a timed lap race, not a gran fondo (and not the motorcycle race). Laps of the Suzuka Circuit International Racing Course — the 5.807 km figure-eight famous from Formula 1 — ridden counterclockwise, the opposite direction to motorsport. This is a timed circuit enduro, not a point-to-point course: solo riders or relay teams accumulate as many laps as possible in 4 or 8 hours, or ride the fixed 40-lap Attack 240 (232.28 km). The lap rolls constantly through the chicane, West Straight, Spoon, the hairpin, the 25R-Degner complex and the descending S-curves — technical circuit features rather than named climbs — on fully paved racing tarmac 10 to 16 metres wide. Total distance and climbing depend entirely on how many laps you complete; the 2025 8-hour leader logged 58 laps, roughly 336.8 km. Signature challenge: Pacing a 4- or 8-hour circuit effort: the lap's rhythm — descending S-curves, the Degner complex, the hairpin, and the rising drag to the line — repeats every 5.807 km, and lap consistency is the whole game. Housekeeping first: 'Suzuka Endurance Road' is not a thing. No event uses that name — it's a hybrid of the Suzuka 8 Hours Enduro (a real amateur bicycle event) and the Suzuka 8 Hours Endurance Road Race (the famous FIM motorcycle race). This profile previously carried the motorcycle race's dates, videos and atmosphere; all of that has been purged. What's left is genuinely worth knowing about: in November 2025 more than 4,000 cyclists took over the Formula 1 circuit for timed enduros — 4 hours, 8 hours solo or in relay teams of up to six, or the fixed 40-lap Attack 240 — riding the 5.807 km lap counterclockwise on closed racing tarmac, with transponder timing, pit lanes and rolling starts. But be honest about the format: this is lap racing against a clock, not a gran fondo. There is no course to discover, no summit, no scenery beyond the circuit complex — the appeal is the circuit itself and the event around it, and registration, rules and communications are in Japanese. Yes if a timed 4/8-hour team or solo enduro on a legendary closed circuit appeals and you can navigate Japanese-language registration. No if you want a point-to-point gran fondo with real terrain — this is the same 5.807 km lap all day.

### Tour de Yorkshire Sportive
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 87 mi | 6,890 ft | Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom | April | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-yorkshire-sportive/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-yorkshire-sportive.md

Tour de France heritage. Yorkshire climbs. Roadside passion. On hiatus since 2019 — but if it returns, ride it. The Tour de Yorkshire Sportive changed its route each year to mirror the professional race's final stage, giving riders a rotating tour of Yorkshire's finest cycling terrain. The consistent element was the terrain character: short, steep, punishing climbs with exposed moorland between them, narrow English lanes, and descents that demanded respect in wet conditions. Buttertubs (6 km at 6% with 20% ramps), Grinton Moor, Cote de Harwood Dale, and similar Yorkshire classics rotated through. The route always included the final 50 km and finish line of the pro race, and riders could watch the professional peloton cross the same line hours later. Signature challenge: Buttertubs. Six kilometers at 6% average with pitches hitting 20%. Exposed, relentless, and iconic. The quintessential Yorkshire climb — short enough to be over quickly, steep enough to make you wish it was over sooner. The Tour de Yorkshire Sportive was born from the most electrifying moment in British cycling history: the 2014 Tour de France Grand Depart. When the Tour came to Yorkshire, 2.6 million people lined the roads. A cycling culture was ignited. The professional Tour de Yorkshire launched in 2015, and the sportive gave amateurs the chance to ride the same roads, hours before the pros.

The format was simple and powerful: ride the route of the final stage — including its iconic Yorkshire climbs — then watch the pro race from the finish line. The routes varied each year: Leeds, Scarborough, Sheffield, each bringing different Yorkshire terrain. Buttertubs, Grinton Moor, Cote de Harwood Dale — the classic climbs rotated through, keeping each edition fresh.

The event is currently on hiatus. The professional Tour de Yorkshire was cancelled from 2020 onwards (COVID, then financial difficulties with Welcome to Yorkshire), and the sportive has not returned. If it does, the combination of Tour de France heritage, Yorkshire's passionate cycling community, and the county's beautiful-brutal terrain makes it one of the UK's strongest sportive propositions. Yes if the event returns and you want to ride iconic Yorkshire climbs with the Tour de France heritage and passionate roadside support. Yes if English cycling culture and the Dales landscape appeal to you. Skip if the event remains on hiatus. Skip if you need guaranteed good weather — Yorkshire in late April is a gamble.

### Two Volcano Sprint
Tier 2 | Score: 67/100 | 758.7 mi | 82,000 ft | Ercolano (Mt Vesuvius) to Nicolosi (Mt Etna), Italy | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/two-volcano-sprint/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/two-volcano-sprint.md

A genuine Vesuvius-to-Etna self-supported ultra — 1,221 km, ~25,000 m, GPS-tracked and unsupported. Not a gran fondo. A single-stage, fixed-route, self-supported ultracycling race from one active volcano to another: roughly 1,221 km and on the order of 25,000 m of climbing from Ercolano on Vesuvius's flank to Nicolosi on Etna's. The 2026 GPX opened straight up Vesuvius, then ran the Amalfi/Cilento side of the Tyrrhenian coast, over Monte Gelbison (about 30 km of climbing with ramps over 12%), past Cristo Redentore above Maratea, through the Pollino, Sila and Aspromonte massifs, across the Strait of Messina by ferry, up a 38 km climb from the Sicilian coast, and finally about 22 km up Etna to roughly 2,000 m before dropping to the finish. Riders follow the compulsory track, carry a live GPS tracker, and handle all food, water, sleep and mechanicals themselves — drafting is prohibited except within a pair entry. The surface is road-bike terrain on paper, but rider reports document rough farm tracks, technical descents and Calabrian potholes reported at up to 30 cm deep. Signature challenge: Racing 1,200+ km with ~25,000 m of climbing unsupported, then finishing on a 22 km ascent of Etna to ~2,000 m after two-plus days without proper sleep. Two Volcano Sprint is a genuine, currently active self-supported ultracycling race in the Transcontinental tradition: one stage, a compulsory ~1,221 km GPX from Vesuvius to Etna with around 25,000 m of climbing, live GPS tracking, and riders handling their own food, sleep and mechanicals — no drafting outside pair entries, no support crews. The 2026 edition put roughly 112 tracked riders on the road and classified 62 solo finishers, with Bruno Wicht winning in 59h23. It's run as a not-for-profit — after tracker costs, entry fees fund an environmental grant — but be clear-eyed about the details: the 'road' classification undersells documented farm tracks, broken tarmac and Calabrian potholes reported at 30 cm deep; published elevation figures conflict (24,000 m is stale, from the shorter early routes; 2026 reporting says 25,000-26,000 m); the planned 2023 edition was cancelled for lack of checkpoint volunteers; and as of this writing no 2027 edition has been announced. This is racing for experienced ultra riders, and our database's gran fondo framing simply doesn't fit it. Only with real multi-day self-supported ultra experience — 1,200+ km unsupported with a mountain finish is not an entry point to the discipline. If you want supported southern-Italy climbing, look elsewhere.

### Alpe d'HuZes
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 51 mi | 21,089 ft | Alpe d'Huez, Isere, France | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpe-dhuzes/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/alpe-dhuzes.md

Twenty-one hairpins. Six ascents. EUR 100 million for cancer research. Cycling's most profound charity event. One climb. Repeated. The 21 hairpins of Alpe d'Huez — 13.8 km at 7.9% average, with sections exceeding 11% — climbed up to six times in a single day. The route is simple to describe and punishing to execute. Each ascent follows the same road: the steep lower hairpins through the forest, the more open middle section, and the final push into the resort village at 1,860m. Each descent follows the same road back to Bourg d'Oisans. The physical experience changes with each repetition — ascent one is exhilarating, ascent three is grim, ascent six is transcendent. The emotional experience depends entirely on why you're climbing. Signature challenge: Repetition. One ascent of Alpe d'Huez is a great cycling experience. Six ascents transform it into something else entirely — a test of physical endurance, mental fortitude, and the power of purpose. The mountain doesn't change, but you do. Alpe d'HuZes is not a cycling event that happens to raise money for charity. It is a charity event that happens to use cycling's most legendary mountain as its vehicle. The distinction matters. When 5,000 riders climb Alpe d'Huez up to six times in a single day — many wearing jerseys bearing the names of people they've lost to cancer — the physical achievement becomes secondary to the emotional one. The 21 hairpins are still the 21 hairpins, the gradients are still punishing, and six ascents produce more vertical than almost any single-day cycling event on Earth. But what elevates Alpe d'HuZes beyond any sportive or gran fondo is the why. EUR 100 million raised. The largest sporting charity event in the Netherlands. This is cycling at its most human. Yes if you want to climb cycling's most famous mountain for a cause that transcends sport. Yes if the Dutch charity community and the emotional atmosphere appeal to you as much as the physical challenge. Skip if you want a traditional sportive with varied terrain and competitive structure. Skip if the EUR 1,500 fundraising minimum is a barrier.

### Bluewater International Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 100 mi | — | Bright's Grove/Sarnia, Ontario, Canada | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/bluewater-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/bluewater-gran-fondo.md

A sold-out, well-run Lake Huron community fondo — real support and real charity, flat-rolling terrain, segment timing only. Out of Mike Weir Park in Bright's Grove on the Lake Huron shore, the routes run quiet, paved rural Lambton County roads — lakeshore, fruit orchards and flat-to-rolling farmland. The organizer classifies the 30 km and 50 km routes as flat and the 100 km and 161 km routes as rolling, and publishes no named or categorized climbs; a detailed rider report identifies the Arkona/Parkhill farmland hills as the hilliest portion of the longer routes and wind as a meaningful course factor. For the 10th anniversary the long route grew to roughly 161 km/100 mi (from the previous ~150 km), and timing is by chip on selected sections only — 4 on the long route, 3 on the 100 km, 1 on the 50 km — with awards decided on cumulative segment time rather than a full-course start-to-finish result. Signature challenge: Repeated efforts across the timed sections on flat-to-rolling roads, with Lake Huron's wind across open farmland as the course's main variable — this event's difficulty is wind and pacing, not elevation. The Bluewater International Granfondo is what a community gran fondo looks like when it's run seriously: a 1,000-rider cap that sold out for the 10th anniversary, four route options from a 30 km family ride to a new ~161 km/100-mile long course, real support (fuel stops, SAG, finish meal), and over $500,000 returned to named local palliative-care causes since 2016. Two honesty notes. First, the terrain: this is flat-to-rolling Lambton County farmland — the organizer publishes no named or categorized climbs, the Arkona-area hills are the hilliest part of the course, and a rider report flags Lake Huron's wind as a meaningful factor. Second, the format: the organizer itself says this is not a race — timing is chip-based on selected segments only (4 on the long route), and awards run on cumulative segment time, not a full-course start-to-finish result. Also know the numbers wobble: the organizer says 161 km, Race Roster says '160K' but describes 162 km, and no current elevation figure is published for the new long course — we've dropped the old 853 m figure rather than carry stale data. Yes for a supported community fondo with genuine charitable impact and family-friendly options. No if you want mountains or a full start-to-finish race — the course is flat-to-rolling and only selected segments are timed.

### Bra-Bra Fenix Internazionale
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 78.3 mi | 7,841 ft | Pollenzo, Bra, Piedmont, Italy | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/bra-bra-fenix-internazionale/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/bra-bra-fenix-internazionale.md

A well-organized, scenic granfondo through UNESCO wine regions offering excellent early-season preparation with reasonable costs and flexible route options. Both the Granfondo (~126 km/~2,390 m) and Mediofondo (~105 km/~1,900 m) start and finish in Pollenzo, then cross the Roero, skirt the Monferrato, and climb into the Langhe/Alta Langa. The two courses split at a junction near Coste Pomo/Sinio, where the Granfondo takes a harder extension through Pedaggera, Serravalle Langhe, Cissone and the SP56/Serralunga sector before the routes come back together (per the official timing tables, the courses rejoin around the end of the Valdicroce climb, ahead of Serralunga). Named selection points along the shared portion include Bra/Orti, Monticello d'Alba, Guarene, Neive Borgo Alto, Neviglie, Trezzo Tinella, Benevello, the Dorsale delle Langhe, Tre Cunei and Albaretto Torre. Strada Paciarini to the Cedro del Libano is a shared late-race climb/GPM point, not the reunion point itself, followed by La Morra, Verduno and back to Pollenzo. The formerly prominent Mur d'la Mura climb, with its reported gradients up to 20% and short gravel sector, was removed from the course for 2026 — older descriptions of it no longer apply. The official 2026 materials reviewed do not publish per-climb gradients, so exact pitches on the Langhe/Alta Langa climbs remain unverified. Signature challenge: The Cedro del Libano ascent via Strada Paciarini — a shared late climb/GPM point, arriving after the Granfondo field has already absorbed its harder Serralunga-sector extension. Bra-Bra Fenix Internazionale is a legitimate amateur road Granfondo founded in 1992 and now in its 33rd edition, run by A.S.D. Gran Fondo Bra Bra out of Pollenzo. The course crosses the Roero and Langhe/Alta Langa wine country on paved roads, with a 2,000+ rider field in 2026. During the 2026 edition, a participant died in a crash near Neviglie; organizers suspended celebratory/collateral activities and said there would be no further competitive communications. Separately, the event's own published course figures are inconsistent: the regulations, timing tables, homepage and race-week press give a range of about 124.7-126 km and 2,375-2,390 m for the Granfondo (103.98-105 km/1,900-1,906 m for the Mediofondo) depending on which official page you read. Yes, if you want a historic Piedmont wine-country granfondo with a real field — but go in aware of the 2026 fatal incident and the organizer's inconsistent published course figures.

### Copper Triangle
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 79 mi | 6,500 ft | Copper Mountain Resort, Colorado | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/copper-triangle/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/copper-triangle.md

3 passes. 79 miles. Never below 9,000 feet. Colorado's premier high-altitude loop. A three-act alpine loop that never lets you forget where you are. The Copper Triangle traces a triangle through the heart of the Colorado Rockies, connecting three mountain passes through three distinct valleys. You climb past industrial mining heritage on Fremont, descend into America's highest city at Leadville, ascend through WWII military history at Camp Hale, and close the loop on the car-free Vail Pass bike path. The entire route sits above 9,000 feet — there is no low-altitude recovery. The grades are moderate, the road surfaces are good, and the scenery is relentless. What makes this ride hard is not the climbing profile on paper. It's the thin air that makes every gradient feel steeper than it reads. Signature challenge: The cumulative altitude. No single pass is a leg-breaker. The grades are moderate, the distances between passes are manageable. But the Copper Triangle never lets you below 9,000 feet. By the time you're climbing Vail Pass — your third summit above 10,000 feet — the oxygen deficit has been compounding for 65 miles. The thin air is the opponent, not the gradient. The Copper Triangle is a masterclass in what altitude does to honest cycling. 79 miles and 6,500 feet of climbing sounds manageable until you register the fine print: the entire route sits above 9,000 feet, the high point reaches 11,318, and you never get a breath of thick air. Three mountain passes — Fremont, Tennessee, Vail — through three Colorado valleys, past Leadville and Camp Hale and Minturn, finishing where you started at Copper Mountain. Twenty years of raising money for the Davis Phinney Foundation. Not the longest ride. Not the most climbing. But an altitude event that quietly exposes the gap between your sea-level fitness and what the Rocky Mountains actually demand. Yes if you want to experience what genuine high-altitude cycling feels like across three mountain passes in a single day. Yes if you value a well-organized charity ride through Colorado's most historic mountain terrain. Skip if you need race competition or if riding above 10,000 feet is a medical concern.

### Gran Fondo Hainan
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 130.8 mi | 7,221 ft | Lingao, Danzhou/Yangpu & Wuzhishan, Hainan Island, China | December | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-hainan/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-hainan.md

A tropical UCI debut with real terrain variety across three separately-entered days — treat the 'stage race' label skeptically pending a 2026 confirmation. A three-day UCI-branded program across Hainan Island rather than a single ridden course: Day 1 is a 110.4km coastal sprint along the Hainan Coastal Scenic Highway from Lingao to Danzhou/Yangpu (557m gain), Day 2 is a flat, wind-exposed 19.4km individual time trial on a repeated 5km loop in Yangpu, and Day 3 is an 80.74km queen stage climbing into the Wuzhishan rainforest to a 787m summit finish at Atuoling. Riders can enter one day, two, or all three — the organizer sells and enters each day separately, with no cumulative general classification published in the results, so despite the UCI's 'three-day stage race' label this behaves more like three independently-run qualifiers sharing a weekend than a true stage race. Signature challenge: The Wuzhishan queen stage's closing 13.4km at 4.1% to the 787m Atuoling summit — the decisive, longest-defined climb of the weekend, though not the only sustained climbing on Day 3: the stage first rises to roughly 755m before a long descent resets the legs for the final ascent. Gran Fondo Hainan is a genuine, UCI-sanctioned event on Hainan Island, separate from the professional Tour of Hainan. Its inaugural 2025 running drew roughly 2,300 stage entries from 34 countries across three days: a flat coastal sprint, a windy Yangpu time trial, and a rainforest queen stage climbing to the 787m Atuoling summit. But 'three-day stage race,' the UCI series' own label for the event, oversells the format — in 2025, each day was sold and entered separately with no published cumulative classification, so this reads as three independently entered and classified qualifiers sharing a weekend and a location rather than a Tour-style stage race. The event's own numbers haven't settled either: official UCI World Series sources published three different queen-stage elevation totals (1,535m, then 1,236m, then a final 1,644m) across three separate announcements, and the organizer's site was still displaying 2025 dates and fees as of this research despite December 2026 being on the UCI calendar. Yes if you want a UCI-qualifying event with genuine terrain variety (coastal flat, TT, rainforest climb) and a December racing window. Verify 2026 dates on the UCI calendar and wait for the organizer to publish registration and fees before booking, since the site hadn't updated from 2025 as of this research.

### Rad am Ring
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 93 mi | 11,024 ft | Nurburgring, Nurburg, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/rad-am-ring/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/rad-am-ring.md

Race the Green Hell. 12,000 cyclists on the world's most famous motorsport circuit — the Nurburgring Nordschleife. A relentless, undulating closed circuit combining the legendary Nordschleife (20.8 km) with the modern Grand Prix circuit (5.1 km). No flat sections exist — you are always either climbing or descending through 84 turns per lap. The forest-enclosed Nordschleife feels otherworldly, while the GP circuit provides the F1 arena start/finish spectacle. Perfect tarmac throughout, but the elevation profile punishes anyone who starts too fast. Signature challenge: The Hohe Acht climb at 17% gradient — the roof of the Nordschleife where every lap extracts its toll. Combined with the relentless undulation of the full circuit (560m elevation per lap), there is no recovery. The Green Hell simply grinds you down. Rad am Ring does something no other cycling event can: it puts you on the Nurburgring Nordschleife. The same 20.8 km of relentless, forest-enclosed circuit where motorsport legends were forged since 1927. Where Rudi Altig won the Road World Championship in 1966. Where Jackie Stewart coined the name 'Green Hell.' Nearly 12,000 cyclists now invade this sacred motorsport ground every July, racing through 84 turns per lap, surviving the 17% Hohe Acht climb, and hitting 100 km/h on the Fuchsrohre descent. The 24h race adds a surreal dimension — riding the Nordschleife at 3 AM through fog with only a headlamp. This is not gravel, this is not a gran fondo — this is road cycling on the most storied racing circuit on Earth, and the experience is absolutely singular. If you have any connection to motorsport culture, this is a mandatory pilgrimage on two wheels. The 24h race is the crown jewel — 24 hours of closed-circuit racing through the Nordschleife, including surreal night laps through forest fog. The public races (25/75/150 km) offer the venue experience in a single day. For German and European cyclists, this is one of the continent's most unique events. For international visitors, combine with a broader European cycling trip.

40 years of where legends are born. Now ride the same roads yourself. Southern California climbing roads through citrus country and oak-studded foothills, punctuated by the iconic professional race climbs. The same road, the same gradient, the same afternoon sun. The Redlands Bicycle Classic has launched more professional cycling careers than any other American race. Since 1985, the Sunset Loop, Oak Glen, and downtown criterium have been the courses where American legends first proved themselves. The Legends' Fondo puts amateur riders on those same roads, led by Phil Gaimon, finishing at the iconic RBC finish line. This isn't about the climbing or the distance — it's about 40 years of history seeping through the asphalt. Ride Oak Glen and you're riding where the next Olympic cyclist might be racing that same weekend. Yes if you value American cycling history and want to ride iconic professional race courses. Yes if you want a well-organized SoCal weekend with professional racing to watch. Skip if you want dramatic scenery or extreme physical challenge.

### Tour de Okinawa
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 124 mi | 6,560 ft | Nago City, Okinawa, Japan | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-okinawa/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-okinawa.md

Japan's biggest citizen road race — subtropical island, shut-down roads, Asian amateur racing at its finest. Deceptively demanding. The two cross-island climbs through Yanbaru forest are the race's signature — honest 5-8% gradients through subtropical canopy that shatter groups and determine results. Between those climbs, the constant coastal undulations from sea level create cumulative fatigue that the raw elevation numbers disguise. The course follows the coastline of northern Okinawa, cutting twice across the island's spine where the mountains live. It is not a mountain course, but it is not flat either — 2,000 meters of climbing from sea level is 2,000 meters of absolute gain. Signature challenge: The accumulation. Neither climb alone is extraordinary, but the combination of subtropical humidity, constant undulation, and two honest forest climbs creates progressive fatigue that catches riders who went out too hard on the flat coastal opening. The race rewards patience and punishes aggression. Tour de Okinawa is the race that Japanese amateur cyclists build their entire season around. It is not the hardest course, not the deepest field by global standards, and not the most internationally recognized. What it is: the most professionally organized citizen road race in Asia, held on a subtropical island with fully closed roads, wrapped in Okinawan hospitality, and steeped in 35 years of racing history. The two Yanbaru climbs separate the strong from the ambitious, and the November timing makes it the perfect season capstone. For Japanese cyclists, this needs no justification — it is the season finale that defines your year. For international riders, Tour de Okinawa rewards those willing to navigate the logistics: you get a UCI-grade racing experience on a subtropical island with some of the best on-course support in amateur cycling. The two Yanbaru climbs are honest and the coastal roads are stunning. Come for the race, stay for the sashimi.

A strong-value 1,600 km self-supported ultra with a real Vosges centerpiece and first-edition uncertainty. A partly free-routed, partly fixed 1,600 km road ultra. Riders leave Utrecht together, choose their own commercially supportable lines between three checkpoints, and complete mandatory parcours along the Luxembourg-Germany border, through the Vosges, and across the cobbled hills near Oudenaarde before following the fixed return through Zeeland. Signature challenge: The 218 km Vosges parcours: nearly 5,000 m of climbing inside one mandatory block, reached after riders have already navigated hundreds of self-supported kilometers. Utrecht Ultra XL takes the original race's approachable route-choice concept and turns it into a serious trans-European ultra: 1,600 km, 14,000 m, a 158-hour clock, a 218 km Vosges block, and cobbles near Oudenaarde. The EUR200 entry is unusually strong value for a tracker, staffed mountain checkpoint, storage, media, and finish support. Its limitation is history: 2026 is the inaugural edition, so the course has not yet accumulated the repeat-edition evidence of Europe's established ultras. Yes if route planning, commercial self-resupply, long mountain blocks, and a six-day clock are the challenge you want. Wait for more editions if proven course continuity matters more than novelty.

### Vermont Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 66/100 | 108.7 mi | 9,680 ft | Bristol, Vermont, USA | — | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/vermont-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/vermont-gran-fondo.md

Vermont's LAMB gaps in one supported day — currently on a confirmed one-year hiatus. Four route options starting and finishing at Bristol Rec Park in Bristol, Vermont, using different combinations of the LAMB gaps — Lincoln, Appalachian, Middlebury, Brandon — that cut through Vermont's Green Mountains: Piccolo (40 mi) climbs no gap at all, Medio (80 mi) crosses two (Middlebury, Brandon), the flagship Gran (roughly 109 miles, ~9,680 ft climbing, also cited as 9,850+ ft in the organizer's own overview) runs clockwise over four (Appalachian, Lincoln, Middlebury, Brandon), and the Gran-X (roughly 149 miles, ~15,090 ft) adds Roxbury and Rochester Gaps for six gaps total in a figure-eight layout. None of the four routes is fully paved: the organizer's detailed course data lists roughly 10 dirt miles each on Piccolo and Medio, 18 on the Gran, and 21.5 on the Gran-X, and the FAQ recommends road or gravel bikes with at least 28-30mm tires. Signature challenge: The four-gap sequence on the Gran — Appalachian, then Lincoln, Middlebury, and Brandon — back to back over roughly 109 miles. The Vermont Gran Fondo is an organized mass-participation ride through the LAMB gaps of Vermont's Green Mountains, held annually since 2014, under Todd Warnock's direction since 2018 and based in Bristol since 2019 (current organizer: Ride It If You Can LLC). It is explicitly non-competitive except for timed gap-climb segments — there's no racing license requirement and no overall finish-order competition. The organizer's own site confirms a hiatus for 2026 ('We're Taking a Break in 2026 — See You in 2027'), though no 2027 date or registration has been published yet. The 2025 edition was held in Bristol on June 28, drawing 371 registrations across four routes. Not in 2026 — there's no edition to enter. If it returns in 2027 as the organizer intends, it's a solid regional option for riders who want Appalachian, Lincoln, Middlebury, and Brandon Gaps in a single supported ride, on gravel-capable tires.

### Adelaide Epic Ride
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 85 mi | 5,906 ft | Adelaide, South Australia, Australia | January | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/adelaide-epic-ride/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/adelaide-epic-ride.md

136 km on a UCI WorldTour stage route through the Adelaide Hills with 1,800 m of climbing, ridden on the same day as the pros. The community ride of Australia's biggest professional cycling race. A sealed-road journey from the Adelaide coast through the southern suburbs and into the Adelaide Hills, following the exact route of the UCI WorldTour Men's Stage 3. The 136 km route begins at Henley Beach at sea level and heads south and east through Adelaide's suburban fringe before the terrain tilts decisively upward into the Adelaide Hills. The character shifts dramatically across the ride: flat coastal kilometres give way to rolling suburban hills, which in turn yield to the punchy categorised climbs that define the stage. Chandlers Hill arrives first — a short, sharp shock to legs that have been spinning on flat road. Wickham Hill follows, a more sustained effort through Adelaide Hills bushland. The final act is Mount Barker Summit, arriving with less than 5 km to the finish in Nairne, when accumulated fatigue and January heat conspire to make every gradient feel twice as steep. The descents between climbs are fast and rewarding — wide, well-surfaced roads swept to professional racing standards. Signature challenge: Mount Barker Summit with less than 5 km to the finish — the final categorised climb after 130+ km of riding and 1,500+ metres of accumulated climbing in January heat. Every pedal stroke on this climb is earned. The gradient is honest, the heat is real, and the finish at Nairne is close enough to be cruel. The Adelaide Epic Ride is the rare community ride that lets you put your wheels on a genuine UCI WorldTour stage route and ride it on the same day as the professionals. The 136 km route from Henley Beach to Nairne through the Adelaide Hills delivers 1,800 metres of honest climbing — Chandlers Hill, Wickham Hill, and Mount Barker Summit are real climbs, not token hills — under the full force of South Australian summer heat. This is not the hardest sportive in Australia. But it is the one most directly connected to the highest level of professional cycling, and that connection is what makes it special. Yes if you want the unique experience of riding a genuine WorldTour stage route on race day, embedded in the Santos Tour Down Under festival atmosphere. Yes if you can handle South Australian summer heat and want a well-supported 136 km ride with real climbing. Skip if you need competitive racing, if you cannot tolerate extreme heat, or if you find $225 AUD steep for a community ride.

### Cape Town Cycle Tour

35,000 riders around the Cape Peninsula — the world's largest individually timed bike race, where the Cape Doctor wind is the real opponent. A 109km loop around one of the most beautiful peninsulas on Earth, with 35,000 individually-timed riders on fully closed roads. The course is more spectacle than suffering — the climbing is modest and the challenge comes from wind, distance, and the sheer scale of the peloton. Chapman's Peak Drive carved into a cliff 600m above the Atlantic is the jewel. The Cape Doctor wind is the wildcard that can turn a pleasant ride into a survival exercise. Signature challenge: The Cape Doctor wind. In calm years (like 2025), record times fall. In windy years, the second half of the course becomes a headwind survival exercise. In 2017, 100km/h winds forced the first-ever cancellation. Cape Town Cycle Tour is unlike anything else in cycling. 35,000 riders on fully closed roads around one of the most beautiful peninsulas on Earth. The climbing is gentle, the scenery is stunning, and the entry fee ($53) is absurdly cheap. But this is not a mountainous challenge — it's a community celebration at scale. The Cape Doctor wind is the real antagonist: it has cancelled the event, collapsed infrastructure, and turned Chapman's Peak into a wind tunnel. When conditions cooperate, it's a perfect day on a bike. Yes, if you appreciate the scale and setting over course difficulty. This is a celebration, not a sufferfest. Chapman's Peak alone is worth the trip. The UCI GFWS status in 2026 adds competitive credibility. Just know that the climbing is modest and the wind is the variable.

### Engadin Radmarathon
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 137 mi | 13,123 ft | Zernez, Engadin Valley, Graubunden, Switzerland | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/engadin-radmarathon/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/engadin-radmarathon.md

Three days of Swiss Alpine precision. Five passes above 2,000m. Glaciers, national parks, and UNESCO heritage — through the Engadin, where the roads are perfect and the scenery is better. A three-act Alpine drama staged across the Engadin Valley. The Friday prologue is a sharp appetizer: 6.7 km straight up toward the Ofenpass through the Swiss National Park, legs burning from the first pedal stroke. Saturday's La Cuorta is the international chapter: through a closed tunnel into the duty-free Italian enclave of Livigno, over the Forcola di Livigno and the Bernina Pass in rapid succession — with the glaciers of Piz Bernina and Piz Palu gleaming above the descent to Pontresina. Sunday's La Svizra is the masterpiece: the Fluela Pass at 2,383m rising from Susch in 13 km of sustained climbing, a fast descent into Davos, the long Landwasser Valley approach to the Albula Pass alongside the UNESCO World Heritage Rhaetian Railway, and the final descent back into the Engadin to Zernez. The cumulative effect of three days, five passes, and 221 km at altitude is a slow-building immersion in some of the finest cycling terrain in the Alps. Signature challenge: The Albula Pass on Sunday. After two days of Alpine climbing — five passes already in the legs — the 26 km approach from the Landwasser Valley alongside the UNESCO World Heritage Rhaetian Railway is the event's emotional and physical crescendo. The climb is not the steepest, not the highest, not the most dramatic. It is the most relentless — and it comes when you have the least to give. The Engadin Radmarathon is what happens when Swiss organizational culture meets some of the most spectacular cycling terrain in the Alps. Three days, five passes above 2,000 meters, 221 km of pristine tarmac through the Engadin Valley — crossing into Italy, riding through the Swiss National Park, climbing alongside a UNESCO World Heritage railway, and staring at the Bernina glacier massif from the saddle. It is not the hardest Alpine sportive (the Otztaler and La Marmotte are harder). It is not the most famous (the Maratona and L'Etape are better known). What it is, consistently, is one of the most beautiful — and one of the best organized. The three-day stage format creates something rare in the sportive world: a journey, not just a ride. You sleep in a small Swiss village, wake up, and climb another pass. By Sunday evening, the Engadin feels like home. Yes if you want a multi-day Alpine stage experience with world-class scenery and Swiss-level organization. Yes if five passes above 2,000m through the Engadin, with cross-border adventure into Italy, is your definition of a good weekend. Skip if Swiss prices are a dealbreaker — accommodation and dining add up fast across a multi-day format. Skip if you want a competitive race environment or a field bigger than 1,500 riders.

Licensed Eroica heritage ride through Rheingau vineyards — light on published course precision. Riders leave the central square in Erbach (a district of Eltville am Rhein) on period-correct bicycles — road-racing bikes built in 1987 or earlier, typically steel frames with downtube shifters, external brake cables, and toe clips — and pass through Rheingau vineyards and the landscape around Schloss Johannisberg before an asphalt forest descent gives way to harder climbing. The long route continues into the Rhine-Taunus Nature Park. Three route options are offered: 122 km/2,150 m, 80 km/1,290 m, and a 42.8 km/600 m short option. The organizer's regulations specify a mix of asphalt and unpaved 'white road' (gravel) sectors, though no gravel-percentage breakdown is published, and no named climbs or gradients appear on the official course pages. It finishes at Weingut Baron Knyphausen (Draiser Hof), about 850 meters from the start, with a wine-region festival atmosphere consistent with the Eroica series' heritage format. Signature challenge: The long route's unnamed gravel and forest climbs — official pages disagree on total ascent (2,150 m in the structured route data vs. roughly 2,400-2,500 m in narrative copy), so the real climbing load is difficult to assess beforehand. Eroica Germania has run since its 2018 premiere, produced by German licensee die wellenmaschine (license held since 2017). It follows the series' core format — 1987-or-earlier road-racing bicycles, typically steel, classically inspired clothing, non-competitive ride rather than a timed race — over mixed asphalt/gravel terrain through the Rheingau wine region. What it doesn't offer is much verifiable course precision: the organizer's own site gives two different elevation totals for the long route, publishes no named climbs or gradients, and provides no breakdown of how much of the course is actually unpaved. Yes if you want an Eroica-series experience on a period-correct bike through German wine country and don't need a precisely scouted, timed course.

### GFNY República Dominicana

Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-dominican-republic.md

A wind-dependent Caribbean challenge that tests tactical racing and mental resilience in a stunning tropical setting. A wind-dependent Caribbean cycling challenge featuring a deceptively fast outbound leg with favorable tailwind through rural tropical terrain, followed by a punishing headwind return that tests mental toughness and pacing discipline. The course transitions from coastal roads to lush hinterland and back, with the Caribbean Sea and impressive hill backdrops providing scenic contrast. Signature challenge: The wind reversal from outbound to return leg. Riders must exercise extreme restraint during the fast, favorable outbound section (km 0-67) despite the pace feeling easy and the field moving quickly. The return journey's headwind separates those who paced conservatively from those who burned matches early. GFNY Dominican Republic is a wind-defined race that rewards tactical patience and mental toughness. The outbound leg's false sense of ease—powered by favorable tailwind through beautiful rural terrain—sets up a humbling return journey. This is not a race to chase early moves; it's a race to conserve energy, read the wind, and unleash in the final 10km when others are suffering. The Caribbean setting elevates the experience beyond pure cycling metrics, and the professional race organization ensures riders feel like legitimate competitors. Best suited for cyclists who enjoy wind strategy and don't mind a challenging finish. GFNY Dominican Republic delivers a unique racing experience where wind becomes the primary opponent rather than terrain. The 149.7km long course offers genuine competitive racing with a well-organized international field, while the 93.8km medium course provides an accessible alternative. The race's greatest strength is its strategic depth—the favorable outbound leg tempts aggressive racing, but the brutal headwind return punishes poor pacing decisions. Punta Cana's resort infrastructure, direct international flights, and beautiful Caribbean scenery make this an attractive destination race. However, the relatively modest elevation gain and lack of technical terrain limit its appeal for climbers or technical specialists. The race shines for cyclists seeking a professional racing experience in an exotic location, particularly those who thrive in wind-based tactical racing. Not ideal for first-time gran fondo participants or those seeking a pure climbing challenge, but excellent for experienced riders wanting to test their racing acumen in paradise.

### GFNY Ottawa
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 73.5 mi | 2,572 ft | Ottawa, Ontario, Canada | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-ottawa/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gfny-ottawa.md

A fully closed 118-kilometer race where Kanata rollers, technical turns, and crosswinds make a flat profile tactically expensive. Ottawa's long race covers 118.3 kilometers and 784 meters of climbing on a fully closed course. The route mixes technical early turns, long false-flat roads, a short northern climb, and two laps, making group economy and repeatable power more important than pure climbing speed. Signature challenge: Beginning the second lap after roughly 60 kilometers without having overspent on the fast first circuit. Ottawa looks easy if you read only the elevation total. That misses the point. The combination of full road closure, technical turns, false flats, crosswinds, and a second lap encourages speed that can turn small positioning mistakes into a very long chase. Race Ottawa if you want a fast, tactical fondo where efficiency and position matter every bit as much as watts per kilogram.

### Gran Fondo Kazakhstan

Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-kazakhstan/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-kazakhstan.md

Legitimate Almaty road race since 2016, oversold as a 'World Championship' it isn't. A lap-based road course starting and finishing at the Halyk Bank parking area on Al-Farabi Street in Almaty. The organizer runs three linked categories on the same asphalt circuit: a 95 km Gran Fondo and 50 km Media Fondo for road bikes, plus a separate 37 km MTB category. The organizer describes the course as hilly, with steep ascents and smooth descents, rather than a single point-to-point mountain profile — but has not published a route-level elevation total or climb-by-climb breakdown to back that characterization. Signature challenge: The repeated hill sequences within the lap circuit — no single named climb dominates, since the organizer markets the course as a hilly asphalt loop rather than a mountain point-to-point. Gran Fondo Kazakhstan is a genuine, timed road race in Almaty — a 95 km Gran Fondo and 50 km Media Fondo on a timed asphalt lap course, plus a separate 37 km MTB category that doesn't compromise the road event's identity. It has run since 2016 and has real continuity: a 2025 edition with organizer-published results, and a confirmed 2026 date. The catch is the marketing. The organizer calls it the "Gran Fondo World Championship," but its own regulations qualify that as a title "according to the GFWT version" — Gran Fondo World Tour branding, not a UCI World Championship. Read the name literally and you'll overrate what this is. Yes if you want an affordable, genuinely timed road race in Central Asia with real organizational continuity. Don't expect a UCI-sanctioned World Championship field or documented high-mountain climbing — this is a hilly asphalt lap course, not a Tien Shan epic.

### UCI Gran Fondo Loutraki
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 69.6 mi | 4,462 ft | Loutraki, Isthmus of Corinth, Greece | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-loutraki/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-loutraki.md

A well-organized UCI World Series qualifier offering Mediterranean scenery and legitimate competition with direct pathway to world championships. The 2026 Gran Fondo Loutraki is a 112 km closed road race through Corinthia and the Peloponnese. Its 1,360 m of climbing and rapid descents make pacing and road handling the defining demands. Signature challenge: Accumulating 1,360 m of climbing across the 112 km route while preserving control for the rapid descents. Gran Fondo Loutraki represents an excellent entry point into UCI Gran Fondo World Series racing with genuine competitive value. The inaugural 2025 event attracted 400+ international riders, and the 2026 edition returns on a 112 km closed route with 1,360 m of climbing. Its qualification pathway elevates its prestige beyond a typical regional event while keeping the format accessible to age-group racers. Gran Fondo Loutraki successfully launched as Greece's first UCI Gran Fondo World Series event in November 2025, establishing itself as a quality international cycling event. The 112 km route intelligently balances accessibility with challenge, featuring flat coastal sections that welcome diverse ability levels alongside rolling inland climbs that test fitness. The automatic qualification system for top 25% finishers in each age category provides meaningful competitive stakes. Professional organization by the Municipality of Loutraki and Hellenic Cycling Federation ensures world-class standards. The location's proximity to Athens and established tourism infrastructure supports international participation. For cyclists seeking UCI-sanctioned racing with genuine world championship qualification opportunities, combined with Mediterranean scenery and strong community atmosphere, Loutraki delivers exceptional value. The event's inaugural success and integration into the prestigious UCI Gran Fondo World Series calendar positions it as a must-do qualifier for ambitious Gran Fondo racers.

Four distances were offered in 2019: Super Fondo (160 km), Gran Fondo (125 km), Medio Fondo (80 km) and Molo Fondo (45 km). The Nordet portion of the route was singled out for scenery. The format leaned toward personal-challenge riding with ride leaders managing pace groups, rather than a single-field competitive race, though selected KOM segments provided a timed/competitive element. Signature challenge: Historically, the Nordet section of the Laurentians route — the scenic core of the ride, no longer verifiable as current given the event's lapsed status. There is no evidence Gran Fondo Mont-Tremblant has run since May 26, 2019. COVID postponed 2020 and 2021, the entire 2022 Crossroads festival was then cancelled outright, and the organizer's stated intention to return in 2023 has no supporting evidence of ever happening. Mont-Tremblant's current event calendar lists Salsa Tremblant on the exact August weekend this database's prior file claimed for Gran Fondo Mont-Tremblant — that date appears to be contamination from an unrelated destination event, not evidence of a revival. ### Gran Fondo Siete Lagos
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 68.4 mi | 4,921 ft | Villa La Angostura ↔ San Martín de los Andes, Neuquén, Argentina | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-siete-lagos/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-siete-lagos.md

Seven lakes, one paved Patagonian test — now Argentina's first stop on the UCI Gran Fondo World Series. A point-to-point road gran fondo along RN40's Ruta de los Siete Lagos, linking Villa La Angostura and San Martín de los Andes through Lanín and Nahuel Huapi national parks — past the Lácar, Machónico, Falkner, Villarino, Espejo, Correntoso, and Nahuel Huapi lakes. The 110km course is fully paved (Argentina's tourism authority documents more than 96km of the corridor as completely asphalted); an MTB category rides the same paved road, so this is not a gravel event despite the mixed-discipline field. Direction alternates by year — 2025 ran Villa La Angostura to San Martín de los Andes, 2026 reverses to San Martín de los Andes to Villa La Angostura, which changes which climbs land early versus late. The profile is a long rolling mountain corridor rather than a single summit finish: an early sustained climb, extended lakeside descents, and two short, steep ramps late in the race. Signature challenge: The opening climb — roughly 15km averaging 3.5% to the course's 1,175m high point — sets the tone early, but the real sting comes late: two short, steep ramps (1.9km at 7.2% and 1.2km at 6.5%) hit tired legs well into the 110km. Gran Fondo Siete Lagos is a growing Patagonian road gran fondo along the Ruta de los Siete Lagos between Villa La Angostura and San Martín de los Andes, and as of 2026 it's the first UCI Gran Fondo World Series round held in Argentina — a dated, externally verified prestige signal, not a self-reported claim. It draws roughly 3,000 riders each November (Patagonian spring, not the March date this profile long listed in error) and has attracted notable sporting names — Lionel Scaloni, Pablo Aimar, and Gabriela Sabatini among them in 2024. The course is fully paved despite an MTB category riding the same road, and the profile rewards riders comfortable with a long early climb followed by short, steep late ramps rather than one big summit test. One caution: no single organizer-published total elevation-gain figure exists — GPS tracks from different editions and directions range roughly 1,300–1,800m, so treat any single number, including ours, as an estimate rather than a certified total. Yes if you want a scenic, well-supported November gran fondo in Patagonia with a growing UCI-Series pedigree. Confirm the current year's direction and don't expect a single-summit profile — it's a long early climb plus two short, steep late ramps.

### Granfondo Yunnan
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 404 mi | — | Mangshi to Jinghong, Yunnan, China (multi-city stage race) | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-yunnan/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/granfondo-yunnan.md

A ~650km, 5-stage amateur GC race across western Yunnan — not the single-day Kunming fondo this profile used to describe. A multi-city, multi-day timed stage race across western Yunnan, not a single one-day fondo. The 2025 (12th) edition ran five GC stages totaling roughly 650+ km plus a non-GC 9 km Duo TT prologue, moving through Mangshi, Tengchong, Fengqing, Pu'er/Simao, and finishing in the Xishuangbanna/Jinghong area — Kunming was not the 2025 event base, despite this database's prior listing. General classification is genuinely competitive (active UCI professionals are excluded), with traffic-controlled stages and organizer-run inter-city bus/hotel logistics between stage towns. Signature challenge: Stage 1's Jiandong Mountain climb (~1,000 m gain) sets the GC tone early; Stage 5 (133 km, ~2,500 m climbing) into the Jinghong/Xishuangbanna finish closes out the tour as the hardest single day. Granfondo Yunnan is a genuine, competitive multi-day amateur stage race — five GC stages across roughly 650+ km through western Yunnan's Mangshi, Tengchong, Fengqing, Pu'er and Xishuangbanna regions, plus a non-GC Duo TT prologue. That's a materially bigger and more complicated undertaking than the single 140 km/2,286m Kunming fondo this database previously described, which appears to have been an unsourced single-stage extract rather than the actual event. The 2025 edition drew more than 2,000 riders and delivered real GC racing with professional exclusions — but it also delivered real disruption, with heavy rain shortening one stage and landslides forcing another to be neutralized. This is a rare amateur stage-race experience, not a weekend fondo, and should be marketed and scored as such. Yes if you want a rare, genuinely competitive multi-day amateur stage race with real GC stakes and don't mind the added logistics of a multi-city tour. Skip if you're looking for a simple one-day fondo — that's not what this is.

150km non-competitive lakeside ride around Omberg and southern Lake Vättern — Bike Week atmosphere, no ranked result. A 150 km paved-road ride starting and finishing in Motala, run under the Vätternrundan organization's Bike Week umbrella. The route takes in the Omberg hills and Lake Vättern shoreline, alternating winding lakeside roads with forest and open agricultural landscapes. Roads remain open to normal traffic throughout — this is not a closed-course race, and the organizer explicitly cautions riders about group-riding risk, recommending no more than two abreast. Signature challenge: The Omberg climbs — the course's only real elevation, set against an otherwise rolling lakeside profile. HalvVättern is exactly what its name says — the half-distance version of Vätternrundan, a 150 km ride around the southern shore of Lake Vättern out of Motala. It's genuinely well organized, with more than 3,000 riders in 2026, clear timing checkpoints, and Vätternrundan's established Bike Week infrastructure. What it is not is competitive: like the rest of the Vätternrundan family, there's no ranked result list, no crowned winner, and no race classification — just a completion time and a diploma. Riders coming from a GFNY- or UCI-style gran fondo background should recalibrate their expectations accordingly. ### K2 Road Cycle Classic

Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/k2-road-ride/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/k2-road-ride.md

Historic 192km Coromandel Peninsula circuit with uncertain continuity since its 2021 edition. An anticlockwise, roughly 192 km sealed-road circuit around the full Coromandel Peninsula, starting and finishing in Coromandel Town: Coromandel to Thames (53 km), Thames to Tairua via Kopu-Hikuai (53 km), Tairua to Whitianga via Coroglen (43 km), and Whitianga back to Coromandel via Kuaotunu (43 km). A shorter K1 (86 km) and the Nicholas Browne Challenge (43 km) run alongside the full circuit. The route is coastal and forested with repeated climbing rather than one dominant summit. Signature challenge: The Kopu-Hikuai climb on the Thames-Tairua leg, followed later by the Pumpkin Hill/Kuaotunu/Whangapoua sequence on the closing leg back into Coromandel Town — the two established decisive sectors of the full peninsula lap. K2 is a genuine, historically well-regarded full-circuit road race around the Coromandel Peninsula, running since 2002 with real elite and recreational history and roughly 192 km/2,300 m of sealed-road climbing. But its current status is shaky. The most recent confirmed edition was 2021 (406 starters); the planned 2022 running was officially postponed after entries collapsed roughly 70% during Omicron, and no confirmed 2023-2025 results or organizer announcement could be found. A 2026 date exists only on a third-party events listing (GoStride), not on any live ARC Events page — and the event's former standalone domain, still linked as 'official' by directories, now resolves to an unrelated gambling/spam site. That's a real trust problem for anyone trying to plan around this race. Only after confirming directly with ARC Events that a 2026 (or later) edition is actually running — the only current listing is third-party and unconfirmed, and the event's own former domain is now compromised.

Korea Epic Ride is a self-supported ultra-distance bikepacking event through Gangwon-do's mountains and East Sea coast, not a conventional timed road gran fondo. Three route options — a fully paved 1,024km/17,670m Epic Road 1000, a 500km/12,240m Offroad route (276km unpaved), and a 328km/8,004m Offroad route (~194km unpaved) — all start from a simultaneous grand depart at Songjeon Beach with no timing stops, no aid stations, and no organizer support along the way. Riders navigate by GPS through remote forest roads, rural mountain settlements, and major passes. Signature challenge: The 25km Hangyeoryeong ascent on the road route, or on the offroad routes, forest sections with gradients exceeding 15% and rough gravel descents through terrain vulnerable to landslides and washouts. The real Korea Epic Ride is a self-supported ultra-distance bikepacking event based in Yangyang, Gangwon-do, with routes from 328km to 1,024km through mountain passes and unpaved forest roads — explicitly 'not a race' per the organizer's own site, with no aid stations, no timing stops, and no organizer support between the grand depart and the finish. It's a real, honestly-run event founded in 2020 by Kiseok Uhm with a genuine six-edition history, but it bears no resemblance to a conventional gran fondo, and the 2026 edition has been cancelled outright. Not this year — the 2026 edition is cancelled. If a future edition is announced, go in understanding this is a fully self-supported ultra-distance mountain/forest-road event, not a timed, aided road race.

### Les Trois Ballons
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 112.5 mi | 13,189 ft | Ronchamp, Haute-Saône, France (finishes at La Planche des Belles Filles) | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/les-trois-ballons/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/les-trois-ballons.md

Dense Vosges climbing gauntlet — Servance, Markstein, Grand Ballon, Ballon d'Alsace — finishing atop La Planche des Belles Filles. Officially branded 'Les 3 Ballons Chef de File,' this cyclosportive starts at the Esplanade du Stade in Ronchamp and climbs through a dense sequence of southern Vosges massifs — Ballon de Servance, Col d'Oderen, Le Markstein, Grand Ballon, and Ballon d'Alsace — before an uphill finish at the summit of La Planche des Belles Filles, whose closing ramps exceed 15%. Riders return to Ronchamp afterward, roughly 14 km of mostly descending travel from the foot of the climb. It shares the Grand Ballon-Markstein corridor with GFNY Grand Ballon (Thann), but the two events are genuinely distinct: different organizers (Top Club France/Sport Communication vs. GFNY), different exact routes, and different dates. Signature challenge: The summit finish at La Planche des Belles Filles, arriving after Servance, Oderen, Markstein, Grand Ballon and Ballon d'Alsace have already been climbed — a true summit-finish sportive rather than a loop back to a flat finish. Les 3 Ballons is a well-established French cyclosportive built around an unusually dense sequence of major Vosges climbs — Servance, Oderen, Markstein, Grand Ballon, Ballon d'Alsace — capped by a genuine summit finish at La Planche des Belles Filles. It shares its home massif and one climbing corridor with GFNY Grand Ballon in nearby Thann, but the two are run by different organizers on different routes on different dates; they should be catalogued as distinct events, not duplicates. Entry pricing (EUR75-85) is reasonable for the density of climbing on offer, though the organizer's own materials disagree with themselves on the exact distance (178 km on one portfolio page, 181 km on the dedicated 2026 course page) — a small but real precision problem. Yes if you want one of the hardest single-day amateur climbing tests in the Vosges with a genuine summit finish. Choose the 93 km Mediofondo if the full 181 km/4,020m Granfondo is beyond your current fitness.

### Pelotonia
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 100 mi | 2,500 ft | Columbus, Ohio, USA | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/pelotonia/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/pelotonia.md

$339 million raised. 7,500 riders. 100% of every dollar to cancer research. The terrain is Ohio. The mission is everything. A point-to-point ride from downtown Columbus across Central Ohio's gently rolling farmland. The route leaves the urban grid within the first 10 miles, transitioning through suburbs and into genuinely rural countryside — corn and soybean fields, white farmhouses, quiet county roads lined with hardwood trees. The terrain is a series of short rollers, none individually significant but cumulatively honest over 100 miles in August heat. The 100-mile route culminates at Kenyon College in Gambier — a hilltop liberal arts campus that transforms into a finish line celebration. The 165-mile two-day option adds a Sunday return from Kenyon through different countryside to New Albany. Signature challenge: The heat. Not the terrain, not the distance, not the climbing — the August Ohio heat and humidity that turns an otherwise moderate century into a genuine test of preparation and resilience. Every experienced Pelotonia rider will tell you the same thing: respect the weather. Pelotonia is the rare cycling event where the suffering has a point beyond personal satisfaction. $339 million raised for cancer research — every dollar from riders going directly to the Ohio State Comprehensive Cancer Center, operational costs covered by corporate partners so nothing leaks to overhead. The riding itself is honest but unremarkable: flat-to-rolling Ohio farmland in August heat, paved roads, no technical demands. What makes Pelotonia extraordinary is the community — 7,500 riders who have raised thousands of dollars each, many riding for deeply personal reasons, united by a single goal that is bigger than any of them. The Opening Ceremony will give you chills. The finish line might make you cry. The terrain will not. Yes if you want to be part of one of the most impactful cycling communities in America. Yes if cancer has touched your life and you want to ride with meaning. Yes if you value community and mission over scenery and competition. Skip if you cannot commit to the fundraising requirement, need competitive racing, or want dramatic terrain.

### Prosecco Cycling
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 62 mi | 5,118 ft | Valdobbiadene, Veneto, Italy | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/prosecco-cycling/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/prosecco-cycling.md

100 kilometers through UNESCO vineyards, Prosecco at the aid stations, Nessun Dorma at the start line. The only gran fondo where the feed zone serves shrimp scampi and sparkling wine. A 100 km circuit through the UNESCO World Heritage Prosecco Hills, starting and finishing in Valdobbiadene. The terrain is relentlessly rolling — short, punchy climbs through terraced vineyards connected by valley-floor sections through medieval villages. The climbing is concentrated in sharp, steep pitches rather than sustained alpine passes. The Muro di Ca' del Poggio is the signature effort: 1.1 km at 12.7% average with a 19% maximum gradient, a Giro d'Italia climb compressed into a furious sprint. Between the four timed climbs, the route meanders through Combai, Follina, Tarzo, Resera, Refrontolo, San Pietro di Feletto, Conegliano, and Collalto before returning via Sernaglia della Battaglia, Col San Martino, and Guia. The rhythm is climb-descend-roll-climb, with the rolling sections offering UNESCO vineyard panoramas at every turn. The route is designed for experience first, suffering second. Signature challenge: The Muro di Ca' del Poggio — 1.1 km of 12.7% average gradient with a 19% maximum, certified by the Italian Cycling Federation and featured in the Giro d'Italia. It is the kind of climb that sorts riders into those who can hold 300+ watts for 5 minutes and those who cannot. The 19% pitches are the steepest gradient most amateur cyclists will ever ride on paved road. The reward at the top — Prosecco and Scampi at the San Pietro di Feletto ristoro — is the most Italian thing that has ever happened at a cycling aid station. Prosecco Cycling is the only gran fondo in the world where the aid stations serve sparkling wine and shrimp scampi. That sentence alone should tell you what kind of event this is. Starting with Puccini's Nessun Dorma blasting across Valdobbiadene's central piazza while waiters wave Prosecco bottles at 2,700 cyclists, the 100 km route threads through a UNESCO World Heritage vineyard landscape during the grape harvest, climbs the Giro d'Italia's Muro di Ca' del Poggio (19% maximum gradient, 1.1 km of pure punishment), and returns to a town-wide celebration of everything that makes Italian cycling culture irreplaceable. The riding is honest but not brutal. The scenery is extraordinary. The food and wine are non-negotiable. This is not an endurance test — it is Italy's end-of-season cycling party, and everyone is invited. Yes if you want the most uniquely Italian cycling experience available — wine, food, UNESCO scenery, and Puccini at the start line. Yes if EUR58 for a ride through a World Heritage landscape with Prosecco at the aid stations sounds like the best deal in European cycling. Yes if the Muro di Ca' del Poggio (19% max, Giro d'Italia climb) is on your bucket list. Skip if you need 150+ km and 3,000+ meters of climbing — this is 100 km and 1,560m, deliberately approachable. Skip if you want a pure competitive environment — all bike types are welcome and the atmosphere is celebratory.

### Race Across Italy 300
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 205.1 mi | 15,092 ft | Silvi Paese, Teramo, Italy | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-italy-300/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-italy-300.md

A genuine ~330km ultracycling race from the Abruzzo coast into the Apennines -- not a gran fondo, and not really 300km anymore. A non-stop, continuously-timed ultracycling race on open public roads, starting and finishing in Silvi Paese (Teramo province, Abruzzo) and looping from the Adriatic coast up into the Apennine foothills and back. Entry formats include solo supported (with a following support vehicle/crew), supported 2- or 4-rider relay teams, solo self-supported, and self-supported pairs -- the self-supported category bans private outside assistance beyond the organizer's single official time station, though riders may use public shops along the route. Despite the '300' in the name, the 2026 course was published as roughly 330 km with about 4,600 m of climbing. The organizer's own pages don't fully agree with each other (325 km on one Italian page vs. 330 km on the homepage, English page, and 2026 media coverage), no public final GPX was found, and the organizer states the route can change -- so treat 330 km as a published figure, not a measured one. Signature challenge: The single official time station is the only guaranteed support point on course -- solo self-supported riders are otherwise on their own for roughly 330 km and 4,600 m of climbing inside an 18-20 hour window. Race Across Italy 300 (RAI300) is a real, currently active ultracycling race -- its fifth edition ran May 2, 2026, from Silvi Paese in Abruzzo. It's continuously timed, GPS-tracked, has category rankings and a no-drafting rule, and offers solo supported, relay, and self-supported entry formats. What it is not is a gran fondo or mass-participation sportive: there's no expo-style field, no closed-road mass-start atmosphere, and no ranked-vs-alphabetical two-tier format to weigh the way you would with a GFNY event. It also isn't the distance its name implies anymore -- the published course has grown from roughly 299 km at its 2023 (second) edition to roughly 330 km by 2026, while keeping the '300' brand name. Yes, if you're specifically looking for a small-field, continuously-timed ultra-distance race with flexible supported/self-supported formats. No, if you want a mass-participation gran fondo experience -- this isn't one.

### Race Around Austria
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 348 mi | 21,325 ft | St. Georgen im Attergau, Austria (CHALLENGE category route — the flagship Extreme race covers ~2,200km/30,000m around all of Austria) | August | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-around-austria/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-around-austria.md

Legitimate Austrian ultracycling institution (CHALLENGE: 560km/~6,500m; flagship Extreme: ~2,200km/30,000m) — not a conventional gran fondo. Race Around Austria is a family of ultracycling time trials based in St. Georgen im Attergau, Upper Austria. This profile's stored vitals (560km/~6,500m) describe the CHALLENGE category — a single loop around Upper Austria run in a 24-hour-race format, with both supported and unsupported solo options plus team categories. The flagship 'Extreme' race is a much bigger undertaking: a supported, nonstop individual time trial of roughly 2,200 km/30,000m around the entire country through eight Austrian states, including the Styrian wine roads, Großglockner, western Alpine passes, the Inn Valley and Salzburg approaches — with no stages and a clock that never stops. A 1,500 km/~17,500m 'RAA 1500' sits between the two. The 2025 and 2026 WUCA World Championships run on the Extreme course (2,160 km, supported mode). Signature challenge: For the CHALLENGE category this profile describes: a single 560km/~6,500m nonstop loop around Upper Austria within a 24-hour format. For the flagship Extreme race (a distinct, much longer event): the Großglockner and western Alpine passes deep into a nonstop, multi-day national circumnavigation. Race Around Austria is a genuine, well-organized national ultracycling institution — first run in 2009, now hosting the WUCA World Championships on its flagship ~2,200km/30,000m Extreme course, with a 560km/~6,500m CHALLENGE category (this profile's stored distance) and a 1,500km RAA 1500 in between. It is fundamentally an ultracycling time trial festival, not a conventional single-day gran fondo, and its presence in this database under gran_fondo scoring dimensions is a taxonomy mismatch worth flagging rather than silently correcting. Whichever distance you enter, expect extraordinary crew, vehicle and travel burden well beyond what a headline entry fee suggests. Yes if you're specifically seeking an ultracycling challenge with real WUCA-championship pedigree and can absorb the crew/travel costs. Not a fit if you're looking for a single-day, closed-course mass-participation gran fondo experience.

### Race Around Poland
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 2237 mi | 108,596 ft | Poland (national circumnavigation, honorary start Warsaw Royal Wilanów) | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-around-poland/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-around-poland.md

Genuine 3,600km/33,100m national circumnavigation ultra with WUCA championship status — a small serious field, not a mass fondo. A full national circumnavigation ultracycling time trial, honorary-started at Warsaw's Royal Wilanów with a timed start outside the city at Obórki, looping the entire Polish border: the eastern frontier via Włodawa and the Ukrainian border, the Bieszczady and Beskids, Czorsztyn and the Tatras, the Karkonosze/Sudetes, the German border, the Baltic coast, Masuria, and the Lithuania/Belarus border area before returning to Warsaw. Riders start individually at 1-4 minute intervals with drafting prohibited — this is an individual time trial, not a mass-start race. Signature challenge: The full 3,600 km/33,100m loop itself — no single climb or sector defines the race; the challenge is sustaining pace and sleep management across 12 days (solo) through eight distinct Polish regions. Race Around Poland is a real, well-organized extreme ultracycling event — a full 3,600km/33,100m loop of the entire country, first run in 2021 and now hosting a genuine WUCA solo-unsupported world championship category. It offers real progression (150km Challenge 300, 900km 1/4 RAP, 1,800km 1/2 RAP, full 3,600km) and both supported and unsupported options. But with only 100 athletes across every distance in 2026, it should never be presented as a large-field mass-participation fondo — it's a small, serious ultracycling field tackling one of Europe's most complete national circumnavigations, and its own website is inconsistent about exactly how many category types it offers (the rules say seven, the homepage says eight). Yes if you're specifically seeking an extreme ultracycling national-circumnavigation challenge and can commit to the solo or team logistics. Not a fit if you're looking for a conventional single-day, mass-participation gran fondo.

### Tour de Brisbane
Tier 2 | Score: 64/100 | 68.3 mi | 4,068 ft | Brisbane, Queensland, Australia | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-brisbane/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-brisbane.md

Innovative urban gran fondo with excellent logistics but modest climbing and prestige. Tour de Brisbane transforms urban infrastructure into a cycling playground, starting at City Botanic Gardens and weaving through Brisbane's heart on fully closed roads. The course loops through the city center, crosses the Brisbane River via major bridges, navigates through tunnels and expressways, and features five technical turns requiring constant attention. Mount Coot-tha provides the only significant climbing challenge, while the remainder emphasizes urban navigation, tactical positioning, and the unique experience of riding through normally car-filled streets. The finish returns to South Bank Cultural Precinct, completing a comprehensive tour of Brisbane's cycling-friendly infrastructure. Signature challenge: Mount Coot-tha's 2km climb at 9% gradient serves as the race's defining moment, arriving at 67km to determine final positioning. While modest by gran fondo standards, the climb's placement late in the event and its role as the course's only significant elevation gain make it tactically crucial. The summit's panoramic Brisbane views reward the effort before the final descent to South Bank finish. Tour de Brisbane represents a genuinely innovative approach to gran fondo racing—taking the closed-road concept into a vibrant city rather than rural mountains. The event delivers on its promise of fully closed urban infrastructure, excellent logistics, and strong community engagement. However, it's fundamentally a different animal than traditional gran fondos: flatter, shorter, and more about urban cycling experience than climbing or distance. For Australian cyclists or those seeking a unique international cycling destination, it's compelling. For riders chasing elevation, prestige, or classic gran fondo suffering, look elsewhere. Yes if you value unique urban cycling experiences, seek UCI Worlds qualification, or want to explore Brisbane's cycling culture. Skip if you're chasing serious elevation, classic gran fondo suffering, or established prestige—this isn't that event.

### Tour of Pembrokeshire

Severe climbing-to-distance ratio through Pembrokeshire coast and Preseli Hills — over 10,000ft across 105 miles. A JCP Solicitors-titled road sportive based at Ysgol Penrhyn Dewi (Dewi Campus), Millard Park, St Davids, offering three distances through rugged Pembrokeshire coastline, narrow country lanes and the Preseli Hills. The organizer (BCS Events, formerly Big Cow Sports) does not publish a definitive list of named climbs, but the Epic route's severity for its distance (over 10,000 ft across 105 miles) is well documented by riders and media. Signature challenge: The cumulative climbing of the Preseli Hills and coastal lanes on the Epic route — severe for a UK sportive of this distance, with exposed weather adding to the difficulty. Tour of Pembrokeshire is a well-organized, currently active Welsh road sportive with three genuinely differentiated distances — the 105-mile Epic (over 10,000 ft of climbing), the 60-mile Classic, and the 25-mile Community ride. The Epic's climbing-to-distance ratio is unusually severe for a UK sportive, and the Pembrokeshire coastline and Preseli Hills scenery back it up. The organizer publishes only threshold elevation figures ('over 10,000 ft') rather than precise surveyed totals, and 2026 participation numbers weren't independently confirmed at the time of this review — but there's no sign of cancellation or decline, and the event has real multi-year continuity under BCS Events. Yes if you want one of the harder one-day UK sportives for its distance, with distinctive coastal scenery. Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/velomediane-criquielion/
