18 named Ardennes climbs and a real namesake — but a randonnée, not a ranked race, with an uncorroborated elevation claim. A La Roche-en-Ardenne loop through the deep Ardennes: out through Vecmont, Ortho, Warempage, Wibrin, Chabrehez and Maboge, back through La Roche, then a second sweep through Samrée, Manhay, Roche-à-Frêne, Rideux, Fisenne, Beffe and Dochamps before finishing where it started. The Grand Challenge is marketed at 165 km, though the organizer's own detailed itinerary and independent route tools put the actual mapped course closer to 167 km. Elevation is where the numbers diverge: the organizer states 3,570 m for 2026, while a route-engine recalculation of the same published 167 km trace comes in around 3,121 m (a separate ~3,200 m figure circulating from a 2024 rider's ride report belongs to a different 171 km/19-climb edition of the course, not a second measurement of the current route) — treat 3,570 m as the organizer-stated figure that is not independently corroborated. The course itself lists 18 named climbs, including the Mur de la Vélomédiane, Saint-Quoilin, Parc à Gibier, Haussire, Roche-à-Frêne and Rideux Nord. Signature challenge: The Mur de la Vélomédiane — the event's namesake wall climb, one of 18 named ascents packed into the Grand Challenge's second half. The Vélomédiane Claudy Criquiélion is a 37-edition-deep Ardennes cyclosportive named for Claude 'Claudy' Criquiélion, the 1984 professional road World Champion, who was the event's patron from its 1989 founding — the name predates his 2015 death and is not a posthumous rebrand. The 2026 Grand Challenge lists 18 named climbs on a course marketed at 165 km, and the organizer's elevation figure (3,570 m) is not independently corroborated: a route-engine recalculation of the same 167 km published trace gives 3,121 m. It's technically a timed randonnée rather than a ranked race — under the post-2019 format, times are published alphabetically, not as an official classification — and the organizer's own course-option distances are inconsistent across its current 2026 pages. Yes, if you want a decades-deep Ardennes climbing test at an approachable price. Go in expecting a timed randonnée with alphabetical results, not a competitive classification, and treat the 3,570m elevation figure as organizer-stated rather than independently surveyed.

### Around the Bay in a Day
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 137 mi | 2,812 ft | Melbourne, Victoria, Australia | October | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/around-the-bay-in-a-day/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/around-the-bay-in-a-day.md

220 km around Port Phillip Bay with a ferry crossing and a Beach Road finish — a Melbourne cycling institution since 1993. A flat, coastal circumnavigation of Port Phillip Bay on sealed roads and paths, punctuated by a 40-minute ferry crossing between Queenscliff and Sorrento. The Classic route runs anti-clockwise: west from Albert Park over the West Gate Bridge, through Werribee and Little River to Geelong, along the Bellarine Peninsula to Queenscliff, across the water by ferry to Sorrento, then back along the Mornington Peninsula and Beach Road to the finish at Albert Park. The terrain is relentlessly flat — the challenge is distance, wind, and endurance rather than gradient. The scenery shifts from urban Melbourne to industrial western suburbs, open farmland, Geelong's waterfront, the coastal Bellarine Peninsula, and finally the iconic Beach Road run home. Signature challenge: The sheer distance — 220 km of predominantly flat coastal riding with little shelter from the wind. The western shore between Werribee and Geelong is where Around the Bay reveals itself: in a headwind, this section is a war of attrition. The ferry provides a reprieve before the return along the Mornington Peninsula and Beach Road. Around the Bay is not the hardest ride in Australia. It is not the hilliest, the most technical, or the most remote. It is one of the most inclusive and culturally embedded cycling events on the continent. Riders circle Port Phillip Bay on a single Sunday in October, cross by ferry, and return along Beach Road. The predominantly flat terrain makes the 220 km Classic an endurance problem rather than a climbing contest. Yes if you value community over competition and want a supported 220 km endurance challenge on predominantly flat coastal roads. Skip if you need sustained climbing, technical terrain, or a competitive racing environment.

Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/best-buddies-challenge-miami.md

A 50-rider charity peloton with Grand Tour champions on the guest list — the price of admission is a $10,000 fundraising ask, not a finish time. Best Buddies Challenge: Miami is a fully supported charity fundraising ride, not a competitive gran fondo. The Saturday road Challenge offers 100-mile and 75-mile options, starting and finishing at the Four Seasons Hotel Miami (1435 Brickell Avenue). The course loops through Brickell/Downtown Miami, across the Julia Tuttle Causeway to South Beach and Miami Beach, north to Bal Harbour, Haulover Beach and Aventura, and separately across the Rickenbacker Causeway to Virginia Key and Key Biscayne, plus Coral Gables and Calle Ocho — five total waterway crossings. Riders move together in a single rolling, police-escorted peloton — the organizer describes it as a 'presidential-style' enclosure with road and intersection closures, support vehicles, medical support, and mechanics — rather than a full-day closure of every road on course; a stated minimum group pace of 18 mph is required to stay with the peloton. A separately priced Sunday gravel event (54/28/16-mile loops from DiMare Farms in the Redlands) also exists as an add-on but is a different ride, not a shorter option for the Saturday road Challenge. No official numerical elevation figure is published for the road course — treat it as essentially flat, with only bridge/causeway crossings providing meaningful rises. Signature challenge: There is no terrain-based signature challenge — the test is holding the enclosed peloton's required 18 mph minimum pace across roughly 100 flat, humid South Florida miles, not any single climb or feature. Best Buddies Challenge: Miami is a small, tightly capped (50-rider) charity fundraising ride benefiting Best Buddies International's intellectual and developmental disability programs — not a competitive gran fondo in any real sense. Riders move together in a rolling, police-escorted peloton at a required minimum pace, not a scored race, along a flat Miami/Miami Beach/Key Biscayne loop starting and finishing at the Four Seasons Hotel Miami. What sets it apart is a genuinely exceptional pro-cycling guest list — Chris Froome, Alberto Contador, and Sir Bradley Wiggins are advertised on the 2026 roster (not yet confirmed as having ridden), while Mark Cavendish (the Tour's stage-win record holder) and Geraint Thomas (2018 Tour de France winner) are documented as having actually ridden in 2024. The real barrier to entry isn't fitness, it's fundraising: the Road Challenge tier requires a $250 registration fee plus a $10,000 fundraising commitment, with Best Buddies charging the difference to your card if you fall short two weeks out. Course elevation is unverifiable and should not be trusted at a specific figure — this is a flat South Florida ride with a few bridge and causeway rises, nothing more. Yes if you can meet the fundraising commitment and want a well-supported, flat South Florida ride alongside a genuinely elite pro-cycling guest list. No if you're looking for a scored, competitive event — there isn't one here.

The route mimics the professional race course, with Challambra Crescent as the decisive climb. The Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Ride trades on two things: a legendary name and a legendary road. It delivers on both. The Great Ocean Road provides the visual payoff, and the Geelong-Surf Coast region's cycling culture creates a genuine festival atmosphere. The ride itself is moderate by gran fondo standards — 153 km with 1,600m of climbing won't break experienced riders — but the experience transcends the physical challenge. Yes if riding the same roads as WorldTour professionals appeals to you. Yes if the Great Ocean Road and the Cadel Evans connection are meaningful to your cycling fandom. ### Gran Fondo San Diego

Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-san-diego.md

Established since 2009, three-distance San Diego century with a timed Japatul Road KOM — open roads, not a closed-course race. The Gran Fondo San Diego features the classic 'Great Western Loop' through East County's scenic backcountry, combining rolling terrain with strategic climbing challenges. The route showcases San Diego's diverse athletic landscape and natural beauty, transitioning from urban downtown San Diego through suburban areas into the rugged backcountry before returning to the waterfront finish. Signature challenge: The timed Japatul Road climb at mile 36, which determines KOM/QOM winners across eight age categories and represents the event's primary competitive climbing test. Gran Fondo San Diego is a real, continuously run event since 2009, now heading into its 19th annual edition in 2027. Three well-differentiated distances (100/60/35 miles), a waterfront Ruocco Park base, and a timed Japatul Road KOM/QOM segment give it genuine structure without pretending the whole ride is a closed-road race — it isn't. The event bills itself as 'open start / no mass start,' which is broadly true but slightly oversold: riders still leave in staggered blocks by route (7:15/7:30/7:45am), obey traffic signals, and ride single file on public roads open to normal traffic. The organizer's own materials also disagree with the City's permit on the exact closure time (5:00pm vs. 5:30pm) and with themselves on whether the long route is 100 or 101 miles — small inconsistencies worth knowing before race day. Yes if you want a well-organized, multi-distance Southern California century with real event infrastructure and a fun waterfront festival. Zadar Granfondo Falkensteiner Borik is a genuine, currently active resort-hosted road fondo now in its seventh year (first run 2019, no 2020 edition), combining Adriatic coastal riding out to the Vir bridge with inland Zadar County climbing. Yes for a well-supported, capped-field Adriatic coastal ride at a fair price — just verify the actual course distance and road-closure scope directly with the organizer beforehand.

GranFondo San Sebastián is the rare amateur event that inherits genuine pro racing DNA. ### Hong Kong Cyclothon
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 31.1 mi | — | Tsim Sha Tsui East, Kowloon, Hong Kong | October | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/hong-kong-cyclothon/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/hong-kong-cyclothon.md

Hong Kong hands cyclists its bridges and tunnels for a day — when the event actually happens. The Hong Kong Cyclothon is built around closed-road access to infrastructure cyclists cannot otherwise ride: Tsing Ma Bridge, Ting Kau Bridge, Stonecutters Bridge, and a series of highway tunnels across the New Territories and Kowloon. The latest published mass-ride program (2024/planned 2025) offered two distances: a 50km ride ("four tunnels, three bridges") running via the Cheung Tsing/Cheung Ching Tunnel, Tsing Ma Bridge, Ting Kau Bridge, Nam Wan Tunnel, Stonecutters Bridge, Eagle's Nest Tunnel, and Sha Tin Heights Tunnel; and a shorter 32km ride ("two tunnels, two bridges") via Cheung Ching Tunnel, Nam Wan Tunnel, Ting Kau Bridge, and Stonecutters Bridge. Both start near the Empire Centre on Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui East, and finish at the Jordan Road flyover in Kowloon. A separate, genuinely competitive UCI 1.1-class professional race runs alongside the mass rides — a different field and format from the closed-road public ride. No official source publishes an exact measured distance or elevation total for either public route; treat 50km/32km as organizer-branded nominal distances, and course details for the still-tentative 2026 edition have not yet been finalized. Signature challenge: Closed-road passage across Tsing Ma Bridge and Stonecutters Bridge is the real draw — and the real risk. Hong Kong's rules allow rerouting or shortening the course based on measured bridge wind speeds; in 2022 the 50km ride was cut to roughly 36km mid-cycle when winds exceeded 35km/h and organizers pulled Tsing Ma and Ting Kau from the route. The Hong Kong Cyclothon is an HKTB-organized mass-participation ride offering closed-road access to Tsing Ma Bridge, Stonecutters Bridge, and several road tunnels normally off-limits to cyclists, bundled with a UCI 1.1 professional race that drew nearly 100 pros across 14 teams (spanning WorldTour, ProTeam, Continental, and national squads) in 2023. It also has a rocky history: cancelled in 2019 (social unrest), skipped entirely in 2020-21 (COVID), cancelled again in January 2022 (COVID restrictions), and cancelled again for 2025 following the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po. When it has run, it's drawn real numbers — 6,000 riders and 20,000 spectators in its 2024 record edition, with Chris Froome among the 50km field. But our prior course description invented specifics no official source supports: a 'Tsing Ma Bridge Wind Tunnel' nickname, a fabricated 1,200ft elevation figure, a 'back-to-back' tunnel sequence that isn't how the tunnels are actually ordered on course, and sensory details (dim lighting, echoing packs, heat spikes) with no traceable source. None of that was needed — the actual course and cancellation history speak for themselves. Yes if you want closed-road access to Tsing Ma, Stonecutters, and Ting Kau bridges plus a real UCI-race atmosphere, and you're comfortable with genuine schedule risk — this event has been cancelled or skipped in five of the last seven years. Confirm the current year's date and route before committing travel.

### Le Race
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 62.1 mi | 6,070 ft | Christchurch to Akaroa, Canterbury, New Zealand | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/le-race/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/le-race.md

New Zealand's one-day road classic. 100 km across an extinct volcano. Olympic medalists in the Hall of Fame. Six hundred riders. One French harbour town. A volcanic crossing, not a circuit. Le Race is a 100 km point-to-point race that traverses Banks Peninsula — the eroded remnant of two extinct shield volcanoes — from Christchurch to Akaroa. The course climbs from sea level to the Port Hills ridgeline, traverses exposed summit roads with 360-degree panoramas, descends to the Little River valley, climbs back up to the Hilltop crater rim, and plunges down to the French harbour village of Akaroa at sea level. The terrain is relentless: you are climbing, descending, or fighting wind on an exposed ridge for virtually the entire 100 km. There is almost no flat road. The course rewards climbers, punishes poor descenders, and exposes anyone who has not prepared for crosswinds on volcanic ridgelines. Signature challenge: The Hilltop climb is the centrepiece, but Le Race's true challenge is the accumulation: Dyers Pass, Summit Road crosswinds, Gebbies Pass descent, the Hilltop grind, more Summit Road, and the steep Long Bay descent — all compressed into 100 km with nearly 1,900 metres of climbing. There is no recovery. There is no flat road. The course is designed by volcanic geology, not by committee, and it does not care about your legs. Michael Vink's course record of 2:37 means averaging nearly 40 km/h with 1,900m of climbing — a mark that shows how brutally honest this course is. Le Race is New Zealand's one-day road cycling classic — 100 kilometres from Cathedral Square in earthquake-rebuilt Christchurch to the French harbour village of Akaroa, across the crater rim of an extinct volcanic complex that juts into the Pacific Ocean. The route climbs Dyers Pass out of the city, traverses the exposed Summit Road with panoramic views of Lyttelton Harbour and the Southern Alps, descends to Little River, then grinds back up to the Hilltop — 30-50 minutes of sustained climbing to the Banks Peninsula crater rim — before plunging down to the French-flavoured finish. The Hall of Fame includes Olympic medalists, world champions, and Commonwealth Games winners. Nate Pringle's 2024 victory — cramping on the final climb, squeezing out one last attack to hold off the chasing bunch — is the kind of desperate, decisive racing this course produces. Six hundred riders line up each March for New Zealand's most prestigious day on a road bike. Yes if you want New Zealand's most prestigious one-day road cycling experience with genuine competitive racing on a world-class course. Yes if you are drawn to volcanic landscapes, dramatic coastal ridgelines, and a finish in the most charming village in New Zealand. Skip if you need a large-field mass-participation atmosphere — this is 600 riders, not 6,000. Skip if the 24+ hour journey to Christchurch from the Northern Hemisphere is a dealbreaker.

### L'Etape Brasil by Tour de France
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 66 mi | 7,546 ft | Campos do Jordao, Sao Paulo State, Brazil (flagship stage; series also visits Cunha and Rio de Janeiro) | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-brazil/

Latin America's biggest amateur cycling event: ASO-organized, closed-road mountain racing through Brazil's Serra da Mantiqueira with Tour de France classification jerseys and 3,500 riders. Mountain road course through the Serra da Mantiqueira -- Brazil's 'Swiss Alps.' The 107 km long course packs 2,300m of climbing into a compact route that winds through pine forests, mountain ridges, and the scenic countryside surrounding Campos do Jordao. The terrain is relentlessly hilly: there is very little flat riding between the climbs. Gradients alternate between sustained 5-7% drags and punchy 10%+ ramps. The course starts and finishes in the Capivari district, creating a natural amphitheater for the start/finish spectacle. Signature challenge: The accumulated climbing density: 2,300m of elevation gain packed into 107 km means you are climbing for approximately 60% of the race. There is no extended flat recovery between climbs. Every descent transitions directly into the next ascent. The compact, relentless nature of the climbing separates this from longer, flatter gran fondos. L'Etape Brasil brings ASO's Tour de France franchise to South America with impressive execution -- 107 km of closed-road mountain climbing through the Serra da Mantiqueira, classification jerseys, Shimano support, and 3,500+ riders chasing yellow in the 'Brazilian Switzerland.' Now in its second decade, this is the largest amateur cycling event in Latin America, and it runs with the professional-grade infrastructure you expect from the Tour de France brand. Campos do Jordao delivers 2,300m of genuine climbing in a charming mountain resort town where dawn starts at 5C give way to warm afternoon celebrations. The Brazilian cycling community brings infectious energy that makes the event experience genuinely special. The limitation is scale and context: this is a franchise event, not the original, and the 107 km course is shorter than the French edition's 170 km. The competitive field is strong domestically but thin internationally. What it does brilliantly is bring world-class cycling event production to a growing market that deserves it. Yes if you want Tour de France atmosphere at a fraction of European pricing. Yes if you are based in South America and want the most professionally organized sportive on the continent. Yes if 2,300m of mountain climbing on closed roads through stunning scenery sounds like your kind of weekend. Skip if you want the prestige of the French original -- this is a franchise, not the main event. Skip if you need deep international competition -- the field is overwhelmingly domestic.

### London to Brighton Bike Ride
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 54 mi | 2,500 ft | London to Brighton, England, UK | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/london-to-brighton/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/london-to-brighton.md

54 miles from London to the sea. The ride that defined mass-participation charity cycling. Ditchling Beacon is the final exam. A 54-mile journey from the heart of London to the English seaside, crossing four counties and climbing over the South Downs. The route begins in the urban bustle of Clapham Common, transitions through South London's suburbs, and quickly enters the green countryside of Surrey. Rolling country lanes through the Weald of Sussex provide the middle miles — undulating terrain through small villages, past farms, and along hedgerow-lined roads. The final 10 miles deliver the ride's dramatic crescendo: the approach to Ditchling Beacon across open downland, the brutal 1-mile climb to the summit of the South Downs, the breathtaking view of the sea from the top, and the fast, euphoric descent into Brighton to finish on Madeira Drive along the seafront. Signature challenge: Ditchling Beacon — 1 mile at 9% average with a 16% maximum gradient. The most famous climb in southern England, tackled by 15,000+ riders every June. Spectators cheering, riders walking, and the view of the sea from the top. This single mile defines the entire ride. The London to Brighton Bike Ride did not invent cycling from a capital city to the coast. But it did more than any other event to establish mass-participation charity cycling as a concept that millions of people now take for granted. Since 1976, over 650,000 riders have left Clapham Common on a Sunday morning in June, rolled through the green lanes of Surrey and Sussex, dragged themselves up Ditchling Beacon, and descended in triumph to Brighton seafront. Fifty million pounds raised for the British Heart Foundation. One climb that has become the most famous in southern England. And a finish on the seafront that feels like every good thing that cycling can deliver — exhaustion, achievement, community, and the sea. This is not a race — it is a rite of passage. Yes if you want to experience the most iconic one-day charity cycling event in Europe. Yes if Ditchling Beacon is on your bucket list. Yes if you believe that 15,000 people sharing a road and a purpose is what cycling should feel like. Skip if you need timing chips, competition, or serious distance. The 54 miles will not test a strong cyclist's fitness — but the experience will stay with you regardless.

A challenging, undulating cross-border gran fondo through the Sudetes mountains. Sudety Tour merits consideration for experienced gran fondo cyclists seeking elevation, technical terrain, and cultural immersion. ### Tour de l'Île de Montréal
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 31 mi | 500 ft | Montreal, Quebec, Canada | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-lile-de-montreal/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/tour-de-lile-de-montreal.md

25,000 riders circle the island of Montreal on car-free streets. A former Guinness World Record holder, now in its 41st year. The Tour de l'Île de Montréal is not about the cycling. It is about 25,000 people on bicycles claiming an entire island for a day. Montreal — a city that lives and breathes cycling culture — shuts down its streets and hands them to riders of every age, every ability, every bicycle type imaginable. The ride is flat, short, and easy. The experience is singular.

You will see Montreal the way it was meant to be seen: from a bicycle, in late spring, with the St. Lawrence glittering beside you and 25,000 strangers sharing the same improbable joy. The route circumnavigates the island at river level, threading through neighborhoods that range from gentrified to gritty, from leafy suburban streets to industrial canal banks. Children ride alongside retirees. Cargo bikes alongside carbon road machines. The atmosphere is festive and communal — more block party than bike ride.

This event once held the Guinness World Record as the largest gathering of cyclists on Earth, with 45,000 riders sustained for six consecutive years in the 1990s. It helped transform Montreal into North America's most bike-friendly city. At $30-36 USD entry, it is one of the best-value cycling events anywhere. Do this ride for the experience of Montreal, not the experience of cycling. Come for the ride, stay for the poutine. You do not race the Tour de l'Île — you ride it. Yes if you want to experience Montreal from a bicycle on car-free streets with 25,000 other cyclists. Yes if you want a family-friendly, affordable, superbly organized mass-participation event. Yes if you want to visit one of the world's great cycling cities during its most beautiful season. Skip if you need athletic challenge, competitive racing, elevation, or technical terrain.

### TransAtlanticWay
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 1504 mi | 88,583 ft | Cork/Kinsale to Derry, Ireland | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/transatlanticway/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/transatlanticway.md

Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way, ridden solo and self-supported over 2,400+ km — a real ultra, not a gran fondo. TransAtlanticWay is a self-supported, continuously timed road ultra following Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way, not a mass-participation gran fondo. The flagship Cú Chulainn route runs north from Cork/Kinsale through West Cork, Kerry, Clare, Galway/Connemara, Mayo, Sligo, and Donegal to finish in Derry — organizer materials are internally inconsistent on the exact distance (the homepage says 2,500km, the route page says 2,400km), with the 2026 GPS tracker recording 2,420.24km for riders who completed the full course. Three shorter routes also run point-to-point along the same corridor: Setanta (~1,700km), and two roughly 1,000km halves — Cean beag Ó dheas (Kinsale to Galway) and Cean beag Ó thuaidh (Galway to Derry). Total elevation gain has no single official current figure; independent rider GPS data across editions clusters in the high-20,000-meter range, but varies by exact route and measurement device. The organizer describes the roads as paved throughout, though rider reports consistently note broken pavement, very narrow lanes, repeated short ramps over 20%, and occasional gravel sections — a road-oriented ultra or gravel bike with wide tires and low gearing suits the course better than a standard road-race setup. Route direction and specific segments shift year to year (the 2025 edition, for example, bypassed part of Donegal due to a road rally), so individual landmarks should be read as characteristic route features, not fixed annual waypoints. Signature challenge: There is no single climb that defines TransAtlanticWay — the challenge is the format itself: a multi-day, self-supported effort along an entire Atlantic coastline, managing sleep, resupply, and mechanical problems alone between two staffed checkpoints, with mandatory GPS tracking and no private support crew allowed. TransAtlanticWay is an established self-supported road ultra along Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way, now in its 11th edition (2026) and founded in 2016 by ultra-distance rider Adrian O'Sullivan. It belongs in the Transcontinental Race/TransAm lineage — multi-day, continuously GPS-tracked, no private support crew or drafting outside registered pairs, riders sourcing their own sleep and food between two staffed checkpoints. That is the core problem with how this profile has sat in this database: TransAtlanticWay is not a gran fondo in any real sense — riders start in waves rather than one shared field, there's no aid-station-supported single day, and no bunch riding (drafting is banned outside registered pairs). It's an entirely different kind of event, and describing it with gran-fondo vocabulary risks a rider showing up expecting supported infrastructure that doesn't exist. On its own terms: field growth from 30 riders (2016) to 160+ (2018), organizer-provided GPS tracking and checkpoints, and consistent completion data through the 2026 edition. The organizer's own course numbers are inconsistent (2,400km vs 2,500km on the same site) and no official elevation figure exists — independent GPS data puts the climbing in the high-20,000-meter range, but that's an estimate, not a certified total. Yes if you're an experienced self-supported ultra-distance rider looking for a Transcontinental-lineage event on remote Irish coastal terrain. No if you're looking for a mass-participation gran fondo with aid stations and bunch riding — that's not this event's format at all.

### Vatternrundan
Tier 2 | Score: 63/100 | 196 mi | 4,593 ft | Motala, Östergötland, Sweden | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/vatternrundan/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/vatternrundan.md

315 km around Lake Vättern through the Swedish midsummer night. 22,000 riders. No results. No rankings. Pure cycling. Vätternrundan is not a race. It has never been a race. Since 1966, when a sports medicine physician and a bike shop owner sent 334 riders around Lake Vättern to study what happens to the human body over 315 km, it has been a personal challenge wrapped in a Nordic ritual. There are no results. No rankings. No prizes. There is only the lake, the midsummer night, and the 22,000 other riders sharing the road.

The sun barely sets — the sky glows amber and indigo through the night hours, never reaching true darkness this close to the solstice. You ride through sleeping villages, past midsummer bonfires, past fields of barley lit by twilight. At midnight, you eat hot soup in a Swedish countryside service station with strangers who will become friends by dawn. At 3:30 AM, the sun rises over the eastern shore and you ride the final 80 km home to Motala with the lake on your left and 230 km in your legs.

It is 315 km of gently rolling road around a lake. And it is one of the most extraordinary experiences in cycling. Yes if you want an ultra-distance experience unlike anything else in cycling — the midsummer night is genuinely magical. Yes if you value community and shared adventure over competition. Yes if you are pursuing the Swedish Classic Circuit. Skip if you want to race — there are no results. Skip if you need dramatic terrain — this is flat Swedish farmland around a lake. Skip if remote Scandinavian logistics are a dealbreaker.

### BalatonFondo
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 110 mi | 5,630 ft | Balatonfüred and the Balaton Uplands, Hungary | May | gran_fondo

A growing Hungarian fondo through the Balaton Uplands — real climbing, but not the lake-circling ride its name implies. Contrary to what the 'Balaton' branding suggests, this is not a lake-circumnavigation event — the Granfondo and Mediofondo start and finish in Balatonfüred, with a neutral rollout to Tihany before the timed racing start, then a circuit north/northwest through the Balaton Uplands (Tótvázsony, Kab-hegy/Kab Hill, Hegymagas, Tagyon, Dörgicse, Mencshely, Vászoly) before returning to Balatonfüred. It does not traverse the lake's southern shore. The 2026 route was substantially redesigned and lengthened from 2025 (134km/Granfondo) to 177km/1,716m — a real, meaningful change riders comparing past reviews to the current course should know about. Signature challenge: The Balaton Uplands climbing circuit (Tótvázsony, Kab-hegy, Hegymagas, Tagyon) north of the lake — rolling hill terrain rather than a flat lakeside cruise, despite the event's lake-branded name. Balatonfondo (currently sponsor-branded 'KÉSZ Group Balatonfondo') is an established Hungarian gran fondo now in its fourth edition (founded 2023), listed on the Hungarian Cycling Federation's official calendar. Despite the lake-branded name, it is not a Lake Balaton circumnavigation: the Granfondo and Mediofondo start and finish in Balatonfüred and loop through the Balaton Uplands to the north, never touching the lake's southern shore. The course has also changed between recent editions — the 2026 Granfondo runs 177km, up from 134km in 2025 — so expectations based on a past edition's distance shouldn't be assumed to carry over. Consider it if you want an established regional European fondo with real hill terrain and don't mind that it isn't a Lake Balaton circumnavigation. Confirm the current year's course and distance directly — both have changed significantly year to year.

### Eroica California
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 107.3 mi | — | Cambria, Central Coast, California, USA | September | sportive
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/eroica-california/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/eroica-california.md

California's L'Eroica outpost — genuine Central Coast dirt and wine-country stops, retired after 2023. Eroica California (also called L'Eroica California) was a vintage-bicycle heritage ride based in Cambria on California's Central Coast — mixed paved and unpaved terrain, not the purely paved sportive this profile previously described. The final-era Heroic route ran approximately 107.3 miles/172.7km with roughly 20-30% unpaved sections (an estimate; no official surface breakdown was published for that specific route). It combined paved Highway 1 coastal riding between Cambria and Cayucos with genuine dirt climbing on Santa Rita Creek Road and Kiler Canyon, plus the paved Old Creek Road climb and the mixed gravel/paved Cypress Mountain climb and Santa Rosa Road descent. A shorter Santa Lucia route had a verified breakdown of 56 paved miles plus roughly 16 gravel miles (about 78% paved/22% gravel). Wine-country stops at Halter Ranch, Cass Winery, and Olea Farm were regular features. Riders on the vintage Classic used pre-1987 (or period-style) steel bicycles with downtube shifters and toe clips, per the general Eroica standard — though California's on-course enforcement of those rules was reportedly looser than the written standard, per participant testimony. A separate, co-located modern-bike ride, NOVA Eroica California (launched 2017), ran on Saturdays with road/gravel/cyclocross bikes and timed sectors; it never replaced the vintage Classic — both ran the same weekend through 2023. The event was last held September 15-17, 2023, and has not returned since. This profile now describes a discontinued event, not a bookable one. Signature challenge: Cypress Mountain — roughly 4.2 miles climbing to 1,083 feet with sections over 10%, followed by the long Santa Rosa Road descent that starts on gravel before transitioning to pavement — was the course's defining mixed-surface test, alongside Santa Rita Creek Road and Kiler Canyon. There is no current Eroica California to rate. The event's last verified edition ran September 15-17, 2023 — its 7th year — after COVID cancelled the 2020 and 2021 editions and the event returned for 2022 and 2023. The planned 2024 edition was cancelled outright with no reason given, and no edition has run since; California does not appear on Eroica's official global calendar for 2025 or 2026. Cambria Tourism Board minutes from 2022 point to real operational strain behind the scenes — an event coordinator who left before the event, reported unprofitability, and time-zone coordination friction with Italy-based Eroica management — credible contributing circumstances, though no source formally confirms them as the reason for the final shutdown. When it ran, it was a genuine vintage-bicycle heritage ride with real Central Coast dirt (Santa Rita Creek Road, Kiler Canyon) alongside paved Highway 1 and inland climbs, plus a co-located modern-bike NOVA Eroica ride — a real event with real terrain, not a marketing shell. An independent, unaffiliated ride called Central Coast Classico launched in the same region in April 2026, but it is not an Eroica-branded event and should not be treated as this event's continuation. No — this event does not currently exist. If you want the experience it offered, look at the independent Central Coast Classico, which picked up similar Cambria-area terrain in 2026 without the Eroica branding.

### Gran Fondo Argentina
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 75.8 mi | — | Parque Sarmiento, Buenos Aires, Argentina | October | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-argentina/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-argentina.md

Buenos Aires opens its motorways for a day — a young, fast-growing closed-road fondo, not (yet) an internationally ranked one. A fast, predominantly flat closed-road urban gran fondo entirely within Buenos Aires city limits — not a pampas or rural fondo. For 2026 (the event's 4th edition), the start and finish move to Parque Sarmiento (Av. Dr. Ricardo Balbín 4750). The 122km long course and 46km short course run on ordinary paved city arterials and motorways — current official regulations name General Paz, Perito Moreno, 25 de Mayo, 9 de Julio Sur, Illia, and Cantilo/Lugones — fully closed to motor traffic and monitored by the city's traffic-camera network — though a fully settled 2026 turn-by-turn sequence was not independently confirmed at research time. Finishers ride a ceremonial lap on the Parque Sarmiento cycling track for the medal ceremony. The prior (2025) edition started from Puerto Madero and passed Paseo del Bajo, the Costanera, and areas near the Monumental and Vélez stadiums — those landmarks should not be assumed to carry over to the 2026 route given the new start/finish. Signature challenge: There is no climbing test here — the challenge is pack speed and positioning across a fast, flat, fully closed motorway network that's normally off-limits to cyclists, not terrain. Gran Fondo Argentina is a young (founded 2023) closed-road mass-participation ride through Buenos Aires with documented city-government backing and reported growth from roughly 2,300 riders in its first edition to an official city-government-reported 4,000 by its third. It is not part of the UCI Gran Fondo World Series or the UCI's international calendar — that distinction, as of 2026, belongs to Gran Fondo Siete Lagos in Patagonia, not this event. This is a national urban event, not an internationally ranked one. The organizer's own course pages are also inconsistent: the current 122km long-course page lists both '323m vertical' and '233m/1,060ft elevation' on the same page, numbers that don't reconcile, so we're not carrying forward a single elevation figure we can't verify. Buenos Aires is genuinely flat, and the appeal here is riding motorways normally closed to cyclists in a full mass-start peloton, not a scenic or climbing test. Yes if you want a flat, fast, closed-road city ride through normally-inaccessible Buenos Aires motorways with real government backing and growing fields. Skip it if you're chasing UCI-series prestige or scenic/climbing terrain — neither is what this race offers.

Ankara's growing capital-city fondo — a short urban climb, then long, exposed steppe roads, not a mountain test. A capital-city gran fondo, not a mountain-climbing one. Signature challenge: The city-centre climbing section past Atakule early in the route — the only sustained, tactically important climbing on an otherwise rolling, exposed course. Gran Fondo Başkent (Maximum Gran Fondo Başkent) is a legitimate Turkish amateur road event — its fifth edition runs in 2026 (founded 2022), on the Turkish Cycling Federation's official Gran Fondo calendar, and it has drawn roughly 1,000-1,200 riders per edition since its 2022 launch, with international representation growing from about 25 to 34 countries even as overall turnout has stayed flat rather than climbed. Yes if you want a well-organized, federation-backed Turkish road fondo with real international turnout and don't need sustained climbing. ### Gran Fondo Eilat
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 87 mi | 4,570 ft | Eilat, Negev Desert, Israel | December | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-eilat/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-eilat.md

A real Negev desert climb and long rolling 'bathtubs' — a serious ~500-rider Israeli fondo with an interrupted history, not a four-figure international one. A genuine Arava/Negev desert route, but mixed rather than continuously mountainous. The 140 km course opens with about 52 fast, flat kilometers on the Arava Road (Route 90) before the principal climb — Mt. Ayit/Ketura toward Neot Smadar, roughly 4.2 km at 6.5% average with pitches to 14%. From there, riders face about 60 km of exposed, rolling hills on Route 12, locally nicknamed the 'bathtubs' for their repeated short climbs and descents, before a finish around Netafim Pass/Mount Yoash and a neutralized descent back toward Eilat (only 116.8 km/1,350 m of the full 140 km is competitively timed). Feed stations sit at Neot Smadar, Camp Shagor on Route 12, and the finish; team cars are prohibited and neutral support runs front and rear instead. Signature challenge: The Route 12 'bathtubs' — roughly 60 km of exposed, repeatedly rolling desert hills after the Mt. Ayit/Ketura climb, where accumulated fatigue and Arava wind do more damage than any single gradient. Gran Fondo Eilat is a legitimate Israeli road event through genuinely dramatic Arava/Negev desert terrain — closed roads, electronic timing, prize money, federation involvement and leading Israeli racers all real. But the database's prior figures overstated it on two fronts: the course is 140 km/1,393 m, not 136.8 km/1,400 m, and the field has run around 500 in the 2022 and 2025 editions (the 2021 launch was smaller, roughly 200), not the prior '1000+' figure, which had no supporting source. The event has also had a broken run: launched 2021, a second edition in 2022, then a gap, a cancelled 2023 UCI Gran Fondo World Series debut due to the war, and a 2025 revival under new organizer Shvoong Sport Events. It is not currently on the UCI Gran Fondo World Series calendar despite past ambitions to join it. Yes if you want a genuine December desert fondo with a real climb and closed-road organization, and don't mind a smaller field and a race that's had gaps in its calendar. Confirm the current year's dates directly with the organizer given the event's history of schedule disruption.

### De Rosa Granfondo Firenze
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 83 mi | 6,562 ft | Florence, Tuscany, Italy | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-firenze/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/gran-fondo-firenze.md

Over the Ponte Vecchio and into the Tuscan hills — Florence turns its Renaissance streets into a starting grid and the Mugello into your proving ground. There are gran fondos with bigger climbs. There are gran fondos with bigger fields. There are gran fondos with more prestige and deeper history. But there is no gran fondo that starts where this one starts. You line up at Piazzale Michelangelo with the entire Florence skyline below you — Brunelleschi's Dome, the Palazzo Vecchio, the Arno catching the morning light — and then you ride down into it. You cross the Ponte Vecchio on a bicycle. Let that sink in. The most photographed bridge in Italy, a medieval jewelers' row that has spanned the Arno since 1345, and you are riding across it in lycra with a race number pinned to your jersey. After the city releases you, the Tuscan hills take over: the climb to Fiesole through cypress groves, the Mugello's rolling countryside dotted with olive groves and stone farmhouses, the feed stations where the volunteers pour you wine alongside the energy drink.

The De Rosa Granfondo Firenze is not Italy's hardest ride or its most famous. It does not have the Muro di Sormano's 27% gradient or the Maratona's 4,000m of Dolomite climbing. What it has is Florence — a city that has defined Western civilization's relationship with beauty for six centuries — as both its starting line and its backdrop. The Via Salviati finish, where Rui Costa won the 2013 World Championship road race on a 20% gradient wall, provides the competitive punch. The Mugello countryside provides the Tuscan pastoral. And the city itself provides something no other gran fondo can offer: the feeling that you are not just racing through scenery, but through history. Pack your climbing legs and your appetite. You will need both. Yes if the idea of racing across the Ponte Vecchio and starting from Piazzale Michelangelo makes your heart beat faster. Yes if you want a challenging but accessible Italian gran fondo wrapped in world-class cultural scenery. Yes if you value the total experience — city, countryside, food, history — over pure climbing brutality or maximum competitive depth. Skip if you want an extreme mountain challenge — look to the Maratona dles Dolomites or La Marmotte instead. Skip if you need a massive, festival-atmosphere field — the Nove Colli or Granfondo Campagnolo deliver that. Skip if you prefer gravel or off-road — the GF Strade Bianche is the Tuscan alternative for dirt road lovers.

### Lake Taupo Cycle Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 99.4 mi | 5,837 ft | Taupō, Waikato, New Zealand | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/lake-taupo-cycle-challenge/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/lake-taupo-cycle-challenge.md

New Zealand's biggest cycling event. 7,000 riders circling a supervolcano's caldera. 47 years of one schoolteacher's idea. A circumnavigation, not a criterium. The 160 km circuit follows state highways around Lake Taupō — New Zealand's largest lake and the caldera of the Taupō supervolcano. The terrain is rolling rather than mountainous, with three named hills providing structure: Waihaha (the false summit), Waihi (the big grind), and Hatepe (the late-course sting). The route passes through geothermal steam fields, rolling Waikato farmland, quiet southern-shore settlements, and the crystal-clear eastern lakeside. On a clear day, the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngauruhoe, and Ruapehu dominate the southern horizon. The course rewards steady pacing over 5-8 hours, not explosive power. Signature challenge: The three hills — Waihaha, Waihi, and Hatepe — are the spine of the course. None of them are Alpine monsters, but each has its character: Waihaha lies with its false summit, Waihi demands sustained effort for the best views of the day, and Hatepe arrives when your legs have already given 120 km of effort. The real challenge is the totality: 160 km, 1,779 metres of climbing, potentially exposed to wind and rain, on a course that never lets you fully rest. The Lake Taupō Cycle Challenge is not a race. It is a pilgrimage. Most last Saturdays of November since 1977 (the event was cancelled in 2020, 2021, and again in Feb 2022 due to Covid-19), thousands of New Zealanders have driven to a small volcanic-plateau town to circle a supervolcano's caldera on their bicycles, because a schoolteacher named Walter de Bont once thought it would be a good idea to ride around the lake with 26 of his mates. That ride became New Zealand's largest cycling event — peaking at 10,000 riders in its heyday and still drawing 7,000 annually after 47 editions. The 160 km circuit takes in geothermal steam fields, rolling Waikato farmland, three named hills that each provide their own variety of suffering, and the crystal-clear eastern shore of the largest lake in New Zealand. On a clear day, you ride toward the snow-capped volcanic peaks of Tongariro and Ruapehu. On a bad day, you ride into wind and rain on exposed state highways. Either way, you finish in a town that has been celebrating your ride all day long. Yes if you want an authentic New Zealand cycling experience with volcanic scenery and genuine community atmosphere. Yes if you want a well-supported century ride (or 200-mile ultra) in the Southern Hemisphere. Skip if you need serious competition — this is a community ride, not a race. Skip if geographic isolation is a dealbreaker — getting to Taupō requires commitment.

### L'Etape Chile by Tour de France
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 68.3 mi | 5,919 ft | Valdivia, Los Rios, Chile | November | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-chile/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-chile.md

L'Etape's debut Chile edition: a real 1,804m coastal course, unproven organization, no published price. The 110km long route runs closed roads from Niebla into Valdivia's Los Ríos region, combining Pacific coastline with river-valley and forest terrain for 1,804m of gain. Two shorter options exist alongside it: a 60km route (1,292m) and a 30km family route (372m), both of which permit e-bikes and MTBs. This is a debut edition with no prior field to have ridden it — official figures come from the organizer's own route pages, not an independent post-event report. Signature challenge: The Niebla-to-Valdivia coastal-to-river traverse on the 110km long course: 1,804m of gain on closed roads. No independent course profile is available to confirm how the climbing is distributed across the route, since the organizer has not yet run an edition. L'Etape Chile is the first L'Etape by Tour de France event held in Chile, landing November 1, 2026 in Niebla/Valdivia's Los Rios region — not the series' first Southern Hemisphere event (L'Etape Brasil has run since 2015), but a genuine new country for the series. The long course is real: 1,804m over 110km on closed roads through Pacific coastline and river-valley terrain, and the winner earns a wildcard into the Etape du Tour de France in Europe. Organizer World Centric Group is projecting over 2,000 riders and 10,000 visitors, but that's a debut-year projection, not a result — there is no prior Chile edition to check it against. No entry fee is published anywhere we could find, which is a real gap for a race asking international riders to book flights to Chile on faith. As of the final registration wave (opened July 24, 2026), organizers report interest from 15-plus countries — solid early demand, not a confirmed sellout. Yes if you want to be part of an L'Etape series debut with genuine Tour de France pedigree and can handle unknowns — no track record, no published entry fee. Wait for a later edition if you want confirmed execution before booking international travel.

### L'Etape Denmark by Tour de France
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 186.4 mi | 8,202 ft | Various start points across Jutland, Denmark — all routes finish in Viborg | June | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-denmark/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/letape-denmark.md

ASO's Tour de France franchise meets Denmark's ancient Viking road. 7,000 riders, five routes up to 300 km, TdF jerseys, and a finish festival in Viborg. A point-to-point journey along Denmark's ancient glacial ridge — the Haervejen road that Vikings, pilgrims, and merchants traveled for a thousand years. The terrain is rolling rather than mountainous, with the Jutland ridgeline delivering constant undulation through heathlands, forests, and historic towns. The landscape is understated and pastoral — wide horizons, open farmland, ancient churches, and Viking-era landmarks. Wind is the primary adversary, channeled across the open terrain by prevailing westerlies. Each route starts from a different Jutland town and converges on Viborg, Denmark's former capital, for a shared finish celebration. The 300 km Queen Stage begins across the border in Flensburg, Germany, adding an international dimension to an already mythic route. Signature challenge: The 300 km Queen Stage from Flensburg to Viborg — 186 miles of sustained effort along the Viking road with 2,500 meters of accumulated climbing. The challenge is not any single climb but the relentless accumulation of effort across rolling terrain, exposed to Jutland's winds, for 14-18 hours. Denmark does not have mountains, but it has distance, wind, and the psychological weight of a route that stretches from Germany to the heart of the Danish peninsula. L'Etape Denmark is what happens when ASO's Tour de France franchise lands in the flattest country in Scandinavia — and somehow it works. The Haervejen, an ancient road traveled by Vikings and pilgrims for centuries, provides the narrative backbone that Denmark's topography cannot. Seven thousand riders from 30 countries converge on five routes, all finishing in Viborg — a city older than the Tour de France by about 900 years. The TdF jersey classifications are legitimate, the feed stations are legendary, and the 300 km Queen Stage from Germany to Denmark is a genuine endurance test. DGI's grassroots organization and 1,000+ local volunteers give the event a community warmth that pure commercial sportives cannot replicate. The climbing is modest by any international standard — Mur de Refsgaarde at 8.2% for 550 meters is the hardest the course gets — but the wind across open Jutland will remind you that flat does not mean easy. Yes if you want a well-organized TdF franchise experience in Scandinavia with genuine community atmosphere. Yes if the 300 km ultra-distance Queen Stage appeals to your endurance ambitions. Yes if you want an accessible entry point to international road cycling events — the five distance options accommodate everyone. Skip if you want serious climbing — Denmark's glacial ridgeline is charming but not challenging by Alpine or Pyrenean standards. Skip if you prioritize deep competitive racing over mass-participation experience.

### Race Across Portugal
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 636.3 mi | 41,010 ft | Vila Meã, Amarante, Porto District, Portugal | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-portugal/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/race-across-portugal.md

A genuine multi-day ultra through the Douro Valley and Peneda-Gerês, not a single-day fondo — a real Race Across Series race in its unproven first year. IMPORTANT — this is not a single-day gran fondo. Race Across Portugal is a continuous, timed, semi-autonomous ultra-distance road race run by Race Across Series (legal promoter Across and Beyond Endurance AG, founder Arnaud Manzanini), the same organizer behind Race Across France, Spain and Benelux. The nominal 1,000 km class combines three loops centered on the single basecamp at Vila Meã, Amarante — a 500 km loop plus 200 km and 300 km loops — through northern Portugal's Porto hinterland, the Douro Valley, Atlantic landscapes and Peneda-Gerês National Park. Riders are self-sufficient between loops but return to a staffed basecamp (food, cots, showers, charging, baggage) rather than riding fully unsupported like the Transcontinental Race. A post-race finisher report put the actual 2026 ridden distance at approximately 1,024 km / 12,500+ m, moderately more than the organizer's rounded 1,000 km nominal figure. No credible public source names individual signature climbs on this course as of this research — treat any specific pass name as unconfirmed until the organizer publishes one. Signature challenge: Completing three loops (500/200/300 km) radiating from a single basecamp through the rolling-to-mountainous Douro Valley and Peneda-Gerês terrain within the 96-hour cutoff, with only brief staffed-basecamp stops between loops rather than daily stages. Race Across Portugal is a real, semi-autonomous ultra-distance road race — the host municipality previewed roughly 150 riders from 16 countries across four distances (200/300/500/1,000 km) for its 2026 inaugural edition, though no post-event finisher count by distance has been published to confirm that as final turnout. It's organized by the Race Across Series team, whose own results archive shows an uneven per-country history (Race Across France dates to 2018, but Belgium/Benelux only to roughly 2021-2022 and Spain to 2025 — not a uniform 'since 2018' across all three). It should never have been catalogued as a single-day gran fondo: nearly 1,000 km over a multi-day continuous clock, three loops radiating from a single basecamp, and a 96-hour cutoff for the flagship class put it firmly in ultra-distance territory, not mass-participation fondo territory. As a first-year event it also carries first-year uncertainty — no confirmed 2027 date yet, and no demonstrated multi-edition track record to judge consistency against. Yes if you're specifically seeking a semi-autonomous ultra-distance challenge with real basecamp support and can commit to the 96-hour flagship format. Not a fit if you're looking for a conventional single-day, mass-participation gran fondo.

### RBC GranFondo Whistler
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 76 mi | 7,500 ft | Stanley Park, Vancouver → Whistler Village | September | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/rbc-granfondo-whistler/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/rbc-granfondo-whistler.md

Sea-to-Sky Highway from Vancouver to Whistler — North America's largest and most celebrated gran fondo, where the scenery outshines the climbing. A 122km point-to-point ride from downtown Vancouver to Whistler along the iconic Sea-to-Sky Highway. The course begins at sea level in Stanley Park, crosses the Lions Gate Bridge car-free, follows the stunning Howe Sound coastline, then climbs gradually through the Coast Mountains to Whistler Village. The challenge is sustained distance rather than steep grades — most of the 2,300m of climbing occurs as a long, gradual drag in the second half after Squamish. Signature challenge: The sustained gradient from Squamish to Whistler — 55km of gradually rising road that grinds riders down through sheer distance rather than steep pitches. The Forte adds the pre-dawn Cypress Mountain Cat 1 climb for those seeking a true mountainous challenge. RBC GranFondo Whistler is North America's answer to the European gran fondo tradition. The Sea-to-Sky Highway is genuinely spectacular, the organization is polished, and the Whistler finish creates a perfect post-ride celebration atmosphere. But the course itself is more scenic cruise than mountain challenge — the climbing is gradual and sustained rather than steep and decisive. The Forte adds real teeth with Cypress Mountain, but the standard Gran Fondo is fundamentally a long, beautiful highway ride. Yes, if you value the full gran fondo experience over pure climbing challenge. The Sea-to-Sky is genuinely beautiful, the organization is top-tier, and the Whistler finish is a celebration. The Forte (152km) is the choice for those wanting real climbing. Best for riders who appreciate scenic production over alpine suffering.

### Round Denmark Bike Race
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 1220.6 mi | 28,405 ft | Helsingør to Farum, Denmark (Zealand, southern islands and Jutland loop) | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/round-denmark-bike-race/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/round-denmark-bike-race.md

A genuine self-supported ultra looping Denmark by ferry and coastal road — grassroots, small, and nothing like a gran fondo. IMPORTANT — this is not a single-day gran fondo. Round Denmark Bike Race is a fixed-route, self-supported ultra-distance bikepacking time trial, run by an independent, non-profit volunteer organizer — genuinely distinct from Race Around Denmark (a separate 1,600 km event run by Uggi Kaldan's RAD team) and from Danmark Rundt (the UCI ProSeries professional stage race, an entirely different event). All riders share a common 08:00 start, then immediately disperse to ride solo/self-paced — placing is decided by finish time, not a shared-peloton race; the clock runs continuously, though riders may stop and sleep, and the route is a mandatory organizer-supplied GPX, not rider-chosen. The 2026 road course was scheduled to start at Kronborg Castle in Helsingør on July 5 and finish near Farum, broadly looping through Zealand and Denmark's southern islands before following Jutland's coasts and inland roads — a loose national loop rather than a literal coastline-hugging circumnavigation, requiring five ferry crossings. The road edition still includes roughly 122-130 km of gravel and about 1 km of cobbles despite its 'road' framing. Denmark is flat, so gradient isn't the challenge here: the load is nearly 2,000 km of exposed coastal wind, variable rain and temperature, accumulated sleep deprivation, self-managed food and repairs, and coordinating five separate ferry schedules — with only limited organizer support (luggage transport to Farum, a post-finish shower/possible overnight stay, and GPS tracking), not on-course provisioning or private crew support. Signature challenge: Nearly 2,000 km of continuous, self-navigated riding with no on-course provisioning or private crew support — riders manage their own sleep, nutrition, mechanical repairs and ferry timing for the entire route, with the current road-course record standing at 5 days, 5 hours, 27 minutes (2023). Round Denmark Bike Race is a real, independently organized, self-supported ultra-distance bikepacking time trial — genuinely distinct from both the larger Race Around Denmark and the professional Danmark Rundt stage race, despite years of database confusion between the three. It should never have been catalogued as a single-day gran fondo: nearly 2,000 km on a fixed organizer GPX, a continuous multi-day clock, five mandatory ferry crossings, and a deliberately small field (a 30-rider cap on the road course, historically far smaller starting fields) put it firmly in grassroots ultra-distance territory. Denmark's flat terrain means the challenge here is entirely about distance, wind, sleep management and self-sufficiency rather than climbing. Yes if you're specifically seeking a small, serious, self-supported ultra-distance challenge and can manage your own logistics, sleep and ferry timing across nearly 2,000 km. Not a fit if you're looking for a conventional single-day, mass-participation gran fondo.

### Sea Otter Classic Gran Fondo
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 90 mi | 5,500 ft | Monterey, California, USA | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/sea-otter-classic-gran-fondo/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/sea-otter-classic-gran-fondo.md

90 miles of wine country roads wrapped inside the world's biggest cycling festival. A tale of two halves. The first 40 miles lull you into comfort through flat agricultural valley roads and vineyard aid stations. Then the Cahoon Summit climb punishes complacency with 10+ miles of sustained effort before the Laureles Grade kicker reminds you that the finish is earned, not given. Signature challenge: The Cahoon Summit climb: 10+ miles of sustained 4-6% gradient through East Carmel Valley Road, arriving after 50 miles of riding when glycogen stores are depleting. The Sea Otter Classic Gran Fondo is not the hardest ride you will do this year, and it is not trying to be. It is 90 miles of gorgeous Salinas Valley wine country wrapped inside the world's largest cycling festival, and that combination is more powerful than either element alone.

The route is honest: flat valley roads for 40 miles, then the real work begins with the Cahoon Summit grind and the steep Laureles Grade kicker to finish. 5,500 feet of climbing will remind your legs that this is a proper fondo, not a parade. But the four vineyard-set aid stations, the April coastal weather, and the knowledge that Laguna Seca Raceway awaits at the finish soften the suffering.

What makes this ride special is everything surrounding it. A 4-day festival pass comes with registration. 1,000+ bike brands at the expo. 14 race disciplines across the weekend. Cycling legends signing autographs. It is the season opener for American cycling, and riding the gran fondo puts you at the center of it. Yes if you want the ultimate cycling culture weekend with a beautiful ride attached. Skip if you need competitive racing, chip times, or want to avoid $300/night hotels.

### Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic
Tier 2 | Score: 61/100 | 206 mi | 5,100 ft | Seattle to Portland, Washington/Oregon, USA | July | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/seattle-to-portland/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/seattle-to-portland.md

206 miles from Seattle to Portland. 6,000 riders. 47 years. The Pacific Northwest's cycling pilgrimage. A 206-mile south-bound corridor from Seattle to Portland on paved country roads, avoiding Interstate 5. The route threads through the green lowlands of western Washington and Oregon — Puget Sound farmland, the Nisqually and Chehalis river valleys, the Cowlitz corridor, and the Columbia River crossing into Oregon. The terrain is predominantly flat to gently rolling, with one honest climb near Puyallup and energy-sapping rollers between Chehalis and Napavine. Small towns punctuate the route every 15-25 miles, each one a checkpoint and a morale boost. The course crosses from Washington into Oregon via the Lewis and Clark Bridge over the Columbia River. The final miles run through St. Helens and Scappoose before crossing Portland's St. Johns Bridge to the finish at Holladay Park. The character is rural, green, and relentlessly forward — 206 miles in one direction, no turning back. Signature challenge: The distance itself. STP has no single feature that defines the course — no brutal climb, no technical descent, no unrideable sector. The challenge is 206 miles of sustained forward motion, managing nutrition and hydration across 8-14 hours of saddle time, and the psychological discipline of riding one direction for an entire day (or two). The Chehalis-to-Napavine rollers on tired legs are the closest thing to a crux, but the real opponent is the odometer. STP is less a bike ride and more a regional migration. Every July, 6,000+ cyclists ride 206 miles from Seattle to Portland on country roads, through farmland and small towns, sleeping in a field in Centralia, and finishing at Holladay Park with a medal and a beer. The terrain is flat. The competition is nonexistent. The technical demands are zero. None of that matters. What matters is that for 47 years, this ride has been the Pacific Northwest's defining cycling event — a two-day rolling community of thousands, stretching from the Puget Sound to the Willamette Valley, covering 206 miles that transform from intimidating to accomplished to annual tradition. You ride STP once because you want to see if you can. You ride it again because it's July and that's what you do. Yes if you want one of America's great city-to-city cycling experiences. Yes if community and tradition matter more than competition. Yes if riding 206 miles through the PNW countryside with thousands of fellow cyclists sounds like your idea of a perfect July weekend. Skip if you need racing, climbing, technical terrain, or anything beyond flat-road endurance.

### Bordeaux-Paris Ultra Cycling Challenge
Tier 2 | Score: 60/100 | 403.9 mi | 14,764 ft | Bordeaux to Saint-Remy-les-Chevreuse (near Paris), France | May | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/bordeaux-paris-ultra-cycling/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/bordeaux-paris-ultra-cycling.md

A historic name attached to a genuinely modern ultra-distance revival — with a rocky recent past. The modern Bordeaux-Paris is an amateur ultra-distance revival, not the motor-paced professional classic that ran 1891-1988 under the same name. It runs 650km from the Stadium Velodrome de Bordeaux to Domaine de Coubertin near Paris, semi-autonomous: riders navigate an unmarked route by GPX, carry mandatory safety and repair gear, and rely on three official feed stations and a mid-course rest area rather than continuous support. There's no competitive classification — only individual completion times inside a 50-hour limit. A shorter ~305km secondary route starts from Chateauroux for riders who want the format without the full distance. Signature challenge: The 50-hour clock itself, across a full day-night cycle with minimal support — sleep management is treated as part of the event, not an afterthought, with organizer-provided mattresses at the mid-course rest area. The name Bordeaux-Paris carries a century of professional cycling history — but the event you'd actually sign up for today is a 650km semi-autonomous ultra-distance ride with no official competitive classification, revived by Extra Sports in 2014 and relaunched in its current GPS-tracked, no-classification format in 2022. It's a real, currently organized event (CLSO by SMH, an FFC-affiliated nonprofit) with a retired professional rider, Pierre Rolland, reported by L'Equipe as the 2026 edition's first finisher despite the event publishing no formal results ranking. But it's not a gran fondo in any conventional sense — there's no field to race against, no closed roads, minimal aid; it's a solo clock-and-navigation test with three feed stations and a mattress at the midpoint. The 2023 and 2024 editions were both cancelled, which the organizer itself has acknowledged left a bad taste for prospective entrants, and the current website mixes 2026 and 2027 documentation in ways worth double-checking before you pay. Only if you specifically want a semi-autonomous, minimally-supported ultra-distance challenge — this is not a supported gran fondo, and you should verify current registration details directly given the site's documented inconsistencies and the 2023/2024 cancellations.

### Cape Rouleur
Tier 2 | Score: 60/100 | 373 mi | 19,685 ft | Franschhoek, Western Cape, South Africa | March | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/cape-rouleur/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/cape-rouleur.md

600 km through the Cape Winelands on closed roads with pro support. Cycling's most luxurious sportive experience. The Cape Rouleur unfolds across five stages radiating from Franschhoek into the Western Cape's finest cycling terrain. Each stage delivers a different character: wine country rolling roads through Stellenbosch, mountain pass climbs through the Hottentots Holland range, coastal sections with views of False Bay, and the dramatic landscapes around Paarl and Wellington. The riding is demanding — 120 km per day average with 1,200m climbing — but the closed roads and support infrastructure remove every variable except your legs and the scenery. The final day typically includes an approach into Cape Town, setting up the optional Cape Town Cycle Tour. Signature challenge: The queen stage mountain passes. After three prior stages of cumulative fatigue, the most demanding climbing of the week arrives. The Western Cape's mountain passes are not Alpine monsters, but at 30C with the Cape Doctor blowing and four days of riding in the legs, 1,500m of climbing in a single stage is absolutely honest. The Cape Rouleur is what happens when you give 200 amateur cyclists the professional treatment in one of the world's most beautiful cycling destinations. HotChillee's formula is proven: closed roads, motorbike outriders, lead car nutrition, mechanics with spare wheels, a race doctor, and a broom wagon. You don't think about traffic, navigation, or mechanical issues. You just ride.

The setting makes it sing. Five stages through the Cape Winelands — Franschhoek, Stellenbosch, and the surrounding wine country — deliver vineyards, mountain passes, and coastal roads in succession. The hospitality in Franschhoek between stages is exceptional. Wine tastings, gourmet South African food, poolside recovery. This is cycling as luxury experience.

The price reflects the quality: GBP 1,350+ entry is steep, and flights to Cape Town add another GBP 500-1,200. But for the cycling tourist who wants five days of world-class riding with zero logistics burden, there is nothing better. Yes if you want a premium multi-stage cycling holiday with world-class support in a stunning setting. Yes if the combination of serious daily riding and Franschhoek wine country hospitality appeals to your inner cycling tourist. Skip if the GBP 3,000-4,000 total cost is prohibitive. Skip if you want a competitive event with timing and rankings.

A historic Vasaloppet-family event that's roughly 97% gravel/forest road — a gravel race mislabeled as a road gran fondo. Signature challenge: The opening climb: 178m of gain over the first 3km, up to the course's 528m high point — then close to 90km of forest road, gravel and boardwalk before Mora. Cykelvasan is a real event with genuine Vasaloppet pedigree — nonprofit-run since 2009, part of Swedish endurance-sport culture, drawing nearly 2,000 riders in its 2009 debut. The problem isn't the race, it's the label: roughly 97% of the 92km main course is forest road, gravel, ski-trail and marshland boardwalk, not pavement. A road cyclist showing up expecting a gran fondo on tarmac will be riding the wrong bike. This is a gravel/MTB event that happens to share a start-finish town pairing with road cycling's vocabulary. Race it on a gravel bike, not a road bike — the surface mismatch with a 'gran fondo' listing is real. If you want the Vasaloppet-family history and don't mind mixed terrain, it's worth entering.

### Etape Loch Ness
Tier 2 | Score: 60/100 | 66 mi | 2,953 ft | Inverness, Scottish Highlands | April | gran_fondo
Profile: https://roadielabs.com/race/etape-loch-ness/
Markdown: https://roadielabs.com/race/etape-loch-ness.md

Scotland's largest closed-road sportive — 66 miles around one of the world's most iconic lochs with 900m of climbing and a King of the Mountain at 12%. A 360-degree loop around one of the world's most famous bodies of water on fully closed roads. The route departs Inverness heading west along the north shore of Loch Ness on the A82, following the loch through the Great Glen — a geological fault line that splits Scotland diagonally from Inverness to Fort William. At Fort Augustus, the route reaches the southern tip of the loch where the Caledonian Canal connects Loch Ness to Loch Oich. Here, riders face the King of the Mountain: a 4.8-mile timed climb above the village gaining 380 metres with gradients reaching 12%. The summit delivers Highland panoramas before the descent to the south shore. The return leg follows narrower, quieter B-roads along the south side of Loch Ness — more atmospheric, more exposed to wind, and with rolling terrain that keeps the legs honest. The final miles approach Inverness from the south, with the last section through the city operating on left-lane closure rather than full road closure. The finish returns riders to the event area near Eden Court, completing the circumnavigation. Signature challenge: The King of the Mountain at Glen Doe above Fort Augustus. 4.8 miles gaining 380 metres with gradients reaching 12%. The only timed competitive element in a non-competitive sportive, it is where the Etape Loch Ness transforms from a scenic ride into a proper cycling challenge. Etape Loch Ness is what happens when you take one of the world's most famous natural landmarks, close the roads around it, and let 6,000 cyclists loose at dawn. The result is a sportive that trades on scenery and atmosphere rather than raw difficulty, and it delivers on that promise completely. The 66-mile loop around Loch Ness on fully closed roads is a cycling experience that few UK events can match — the loch emerging from morning mist, the Highland mountains rising on either side, Fort Augustus at the halfway point, and the King of the Mountain climb to test your legs and your resolve. This is not a race that will break elite cyclists, but it is an experience that will stay with every rider who does it. The £2 million raised for Macmillan Cancer Support gives it a soul that pure sporting events often lack. Yes, if riding closed roads around Loch Ness at dawn with 6,000 cyclists appeals to you as an experience. Yes, if you want a well-organized sportive that welcomes all abilities while still offering a legitimate climbing challenge. Skip if you need serious competitive racing depth — this is participatory. Skip if sub-100km on paved roads doesn't challenge you. And check the weather forecast before packing — Scottish April weather demands respect and proper kit.

Gran Fondo Chile is a genuine UCI Gran Fondo World Series stop — confirmed directly on ucigranfondoworldseries.com and the official UCI competition record (class UGF, 2026/CPT/78757) — not the L'Etape Chile event our own data previously pointed its registration link to. That's the good news: real UCI affiliation, an experienced multi-country organizer, and a scenic 114km loop around Lago Ranco with 1,554m of climbing. Yes if you specifically want the UCI Gran Fondo World Series qualifier and don't mind first-edition uncertainty — confirm registration is live before committing.
